school-c10-science-a.description: Class 10 Science chapter by chapter: chemical reactions, acids and bases, metals, carbon compounds, life processes and control & coordination — exam-ready.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Chemical Reactions and Equations
courses.summary: How to recognise a chemical reaction, write and balance chemical equations with state symbols, and classify reactions as combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox — plus corrosion and rancidity in daily life.
outcomes: Learners can identify a chemical change from observations
Learners can write and balance chemical equations with state symbols
Learners can classify reactions and give standard examples
Learners can identify the substance oxidised and reduced in a redox reaction
Learners can explain corrosion and rancidity and how to prevent them

lessons.title: Recognising a chemical reaction

scenes.text: In the lab, Anu holds a cleaned magnesium ribbon in a flame with tongs.
It burns with a dazzling white light and leaves a white powder.
Something new has formed — magnesium oxide. A chemical reaction has happened.

steps.title: Signs of a chemical reaction
steps.body:
A chemical reaction forms **new substances**. Look for one or more of:

- change in **state** (gas given off, solid formed)
- change in **colour**
- **evolution of a gas** (bubbles)
- change in **temperature** (heat given out or taken in)
- formation of a **precipitate** (insoluble solid)
- emission of **light**

steps.title: Solved example 1 — three classic activities
steps.body:
**(a) Burning magnesium:** dazzling white flame, white powder MgO forms.

**(b) Lead nitrate + potassium iodide solutions:** a **yellow precipitate** of lead iodide forms.

**(c) Zinc granules + dilute sulphuric acid:** bubbles of **hydrogen** gas, and the flask becomes warm.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why clean the ribbon?
steps.body: Magnesium ribbon is cleaned with sandpaper before burning to remove the layer of **magnesium oxide** (formed by slow reaction with air) so that fresh metal reacts with oxygen.

steps.title: Word equation
steps.body:
A reaction written in words: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.

**Reactants** are on the left, **products** on the right; the arrow means 'gives' or 'forms'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling melting of ice or dissolving sugar a chemical reaction (no new substance; these are physical changes).
- Forgetting that a gas test helps confirm: hydrogen burns with a **pop** sound.
- Holding magnesium ribbon with bare hands or looking straight at the flame — use tongs and avoid staring at the bright light.

activity.prompt: Chemical change or physical change?

quiz.q: Burning magnesium ribbon produces
options: a white powder of magnesium oxide
quiz.why: Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide, a white powder, with a dazzling white flame.

quiz.q: Lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions give a
quiz.why: Lead nitrate and potassium iodide react to form lead iodide, which is a yellow precipitate.

quiz.q: Gas evolved when zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid:
quiz.why: Zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sign of a chemical reaction?
quiz.why: Change of shape only is a physical change, as no new substance forms. Colour change, gas evolution and temperature change can signal a chemical reaction.

quiz.q: Magnesium ribbon is cleaned before burning to remove
quiz.why: Magnesium in air gets a coating of magnesium oxide, which stops it burning easily. Cleaning removes this layer.

lessons.title: Writing and balancing chemical equations

scenes.text: Lavoisier's idea: in a chemical reaction mass is neither created nor destroyed.
So the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides of an equation.
Rahul's first try, Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂, is unbalanced. Let us fix it step by step.

steps.title: Skeletal to balanced
steps.body:
A **skeletal equation** uses formulae but may be unbalanced: Mg + O₂ → MgO.

A **balanced equation** has equal numbers of each kind of atom on both sides (law of conservation of mass): **2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO**.

**Rules:** change only the **coefficients** (numbers in front), never the subscripts in formulae.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂ (hit-and-trial)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Start with the compound with most atoms, Fe₃O₄. O: 1 on left, 4 on right → put 4 before H₂O.

**Step 2:** H: now 8 on left, 2 on right → put 4 before H₂.

**Step 3:** Fe: 1 on left, 3 on right → put 3 before Fe.

**Balanced:** 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)

steps.title: Solved example 2 — more practice
steps.body:
- H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
- 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
- BaCl₂ + K₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2KCl
- 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
- CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

steps.title: Making equations informative
steps.body:
- **State symbols:** (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution.
- **Conditions** above/below the arrow: heat (Δ), pressure, catalyst, sunlight.
- Example: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₃OH(l) at 340 atm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ to balance oxygen — that makes a different substance.
- Writing O instead of O₂ for oxygen gas.
- Not rechecking every element after the last coefficient.

activity.prompt: Balance the equation for sodium and water (enter the coefficients; write 1 if needed).

quiz.q: A balanced equation obeys the law of
quiz.why: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, which follows the law of conservation of mass.

quiz.q: Balanced form of Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂:
quiz.why: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂ has Fe 3, H 8 and O 4 on each side, so it is balanced.

quiz.q: The symbol (aq) means
quiz.why: The state symbol (aq) means aqueous, that is, dissolved in water.

quiz.q: To balance an equation you may change
quiz.why: To balance an equation we change only the coefficients. Changing formulae or subscripts would change the substances.

quiz.q: Balanced combustion of methane:
quiz.why: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has C 1, H 4 and O 4 on both sides, so it is balanced.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Chemical Reactions and Equations)

lessons.title: Combination and decomposition reactions

scenes.text: Before Diwali, painters mix quicklime (CaO) with water. The bucket hisses and becomes very hot.
The slaked lime is brushed on walls; a few days later the walls shine.
Two reactions are hiding here — one combines substances, the next makes a shiny new solid.

steps.title: Combination reaction
steps.body:
Two or more substances combine to form **a single product**.

- CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + heat (quicklime → slaked lime)
- Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O (thin shiny layer of calcium carbonate on walls after 2–3 days)
- C + O₂ → CO₂; 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

Reactions that **release heat** are **exothermic** (burning, respiration: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy; decomposition of vegetable matter into compost).

steps.title: Decomposition reaction
steps.body:
A single reactant breaks into **two or more** simpler products. It needs energy:

- **Thermal (heat):** 2FeSO₄ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ + SO₃ (green crystals turn brown; smell of burning sulphur); CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (making quicklime); 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (brown fumes of NO₂)
- **Electrolytic (electricity):** 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (hydrogen volume is twice oxygen)
- **Photolytic (light):** 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (white silver chloride turns grey in sunlight); 2AgBr → 2Ag + Br₂ (used in black-and-white photography)

Most decomposition reactions **absorb** energy — they are **endothermic**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body:
(a) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: combination, exothermic.

(b) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (on heating): thermal decomposition, endothermic.

(c) 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electric current): electrolytic decomposition.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — electrolysis of water
steps.body: In the experiment, the gas at the cathode (−) is **hydrogen** and at the anode (+) is **oxygen**. Hydrogen's volume is **double** because water has 2 H atoms for each O atom. A burning candle near hydrogen gives a pop; oxygen makes a glowing splinter burst into flame.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling CaO + H₂O a decomposition (it is combination).
- Storing silver chloride in clear bottles (it decomposes in light — use dark bottles).
- Saying respiration is endothermic (it releases energy).

activity.prompt: Combination or decomposition?

quiz.q: Quicklime reacts with water to form
quiz.why: Quicklime (CaO) reacts with water to form slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, and a lot of heat is released.

quiz.q: The shiny finish on whitewashed walls is due to
quiz.why: Slaked lime on the wall reacts with CO₂ from the air to form calcium carbonate, which gives the shine.

quiz.q: Heating ferrous sulphate crystals gives a smell of
quiz.why: On heating, ferrous sulphate gives off SO₂ and SO₃, which smell like burning sulphur.

quiz.q: Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight because it
quiz.why: Silver chloride decomposes in sunlight into silver and chlorine. The silver makes it turn grey.

quiz.q: In electrolysis of water, volume of hydrogen : oxygen =
quiz.why: Water is H₂O, with 2 hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom. So electrolysis gives hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 : 1 volume ratio.

quiz.q: Respiration is
quiz.why: Respiration releases energy from food, so it is an exothermic reaction.

lessons.title: Displacement and double displacement reactions

story.title: The iron nail in blue solution

scenes.text: Sana dips an iron nail into blue copper sulphate solution.
After 20 minutes the nail has a brownish coat and the blue colour fades to pale green.
Iron has pushed copper out of its compound. More reactive elements displace less reactive ones.

steps.title: Displacement reaction
steps.body:
A **more reactive** element displaces a **less reactive** element from its compound.

- Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) (blue → light green; brown copper on nail)
- Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
- Pb(s) + CuCl₂(aq) → PbCl₂(aq) + Cu(s)

Zinc and iron are more reactive than copper.

steps.title: Double displacement reaction
steps.body:
Two compounds **exchange ions**: AB + CD → AD + CB.

Often a **precipitate** (insoluble solid) forms — a **precipitation reaction**:

- Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) (white ppt) + 2NaCl(aq)
- Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) (yellow ppt) + 2KNO₃(aq)

Neutralisation (acid + base → salt + water) is also a double displacement.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — predict
steps.body: Will copper displace iron from FeSO₄? **No** — copper is less reactive than iron. So Cu + FeSO₄ → no reaction.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — identify
steps.body: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). Ions are exchanged and a white precipitate of AgCl forms → **double displacement (precipitation)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing displacement (an element replaces another) with double displacement (two compounds swap partners).
- Expecting a less reactive metal to displace a more reactive one.
- Forgetting to name the precipitate and its colour in answers.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction with its type and observation.

quiz.q: When an iron nail is placed in copper sulphate solution, the solution becomes
quiz.why: Iron displaces copper, forming iron(II) sulphate, which is light green. The blue copper sulphate colour fades.

quiz.q: BaSO₄ formed from Na₂SO₄ and BaCl₂ is a
quiz.why: Barium sulphate is insoluble in water and appears as a white precipitate.

quiz.q: Which will NOT happen?
quiz.why: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate. The other displacements are possible.

quiz.q: A reaction in which an insoluble solid forms is a
quiz.why: A reaction in which an insoluble solid, a precipitate, forms is a precipitation reaction.

quiz.q: Double displacement involves
options: exchange of ions between two compounds
quiz.why: In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange their ions: AB + CD → AD + CB.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Chemical Reactions and Equations)

lessons.title: Oxidation, reduction, corrosion and rancidity

story.title: The black copper and the stale chips

scenes.text: When copper powder is heated in a china dish, its brown surface turns black.
Meanwhile, an open packet of chips left out for a week tastes and smells bad.
Both changes involve oxygen. Oxidation is everywhere — in labs, kitchens and on rusting gates.

steps.title: Oxidation and reduction
steps.body:
- **Oxidation:** gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
- **Reduction:** loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
- When both happen together, it is a **redox** reaction.

Example: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO (brown → black; copper is oxidised).

CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (on heating): **CuO is reduced** (loses O), **H₂ is oxidised** (gains O). The black coating turns brown again.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — identify
steps.body:
ZnO + C → Zn + CO: ZnO is reduced, C is oxidised. **Oxidising agent: ZnO; reducing agent: C.**

MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + 2H₂O + Cl₂: HCl loses hydrogen → oxidised (to Cl₂); MnO₂ loses oxygen → reduced.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — the oxidising agent
steps.body: The substance that **gives** oxygen (or removes hydrogen) is the **oxidising agent**; it is itself reduced. The substance that **takes** oxygen is the **reducing agent**; it is itself oxidised.

steps.title: Corrosion
steps.body:
When a metal is attacked by substances around it (moisture, air, acids), it **corrodes**. Rust on iron (needs both **air and water**), black coating on silver (silver sulphide), green coating on copper (basic copper carbonate).

Prevention: painting, oiling/greasing, **galvanising** (coating with zinc), chrome plating, making alloys.

Corrosion costs a great deal every year — car bodies, bridges, iron railings and ships all need protection.

steps.title: Rancidity
steps.body:
Fats and oils in food get **oxidised** and become **rancid** — the smell and taste change.

Prevention: add **antioxidants**, store in **airtight** containers, keep in a refrigerator, and flush packets with **nitrogen** (chip packets are filled with nitrogen to keep out oxygen).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying only gain of oxygen counts — loss of hydrogen is also oxidation.
- Naming the oxidising agent as the substance oxidised (it is the opposite).
- Saying chip packets are filled with oxygen or air (they use nitrogen).

statements.s: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, copper oxide is reduced.
Rusting needs only oxygen, not water.
statements.why: Both air and moisture are needed.

statements.s: Chip packets are flushed with nitrogen to prevent rancidity.
Galvanising means coating iron with zinc.
The reducing agent is the substance that gets reduced.

quiz.q: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, the substance oxidised is
quiz.why: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, carbon gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. ZnO loses oxygen, so it is reduced.

quiz.q: Heating copper in air gives a black coating of
quiz.why: Heated copper reacts with oxygen to form black copper(II) oxide: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO.

quiz.q: Black coating on silver articles is
quiz.why: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds in the air to form black silver sulphide.

quiz.q: Rancidity is caused by
quiz.why: Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils, which gives them a bad smell and taste.

quiz.q: Which prevents rusting?
quiz.why: Painting covers iron so air and water cannot reach it, which prevents rusting. Wet or salty conditions speed it up.

quiz.q: Loss of hydrogen is called
quiz.why: Loss of hydrogen is oxidation. Gain of hydrogen is reduction.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Chemical Reactions and Equations)

questions.q: Which is a chemical change?
questions.why: Rusting of iron forms a new substance, iron oxide, so it is a chemical change. Boiling, melting and breaking are physical changes.

questions.q: The symbol (g) in an equation means
questions.why: In a chemical equation, (g) is the state symbol for gas.

questions.q: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO is a
questions.why: Two substances combine to form a single product, magnesium oxide, so it is a combination reaction.

questions.q: Colour of lead iodide precipitate:
questions.why: Lead iodide, PbI₂, is a yellow precipitate.

questions.q: Which gas burns with a pop sound?
questions.why: Hydrogen burns with a pop sound when a burning splinter is brought near it.

questions.q: The balanced form of Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃ is
questions.why: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ has Al 4 and O 6 on each side, so it is balanced.

questions.q: Assertion: Decomposition of calcium carbonate is endothermic. Reason: heat must be supplied to break it into CaO and CO₂.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Heat is needed to break CaCO₃ into CaO and CO₂, so energy is absorbed and the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: Brown fumes on heating lead nitrate are of
questions.why: Heating lead nitrate gives lead oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen. The brown fumes are NO₂.

questions.q: Which is a double displacement reaction?
questions.why: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃ is a double displacement reaction, as the ions exchange partners and AgCl precipitates.

questions.q: In MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + 2H₂O + Cl₂, the oxidising agent is
questions.why: MnO₂ loses oxygen (is reduced) and oxidises HCl to Cl₂, so MnO₂ is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Case: A student puts an iron nail in CuSO₄ solution and records: brown deposit on nail; solution turns green. Which statement explains this?
options: Copper is more reactive than iron
Iron is more reactive than copper and displaces it
questions.why: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate. Copper deposits as a brown layer and iron(II) sulphate makes the solution light green.

questions.q: Case continued: if a copper wire is put in FeSO₄ solution instead,
questions.why: Copper is less reactive than iron, so it cannot displace iron from FeSO₄ and no reaction occurs.

questions.q: Which reaction is photolytic decomposition?
questions.why: Silver bromide breaks down into silver and bromine only in sunlight. A reaction that needs light is photolytic decomposition.

questions.q: When copper oxide is heated in a current of hydrogen, the black solid becomes
questions.why: Hydrogen reduces black copper oxide to copper, which is brown, and forms water.

questions.q: Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning, and why is the reaction exothermic?
options: To remove the oxide layer; heat and light are released
To make it shiny; heat is absorbed
To remove water; no heat change
To add oxygen; heat is absorbed
questions.why: Magnesium is cleaned to remove the oxide layer that would slow burning. The burning gives heat and light, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g). How many moles of H₂ form from 6 moles of Fe?
questions.why: From the equation, 3 mol Fe gives 4 mol H₂. So 6 mol Fe gives 6 × 4/3 = 8 mol H₂.

questions.q: A solution of a substance X is used for whitewashing. X and the product on the walls are
questions.why: X is quicklime, CaO, which forms slaked lime Ca(OH)₂ with water. On the wall Ca(OH)₂ reacts with CO₂ to form calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Acids, Bases and Salts
courses.summary: Indicators, the chemical properties of acids and bases, what happens in water, the pH scale and why it matters in our bodies and soils, and important salts — common salt, caustic soda, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda and plaster of Paris.
outcomes: Learners can test acids and bases with natural, synthetic and olfactory indicators
Learners can write reactions of acids and bases with metals, carbonates, oxides and each other
Learners can explain the role of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions and safe dilution
Learners can use the pH scale in real-life contexts
Learners can describe the preparation and uses of key salts and water of crystallisation

lessons.title: Indicators: telling acids from bases

scenes.text: Meera spills curry with turmeric on her white shirt and scrubs it with soap.
The yellow stain turns reddish-brown! After rinsing with water, it goes back to yellow.
Turmeric is a natural indicator — soap is basic. Indicators reveal acids and bases by colour or smell.

steps.title: Types of indicators
steps.body:
- **Litmus** (from lichen): acids turn blue litmus **red**; bases turn red litmus **blue**.
- **Turmeric:** turns **reddish-brown** in bases; stays yellow in acids.
- **Red cabbage, petunia, hydrangea** petals also change colour.
- **Synthetic:** **phenolphthalein** (colourless in acid, **pink** in base); **methyl orange** (red in acid, yellow in base).
- **Olfactory** (smell) indicators: **onion, vanilla essence, clove oil** — their odour disappears in a base but not in an acid.

steps.title: Everyday acids and bases
steps.body:
Acids taste sour: vinegar (acetic acid), lemon and orange (citric acid), tamarind (tartaric acid), tomato (oxalic acid), curd/sour milk (lactic acid), ant and nettle stings (methanoic acid).

Bases taste bitter and feel soapy: soap, baking soda, milk of magnesia, lime water. **Never taste lab chemicals.**

steps.title: Solved example 1 — identify three solutions
steps.body:
Three test tubes contain distilled water, an acid and a base. You have only red litmus.

**Step 1:** Dip red litmus into each; the one that turns it blue is the **base**.

**Step 2:** Dip the litmus that has turned blue into the other two tubes. The one that turns it **red** again is the **acid**; the one with no change is **distilled water**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — onion test
steps.body: A cloth strip soaked in onion smell is dipped in dilute NaOH: the smell disappears → base. In dilute HCl: smell remains → acid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying phenolphthalein turns pink in acids (it stays colourless).
- Thinking all substances with hydrogen are acids (glucose and alcohol are not).
- Tasting or smelling chemicals directly in the lab.

activity.prompt: Match the indicator with its colour in a basic solution.

quiz.q: Blue litmus turns red in
quiz.why: Acids turn blue litmus red.

quiz.q: Phenolphthalein in a basic solution is
quiz.why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink in a basic solution.

quiz.q: Which is an olfactory indicator?
quiz.why: An olfactory indicator changes its smell in acid or base. Clove oil loses its smell in a base, so it is an olfactory indicator.

quiz.q: The acid in tamarind is
quiz.why: Tamarind contains tartaric acid.

quiz.q: Turmeric turns reddish-brown with
quiz.why: Turmeric turns reddish-brown in basic solutions. Soap solution is basic, while lemon juice, vinegar and tomato juice are acidic.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Acids, Bases and Salts)

lessons.title: Chemical properties of acids and bases

scenes.text: Kabir drops a piece of eggshell (calcium carbonate) into dilute hydrochloric acid.
It fizzes! He passes the gas through lime water, which turns milky.
Acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide — one of several patterns worth memorising.

steps.title: Reactions of acids
steps.body:
- **Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen:** Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑ (H₂ burns with a pop).
- **Carbonate/hydrogencarbonate + acid → salt + CO₂ + water:** Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂; NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
- **Lime-water test:** Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ (milky) + H₂O; with excess CO₂: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (soluble, milkiness disappears).
- **Metal oxide + acid → salt + water:** CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O (solution turns blue-green). So metal oxides are **basic oxides**.

steps.title: Reactions of bases and neutralisation
steps.body:
- **Base + some metals:** 2NaOH + Zn → Na₂ZnO₂ (sodium zincate) + H₂ (not true for all metals).
- **Neutralisation:** acid + base → salt + water: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.
- **Non-metal oxide + base → salt + water:** Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O, so non-metal oxides are **acidic oxides**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — identify the gas
steps.body:
A metal compound A reacts with dilute HCl to give effervescence; the gas extinguishes a burning candle. If one product is calcium chloride, A is **CaCO₃**.

CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — neutralisation in pink solution
steps.body: Add 2 drops of phenolphthalein to dilute NaOH (pink). Add dilute HCl drop by drop: the pink colour disappears when the base is neutralised. Add a drop of NaOH again: pink returns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all metals give hydrogen with bases (only some, like zinc and aluminium).
- Writing CO instead of CO₂ for the gas from carbonates.
- Forgetting that excess CO₂ makes lime water clear again.

activity.prompt: Order the lime-water observations as CO₂ is bubbled for a long time.

quiz.q: Metal + acid gives
quiz.why: A metal reacting with an acid gives a salt and hydrogen gas.

quiz.q: Gas evolved with sodium carbonate and HCl:
quiz.why: A carbonate reacting with an acid releases carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: CuO dissolving in HCl gives a
quiz.why: Copper oxide is a base and reacts with HCl to form copper chloride, which makes a blue-green solution.

quiz.q: Non-metallic oxides are
quiz.why: Non-metallic oxides are acidic because they react with bases.

quiz.q: Zinc with NaOH gives
quiz.why: Zinc is amphoteric and reacts with NaOH to give sodium zincate and hydrogen gas.

quiz.q: Neutralisation produces
quiz.why: In neutralisation an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Acids, Bases and Salts)

lessons.title: Acids and bases in water

story.title: Why does dry HCl gas not change litmus?

scenes.text: In a demonstration, dry HCl gas does not change dry blue litmus paper.
But moist litmus turns red at once.
Acids show their behaviour only in water, where they release H⁺ ions. Ions also let solutions conduct electricity.

steps.title: Ions are the key
steps.body:
- Acids in water produce **hydrogen ions** H⁺(aq), which exist as **hydronium ions** H₃O⁺: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
- Bases in water produce **hydroxide ions** OH⁻: NaOH(s) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
- Bases that dissolve in water are called **alkalis** (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂). All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.
- Solutions of glucose and alcohol do not give H⁺ ions, so they are not acidic and do not conduct (bulb test).

steps.title: Strong vs weak; concentrated vs dilute
steps.body:
- **Strong** acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃) give many H⁺ ions; **weak** acids (acetic acid) give fewer.
- **Concentration** is about how much acid is in a given volume, not strength.
- **Dilution is highly exothermic.** Always **add acid to water slowly with stirring**, never water to concentrated acid — the heat can make the mixture splash and the glass may crack.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — conductivity test
steps.body: Graphite/iron electrodes in dilute HCl light the bulb → ions present. In glucose solution the bulb does not glow → no ions. Conclusion: **acids give ions in water**; not every hydrogen compound is an acid.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — effect of dilution
steps.body: Diluting an acid **decreases** the concentration of H₃O⁺ ions per unit volume, so its pH **rises** towards 7 (it becomes less acidic).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding water to concentrated acid.
- Confusing 'strong' (degree of ionisation) with 'concentrated'.
- Thinking distilled water conducts well (it does not — very few ions).

statements.s: Dry HCl gas turns dry blue litmus red.
statements.why: It needs water to form H⁺ ions.

statements.s: All bases are alkalis.
Acid should be added to water, not water to acid.
Glucose solution conducts electricity well.
H⁺ ions exist in water as H₃O⁺.

quiz.q: Acids in water produce
quiz.why: Acids release H⁺ ions in water, and these combine with water to form hydronium ions, H₃O⁺.

quiz.q: A base soluble in water is called
quiz.why: A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali.

quiz.q: Diluting an acid makes its pH
quiz.why: Diluting an acid lowers its H⁺ concentration, so its pH rises towards 7.

quiz.q: Why must acid be added to water slowly?
quiz.why: Mixing an acid with water releases a lot of heat. Adding acid slowly to water prevents splashing and dangerous heating.

quiz.q: Which conducts electricity?
quiz.why: Dilute HCl has ions that carry current. Glucose solution and alcohol have no ions, and pure water has almost none.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Acids, Bases and Salts)

lessons.title: The pH scale and why it matters

scenes.text: Arjun is stung by a honeybee during a picnic. It burns.
His grandmother rubs a paste of baking soda on the spot and the pain eases.
The sting injects an acid (methanoic acid); a mild base neutralises it. pH explains why.

steps.title: The scale
steps.body:
**pH** ('potenz', power of hydrogen) runs from **0 to 14**.

- **pH 7:** neutral (pure water)
- **pH < 7:** acidic — the lower, the stronger the acid (more H⁺)
- **pH > 7:** basic — the higher, the stronger the base (more OH⁻)

**Universal indicator** shows different colours across the pH range.

steps.title: pH in everyday life
steps.body:
- **Our body** works within a narrow pH range of about 7.0–7.8.
- **Acid rain:** rain with pH below 5.6 makes river water acidic, harming aquatic life.
- **Digestion:** the stomach makes hydrochloric acid; excess causes pain/irritation — **antacids** like milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂, a mild base) neutralise it.
- **Tooth decay** starts when mouth pH falls below **5.5**; bacteria make acids from sugar left in the mouth. Basic toothpastes neutralise the acid. Tooth enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) is the hardest substance in the body but dissolves in acid.
- **Soil:** plants need a suitable pH; farmers treat acidic soil with lime (a base).
- **Stings:** bee and ant stings and nettle hairs inject methanoic acid; baking soda helps. The leaf of the dock plant, which often grows beside nettles, is a traditional remedy.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — order by pH
steps.body: Solutions A (pH 4), B (pH 1), C (pH 11), D (pH 7), E (pH 9). Increasing H⁺ concentration: **C < E < D < A < B**. Strongly basic: C; neutral: D; strongly acidic: B.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — fresh milk to curd
steps.body: Fresh milk has pH about 6. As it turns to curd, lactic acid forms and the pH **falls**. A milkman adds a little baking soda to fresh milk to shift pH slightly towards basic so it takes longer to set into curd.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying pH 1 is weaker than pH 5 (lower pH = more acidic).
- Thinking pH 7 means 'no ions at all' — water has equal tiny amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻.
- Using vinegar on a bee sting (it is acidic too).

activity.label: Slide the pH and read what kind of solution it is.

bands.text: Strongly acidic (like stomach acid or lemon juice).
Weakly acidic (like vinegar, tomato, black coffee). Below 5.5 tooth enamel starts to dissolve.
Slightly acidic (like milk or rain without pollution).
Weakly basic (like blood ~7.4, baking soda solution).
Basic (like milk of magnesia, lime water).

quiz.q: A solution with pH 3 is
quiz.why: A pH below 7 means the solution is acidic, so pH 3 is acidic.

quiz.q: Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below
quiz.why: Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth falls below 5.5, as the enamel begins to dissolve.

quiz.q: Antacids used for indigestion are
quiz.why: Antacids are mild bases that neutralise excess stomach acid.

quiz.q: Rain is called acid rain when its pH is below
quiz.why: Rain with pH below 5.6 is called acid rain.

quiz.q: Increasing H⁺ concentration order of pH 11, 9, 7, 4, 1:
quiz.why: A lower pH means a higher H⁺ concentration. So increasing H⁺ concentration goes from pH 11, 9, 7, 4 to 1.

quiz.q: Bee stings inject
quiz.why: A bee sting injects methanoic (formic) acid, which causes the pain and burning. A mild base like baking soda eases it.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Acids, Bases and Salts)

lessons.title: Salts and their uses

scenes.text: In the kitchen, Zoya finds table salt, baking soda, and in the bathroom a packet of washing soda.
Her grandfather's broken arm was once set in plaster of Paris.
All of these are salts made in industry from common salt or limestone. Let us meet them.

steps.title: Salts and their pH
steps.body:
Salts with the same positive or negative radical form a **family** (NaCl and Na₂SO₄ — sodium salts; NaCl and KCl — chloride salts).

- Strong acid + strong base → **neutral** salt (NaCl, pH 7)
- Strong acid + weak base → **acidic** salt (NH₄Cl)
- Weak acid + strong base → **basic** salt (Na₂CO₃, CH₃COONa)

**Common salt** comes from sea water (evaporation) and from **rock salt** deposits.

steps.title: Chemicals from common salt
steps.body:
- **Sodium hydroxide — chlor-alkali process:** electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g) + H₂(g). Cl₂ at the anode, H₂ at the cathode, NaOH near the cathode. ('Chlor' for chlorine, 'alkali' for NaOH.)
- **Bleaching powder:** Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. Used to bleach cotton, linen and wood pulp, as an oxidising agent, and to disinfect drinking water.
- **Baking soda (NaHCO₃):** NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ + NH₃ → NH₄Cl + NaHCO₃. On heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. Uses: **baking powder** (baking soda + a mild edible acid like tartaric acid — CO₂ makes cakes soft and spongy), antacids, soda-acid fire extinguishers.
- **Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O):** made by recrystallising sodium carbonate. Uses: glass, soap and paper industries, making borax, cleaning, removing permanent hardness of water.

steps.title: Water of crystallisation and plaster of Paris
steps.body:
**Water of crystallisation** is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a crystalline salt: CuSO₄·**5**H₂O (blue), Na₂CO₃·**10**H₂O, CaSO₄·**2**H₂O (gypsum).

Heating blue copper sulphate crystals drives off the water — they turn **white**; adding water turns them blue again.

**Plaster of Paris:** heating gypsum at **373 K** gives CaSO₄·½H₂O. With water it sets back into hard gypsum. Uses: plaster for supporting fractured bones, toys, decorative materials, smoothing surfaces. Store it in a moisture-proof container.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — identify the salt
steps.body: A white powder is added to cake batter; on heating, a gas makes the cake rise. The powder is **baking soda/baking powder**; the gas is **CO₂**. Tartaric acid in baking powder neutralises the bitter Na₂CO₃ that would otherwise form.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — gases at electrodes
steps.body: In the chlor-alkali process, the gas at the anode is **chlorine** (used for PVC, pesticides, disinfectants), at the cathode **hydrogen** (fuels, margarine, ammonia for fertilisers); **NaOH** (soaps, paper, artificial fibres) is formed near the cathode.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing CaSO₄·2H₂O for plaster of Paris (that is gypsum; PoP is CaSO₄·½H₂O).
- Saying baking soda and washing soda are the same compound.
- Forgetting the number of water molecules in hydrated salts.

activity.prompt: Match each salt to its formula or use.

quiz.q: Products of the chlor-alkali process:
quiz.why: In the chlor-alkali process, electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution) gives sodium hydroxide at the cathode region, chlorine at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode.

quiz.q: Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum at
quiz.why: Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum at 373 K (100 °C). At a much higher temperature gypsum loses all its water.

quiz.q: Number of water molecules in washing soda:
quiz.why: Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, so it has 10 molecules of water of crystallisation.

quiz.q: Blue copper sulphate crystals turn white on heating because they
quiz.why: Blue copper sulphate crystals contain water of crystallisation. On heating they lose it and become white anhydrous CuSO₄.

quiz.q: Salt of a strong acid and weak base, e.g. NH₄Cl, is
quiz.why: NH₄Cl is the salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH₄OH). Its solution is acidic, with pH below 7.

quiz.q: Baking powder contains baking soda and
options: a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid
quiz.why: Baking powder is baking soda plus a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. The acid neutralises the Na₂CO₃ formed on heating, so there is no bitter taste.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Acids, Bases and Salts)

questions.q: Methyl orange in an acidic solution is
questions.why: Methyl orange is red in acidic solution and yellow in basic solution.

questions.q: pH of pure water is
questions.why: Pure water is neutral, so its pH is 7.

questions.q: Acid present in curd:
questions.why: Curd contains lactic acid, formed when bacteria act on milk.

questions.q: Formula of baking soda:
questions.why: Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃. NaOH is caustic soda and Na₂CO₃ is washing soda.

questions.q: Gas produced when zinc reacts with NaOH:
questions.why: Zinc reacts with NaOH to form sodium zincate and hydrogen gas.

questions.q: Which is used for disinfecting drinking water?
questions.why: Bleaching powder releases chlorine, which kills germs, so it is used to disinfect drinking water.

questions.q: Assertion: HCl solution conducts electricity but glucose solution does not. Reason: HCl forms ions in water; glucose does not.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. HCl forms H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water, and ions carry current, while glucose does not form ions and so does not conduct.

questions.q: A solution turns red litmus blue. Its pH is likely
questions.why: A solution that turns red litmus blue is basic, so its pH is above 7. Among the choices pH 10 is basic.

questions.q: Which salt gives a basic solution in water?
questions.why: Na₂CO₃ is the salt of a weak acid (carbonic acid) and a strong base (NaOH), so its solution is basic. NaCl and KNO₃ are neutral and NH₄Cl is acidic.

questions.q: On heating baking soda, the products are
questions.why: On heating, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.q: Case: A farmer finds his soil pH is 4.5 and crops are weak. The best advice is to add
questions.why: Soil at pH 4.5 is too acidic. A base such as quicklime or slaked lime neutralises the acid and raises the pH.

questions.q: Case continued: after treatment the farmer wants about pH 6.5–7. This means the soil should be
questions.why: A pH of 6.5–7 is close to 7, so the soil would be nearly neutral, which suits most crops.

questions.q: Why does plaster of Paris need to be stored in a moisture-proof container?
options: It reacts with water and sets into gypsum
questions.why: Plaster of Paris reacts with water to form hard gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O. Moisture in the air would make it set in the container.

questions.q: A metal carbonate X reacts with an acid to give a gas that turns lime water milky; X's solution is used to remove permanent hardness. X is
questions.why: Washing soda, Na₂CO₃, releases CO₂ (which turns lime water milky) with an acid, and it removes permanent hardness of water.

questions.q: 10 mL of NaOH is exactly neutralised by 8 mL of a given HCl. Volume of the same HCl to neutralise 20 mL of the same NaOH:
questions.why: Neutralisation needs equal amounts of acid and base. 8 mL of HCl neutralises 10 mL of NaOH, so 20 mL of NaOH needs twice as much: 16 mL.

questions.q: Which equation for the formation of bleaching powder is correct?
questions.why: Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O.

questions.q: Fresh milk (pH 6) is made slightly alkaline by a milkman. Why does it take longer to set as curd?
options: Lactic acid formed first neutralises the added base, delaying the pH drop
questions.why: The lactic acid formed by the bacteria first neutralises the added base. Only after that does the pH fall enough to set the curd, so it takes longer.

questions.q: Which pair are both acidic salts? (salts of strong acid + weak base)
questions.why: NH₄Cl and (NH₄)₂SO₄ are salts of strong acids with the weak base ammonia, so both are acidic in solution. The others are basic or neutral.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Metals and Non-metals
courses.summary: Physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals, the reactivity series, how ionic compounds form and behave, how metals are extracted and refined, and how corrosion is prevented — including alloys.
outcomes: Learners can compare physical properties and know the exceptions
Learners can write reactions of metals with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions
Learners can show ionic bond formation with electron-dot structures
Learners can explain extraction steps for metals of low, middle and high reactivity
Learners can explain corrosion experiments and the use of alloys

lessons.title: Physical properties and exceptions

story.title: The temple bell and the pencil lead

scenes.text: A temple bell is made of metal because it rings loudly — metals are sonorous.
A pencil 'lead' is graphite, a non-metal — yet it conducts electricity.
General rules are useful, but Class 10 exams love the exceptions too.

steps.title: Metals vs non-metals
steps.body:
**Metals** are usually: lustrous (shiny), hard, **malleable** (beaten into sheets), **ductile** (drawn into wires), good conductors of heat and electricity, **sonorous**, solids with high melting points.

**Non-metals** are usually: dull, brittle, poor conductors, solids or gases (bromine is a liquid).

steps.title: Exceptions to remember
steps.body:
- **Mercury** is a liquid metal at room temperature.
- **Sodium and potassium** are soft enough to cut with a knife; low melting points.
- **Gallium and caesium** melt in your palm.
- **Lead and mercury** are comparatively poor conductors of heat; **silver and copper** are the best conductors.
- **Gold and silver** are the most malleable and ductile (1 g of gold can be drawn into a wire about 2 km long).
- **Iodine** is a lustrous non-metal; **graphite** conducts electricity; **diamond** (a form of carbon) is the hardest natural substance with a very high melting point.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why cooking vessels are metal
steps.body: Pans are made of metals (iron, aluminium, copper) because metals are good **conductors of heat**; handles use plastic or wood because those are poor conductors.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — classify by property
steps.body: An element is soft, cuts with a knife, and reacts vigorously with water: a reactive **metal like sodium**. An element is a dull, brittle yellow solid: **sulphur**, a non-metal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all metals are hard (Na and K are soft).
- Saying all non-metals are non-conductors (graphite conducts).
- Forgetting that bromine is a liquid non-metal.

activity.prompt: Metal or non-metal?

quiz.q: The liquid metal at room temperature is
quiz.why: Mercury is the metal that is liquid at room temperature. Bromine is also liquid but it is a non-metal.

quiz.q: The property used in drawing wires is
quiz.why: Ductility is the property of being drawn into wires. Malleability is being beaten into sheets.

quiz.q: A non-metal that conducts electricity:
quiz.why: Graphite is a non-metal form of carbon that conducts electricity because it has free electrons.

quiz.q: Metals that melt in the palm:
quiz.why: Gallium and caesium have very low melting points and melt in the palm.

quiz.q: Best conductors of electricity:
quiz.why: Silver and copper are the best conductors of electricity. Lead and mercury are poor conductors.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Metals and Non-metals)

lessons.title: Chemical properties and the reactivity series

scenes.text: In the school lab, sodium is stored under kerosene oil.
Exposed to air it catches fire; in water it reacts violently.
Metals differ greatly in how readily they react. Arranging them gives the reactivity series.

steps.title: Metals with oxygen, water and acids
steps.body:
- **Oxygen:** metal + O₂ → metal oxide (basic). 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO (black); 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃. Na and K burn vigorously, so they are kept in kerosene. Zinc and aluminium oxides are **amphoteric**: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O.
- **Water:** Na and K react violently with cold water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + heat); calcium less violently (it floats as H₂ bubbles stick to it); magnesium with hot water; Al, Fe, Zn only with steam (3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂); Pb, Cu, Ag, Au do not react.
- **Dilute acids:** metal + acid → salt + H₂ (Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂). With nitric acid, H₂ is usually not obtained because HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent — except with Mg and Mn and very dilute acid.
- **Salt solutions:** a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.

steps.title: Reactivity series (most → least)
steps.body:
**K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au**

Metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from dilute acids; those below do not. **Aqua regia** (3 parts conc. HCl : 1 part conc. HNO₃) can dissolve gold and platinum.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — predict
steps.body: Will silver react with dilute HCl? Silver is below hydrogen → **no reaction**. Will zinc displace iron from FeSO₄? Zn is above Fe → **yes**: Zn + FeSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Fe.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — non-metals
steps.body: Non-metals form **acidic or neutral** oxides (SO₂, CO₂ acidic; CO, H₂O neutral). They do **not** displace hydrogen from dilute acids because they cannot give electrons to H⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all metal oxides are basic (ZnO, Al₂O₃ are amphoteric).
- Expecting copper to give hydrogen with dilute HCl.
- Forgetting that iron reacts with steam, not cold water.

activity.prompt: Arrange these metals from most reactive to least reactive.

quiz.q: Metal kept in kerosene:
quiz.why: Sodium reacts vigorously with air and water, so it is kept in kerosene.

quiz.q: An amphoteric oxide is
quiz.why: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases, so it is amphoteric. MgO and Na₂O are basic and CO₂ is acidic.

quiz.q: Which metal reacts with steam but not with cold or hot water?
quiz.why: Iron does not react with cold or hot water but reacts with steam: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. Calcium and sodium react with cold water.

quiz.q: Aqua regia is a mixture of conc. HCl and conc. HNO₃ in the ratio
quiz.why: Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO₃ in the ratio 3 : 1. It can dissolve gold and platinum.

quiz.q: Which does NOT give H₂ with dilute HCl?
quiz.why: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not displace hydrogen from dilute HCl.

quiz.q: Calcium floats on water while reacting because
options: hydrogen bubbles stick to its surface
quiz.why: Calcium floats because bubbles of hydrogen gas stick to its surface. It is not lighter than water.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Metals and Non-metals)

lessons.title: Ionic compounds

scenes.text: Sodium is a dangerous metal and chlorine a poisonous gas — together they make table salt.
Sodium hands over one electron to chlorine; both reach a stable octet.
Opposite ions attract strongly — that is the ionic bond.

steps.title: Formation by electron transfer
steps.body:
Metals lose electrons to form **cations**; non-metals gain electrons to form **anions**. The electrostatic attraction between them is an **ionic (electrovalent) bond**.

- Na (2, 8, 1) → Na⁺ (2, 8) + e⁻
- Cl (2, 8, 7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)
- Mg (2, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons → Mg²⁺; two Cl atoms each gain one → **MgCl₂**.

steps.title: Properties of ionic compounds
steps.body:
- Hard, brittle **solids** (strong attraction between ions).
- **High melting and boiling points** (much energy needed to break the attraction).
- Generally **soluble in water**, insoluble in kerosene and petrol.
- **Conduct electricity in molten state or in solution** (ions move), but not as solids (ions fixed).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — electron-dot structure of MgO
steps.body: Mg (2, 8, 2) gives 2 electrons to O (2, 6) → Mg²⁺ (2, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8). Draw Mg with two dots transferring to O's outer shell, then [Mg]²⁺ [:Ö:]²⁻ — formula **MgO**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — explain
steps.body: Why does solid NaCl not conduct but its aqueous solution does? In the solid, ions are held in fixed positions; in solution, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are free to move and carry charge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing shared electron pairs in ionic compounds (that is covalent bonding).
- Saying ionic solids conduct electricity.
- Writing MgCl instead of MgCl₂ (charges must balance).

statements.s: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the solid state.
statements.why: Ions are not free to move.

statements.s: NaCl has a high melting point.
Mg forms Mg²⁺ by losing two electrons.
Ionic compounds dissolve well in kerosene.
statements.why: They dissolve in water, not in kerosene.

statements.s: Chlorine forms Cl⁻ by gaining one electron.

quiz.q: Electronic configuration of Na⁺:
quiz.why: Sodium has configuration 2, 8, 1. Losing one electron gives Na⁺ with 2, 8.

quiz.q: Formula of the compound from Mg and Cl:
quiz.why: Mg gives 2 electrons, forming Mg²⁺, and each Cl takes one electron, forming Cl⁻. So the formula is MgCl₂.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when
quiz.why: Ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved, because then the ions are free to move. In the solid state the ions are fixed.

quiz.q: An ionic bond is formed by
quiz.why: An ionic bond forms by the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds have high melting points because
options: strong forces of attraction between ions
quiz.why: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between ions need a lot of energy to break, so ionic compounds melt at high temperatures.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Metals and Non-metals)

lessons.title: Occurrence and extraction of metals

scenes.text: Miners dig out an ore — a rock containing a metal compound plus lots of sand and soil.
Furnaces, carbon and electricity turn that ore into gleaming metal.
The method depends on where the metal sits in the reactivity series.

steps.title: Ores and steps
steps.body:
**Minerals** are naturally occurring compounds; those from which a metal can be extracted profitably are **ores**. Impurities in the ore are called **gangue**.

**Steps:** 1. Enrichment (removing gangue) → 2. Getting the metal from the concentrated ore → 3. **Refining**.

- **Low reactivity** (Hg, Cu): heating alone. 2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂; 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂. 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂; 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂.
- **Middle** (Zn, Fe, Pb): convert to oxide — **roasting** sulphide ores in excess air (2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂), **calcination** of carbonate ores in limited air (ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂) — then **reduce** with carbon: ZnO + C → Zn + CO.
- **High** (Na, Mg, Ca, Al): **electrolysis of molten chlorides/oxides**; metal at the cathode, e.g. Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; chlorine at the anode.

steps.title: Thermite reaction
steps.body: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ + heat. So much heat is released that iron is produced in the molten state — used to **join railway tracks** and cracked machine parts. Aluminium acts as the reducing agent.

steps.title: Electrolytic refining
steps.body: Example, copper: **anode** = thick block of impure copper; **cathode** = thin strip of pure copper; **electrolyte** = acidified copper sulphate solution. On passing current, pure copper deposits on the cathode; soluble impurities go into solution and insoluble ones collect below the anode as **anode mud**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — choose a method
steps.body: Extract (a) mercury from cinnabar — heat in air; (b) zinc from zinc blende (ZnS) — roast then reduce with carbon; (c) sodium from rock salt — electrolysis of molten NaCl (carbon cannot reduce Na₂O because Na is more reactive than carbon).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up roasting (sulphide, excess air) and calcination (carbonate, limited air).
- Saying electrolysis of aqueous NaCl gives sodium metal (molten NaCl is needed).
- Placing pure copper at the anode in refining.

activity.prompt: Match each process with its example.

quiz.q: Impurities in an ore are called
quiz.why: The unwanted earthy impurities in an ore are called gangue.

quiz.q: Calcination is used for
quiz.why: Calcination is heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air, which drives off CO₂ and leaves the metal oxide.

quiz.q: Sodium is extracted by
quiz.why: Sodium is highly reactive, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.

quiz.q: Thermite reaction is used to
quiz.why: The thermite reaction between iron(III) oxide and aluminium gives molten iron, used to join railway tracks.

quiz.q: In electrolytic refining of copper, the cathode is
options: a thin strip of pure copper
quiz.why: In electrolytic refining the cathode is a thin strip of pure copper, on which pure copper deposits. The anode is impure copper.

quiz.q: Mercury is obtained from its sulphide ore by
quiz.why: Mercury is a low-reactivity metal. Heating its sulphide ore (cinnabar) in air gives mercury.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Metals and Non-metals)

lessons.title: Corrosion and alloys

scenes.text: The iron gate at Riya's home rusts every monsoon, but the steel spoons in the kitchen stay shiny.
Her teacher sets up three test tubes with iron nails to find what causes rust.
Protecting metals and mixing them into alloys saves huge amounts of money.

steps.title: Rusting experiment
steps.body:
- **Tube A:** nails in tap water open to air → **rust**.
- **Tube B:** nails in boiled distilled water (no dissolved air) with a layer of oil on top → **no rust**.
- **Tube C:** nails with anhydrous calcium chloride (keeps air dry) → **no rust**.

Conclusion: **rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water (moisture)**. Silver tarnishes black (silver sulphide); copper turns green (basic copper carbonate).

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Painting, oiling, greasing, **galvanising** (coating iron/steel with zinc — protects even if the coating is scratched), chrome plating, anodising and making **alloys**.

steps.title: Alloys
steps.body:
An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal.

- **Steel:** iron + about 0.05% carbon — hard and strong (pure iron is soft and stretches when hot).
- **Stainless steel:** iron + nickel + chromium — hard, does not rust.
- **Brass:** copper + zinc. **Bronze:** copper + tin.
- **Solder:** lead + tin — low melting point, used to weld electrical wires.
- **Amalgam:** an alloy with mercury.
- **Pure gold = 24 carat**, too soft; ornaments use **22 carat** (22 parts gold with 2 parts copper or silver).

Alloys usually have **lower electrical conductivity and lower melting points** than the pure metals.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — explain
steps.body: Why is galvanised iron better than painted iron? If paint is scratched, the exposed iron rusts. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so even when the zinc layer is scratched, zinc corrodes in preference and protects the iron.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying rusting needs only water.
- Calling 22 carat gold 'pure' gold.
- Confusing brass (Cu + Zn) with bronze (Cu + Sn).

activity.prompt: Complete the alloy facts.
activity.text: Brass = copper + ___; bronze = copper + ___; solder = lead + ___.

quiz.q: Rusting of iron requires
quiz.why: Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water. Neither alone is enough.

quiz.q: Galvanising means coating iron with
quiz.why: Galvanising is coating iron with a layer of zinc to protect it from rusting.

quiz.q: Solder is used for welding electrical wires because it has
quiz.why: Solder is an alloy of lead and tin with a low melting point, so it melts easily to join wires.

quiz.q: 22 carat gold contains gold and
quiz.why: 22 carat gold is mostly gold alloyed with copper or silver, which makes it harder.

quiz.q: Stainless steel is iron mixed with
quiz.why: Stainless steel is iron mixed with nickel and chromium, which stops it from rusting.

quiz.q: Copper vessels develop a green coating of
quiz.why: Copper in moist air slowly forms a green coating of basic copper carbonate.
