questions.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.why: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature among the choices. Gallium melts only slightly above room temperature.

questions.q: Metals are good conductors of heat. Which is a comparatively poor conductor?
questions.why: Lead (and mercury) are comparatively poor conductors of heat, unlike copper, aluminium and silver.

questions.q: Brass is an alloy of
questions.why: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

questions.q: The most reactive among these:
questions.why: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series, so it is the most reactive of these.

questions.q: An oxide that reacts with both HCl and NaOH:
questions.why: ZnO is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and bases. CO₂ is acidic, and Na₂O and CaO are basic.

questions.q: Hydrogen is not evolved when metals react with nitric acid because
options: nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent
questions.why: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises the hydrogen formed to water, so H₂ gas is not evolved (except with very dilute acid and Mg or Mn).

questions.q: Assertion: Ionic compounds have high melting points. Reason: strong electrostatic forces hold the ions together.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Strong electrostatic forces hold the ions together, and much energy is needed to separate them, which gives a high melting point.

questions.q: Which reaction is possible?
questions.why: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate. The other reactions try to displace a more reactive metal, which cannot happen.

questions.q: Roasting is carried out in
questions.why: Roasting is heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air, which converts it to the oxide.

questions.q: Case: An element X (atomic number 12) reacts with element Y (atomic number 17). The compound formed has formula
questions.why: X has atomic number 12 (2, 8, 2), so it loses 2 electrons. Y has atomic number 17 (2, 8, 7), so it gains 1. The formula is XY₂.

questions.q: Case continued: the bond in this compound is
questions.why: Electrons are transferred from the metal X to the non-metal Y, so the bond is ionic.

questions.q: In the thermite reaction, the reducing agent is
questions.why: In the thermite reaction aluminium takes oxygen from iron oxide, so aluminium is the reducing agent.

questions.q: In electrolytic refining of copper, insoluble impurities collect as
questions.why: Insoluble impurities settle below the anode as anode mud. Gangue is the earthy matter in an ore and slag is formed in smelting.

questions.q: Why can carbon not reduce oxides of sodium or aluminium?
options: These metals have more affinity for oxygen than carbon
questions.why: Sodium and aluminium have a stronger affinity for oxygen than carbon does, so carbon cannot take oxygen from their oxides.

questions.q: A metal M is found free in nature, does not react with dilute HCl but dissolves in aqua regia. M is likely
questions.why: A metal that occurs free, does not react with dilute HCl and dissolves in aqua regia is gold, a very unreactive noble metal.

questions.q: Equation for copper sulphide self-reduction:
questions.why: In copper extraction, Cu₂S is partly roasted to Cu₂O, which then reacts with the remaining Cu₂S: 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂.

questions.q: Three tubes: A (nail in tap water, open), B (boiled water + oil layer), C (anhydrous CaCl₂). After a few days rust is seen in
questions.why: Rust needs both air and water. Tube A has both, B has water without air (boiled and sealed with oil) and C has air but no moisture, so only A rusts.

questions.q: An element forms an oxide that turns blue litmus red and does not conduct as a solid. It is most likely
questions.why: An oxide that turns blue litmus red is acidic, and acidic oxides are formed by non-metals. So the element is a non-metal like sulphur.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Carbon and its Compounds
courses.summary: Covalent bonding, why carbon forms millions of compounds, homologous series and IUPAC naming, combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions, ethanol and ethanoic acid, and how soaps and detergents clean.
outcomes: Learners can draw electron-dot structures of simple covalent molecules
Learners can explain catenation, tetravalency and allotropes of carbon
Learners can name compounds with functional groups and identify homologous series
Learners can write combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions
Learners can describe properties and reactions of ethanol and ethanoic acid
Learners can explain micelle formation and the action of soaps and detergents

lessons.title: Covalent bonding

scenes.text: Carbon has 4 outer electrons. Losing or gaining 4 electrons needs too much energy.
So carbon shares electrons with other atoms — like friends sharing a pizza so everyone gets a full plate.
Shared electron pairs are covalent bonds, and they shape all of organic chemistry.

steps.title: What a covalent bond is
steps.body:
A **covalent bond** forms when two atoms **share** a pair of electrons so that each attains a stable noble-gas configuration.

- **Single bond** (1 shared pair): H–H in H₂; Cl–Cl in Cl₂; four C–H in methane CH₄.
- **Double bond** (2 pairs): O=O in O₂.
- **Triple bond** (3 pairs): N≡N in N₂.

Carbon's atomic number is 6 (2, 4). It forms 4 covalent bonds — it is **tetravalent**.

steps.title: Properties of covalent compounds
steps.body:
- Usually **low melting and boiling points** (weak forces between molecules).
- Generally **poor conductors** of electricity (no ions).
- Many are liquids or gases at room temperature.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — methane (CH₄)
steps.body: Carbon shares its 4 electrons with 4 hydrogen atoms, each H giving 1 electron. Electron-dot: C in the centre with 4 shared pairs, one to each H. Every H has 2 electrons (like He); C has 8 (like Ne).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — nitrogen (N₂)
steps.body: Each N (2, 5) needs 3 more electrons, so the two atoms share **three pairs**: N≡N, a triple bond. Each N also keeps one lone pair.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing a double bond in H₂ (hydrogen can share only one pair).
- Saying carbon forms ions C⁴⁺ or C⁴⁻ easily.
- Forgetting lone pairs on N and O in electron-dot diagrams.

activity.prompt: Match each molecule with its bond type.

quiz.q: Covalent bonds form by
quiz.why: A covalent bond forms by sharing of electrons between atoms.

quiz.q: Number of shared pairs in N₂:
quiz.why: Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons and needs 3 more, so two N atoms share 3 pairs, forming a triple bond.

quiz.q: Covalent compounds are generally
quiz.why: Covalent compounds have no free ions or electrons, so they are generally poor conductors of electricity.

quiz.q: Valency of carbon:
quiz.why: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and forms 4 bonds, so its valency is 4.

quiz.q: Bond in O₂:
quiz.why: Each oxygen atom needs 2 more electrons, so two O atoms share 2 pairs, forming a double bond.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

lessons.title: Versatile carbon: chains, rings and homologous series

scenes.text: Like LEGO bricks that join in endless ways, carbon atoms link to each other in chains, branches and rings.
The same element is in diamond, pencil graphite and football-shaped C₆₀.
Families of compounds that differ by CH₂ form homologous series.

steps.title: Why so many compounds?
steps.body:
- **Catenation:** carbon links to other carbon atoms to form long **chains**, **branched chains** and **rings**; C–C bonds are strong and stable.
- **Tetravalency:** carbon bonds with C, H, O, N, S, Cl and many other elements.

**Allotropes of carbon:** diamond (each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D structure — hardest), graphite (each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers, one electron free — a good conductor and lubricant), **fullerenes** (C₆₀ shaped like a football).

steps.title: Saturated, unsaturated and series
steps.body:
- **Saturated** hydrocarbons (alkanes) have only single bonds: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈).
- **Unsaturated:** alkenes (C=C) CₙH₂ₙ (ethene C₂H₄); alkynes (C≡C) CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne C₂H₂).
- Ring compounds: cyclohexane C₆H₁₂; benzene C₆H₆.
- **Homologous series:** compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, differing successively by **–CH₂–** (14 u). Physical properties (melting/boiling point) change gradually.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — isomers
steps.body: Butane C₄H₁₀ has two structures: a straight chain (n-butane) and a branched chain (isobutane). Compounds with the same formula but different structures are **structural isomers**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — homologous series
steps.body: CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH: each differs by CH₂ (14 u), same –OH group → a homologous series of alcohols. Next member: C₅H₁₁OH.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying graphite is hard like diamond.
- Writing the alkene formula as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
- Thinking the molecular mass of successive members differs by 12 u (it is 14 u).

activity.prompt: Saturated or unsaturated?

quiz.q: The property of carbon to form chains is
quiz.why: The ability of carbon to join with other carbon atoms to form long chains is called catenation.

quiz.q: Successive members of a homologous series differ by
quiz.why: Successive members of a homologous series differ by a CH₂ unit, which is a mass of 14 u.

quiz.q: General formula of alkynes:
quiz.why: Alkynes have a triple bond and the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, for example C₂H₂.

quiz.q: Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity?
quiz.why: Graphite conducts electricity because it has free electrons. Diamond has none, so it does not.

quiz.q: Structural isomers have
quiz.why: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures, for example n-butane and isobutane.

quiz.q: C₆₀ is called
quiz.why: C₆₀ is a fullerene, a football-shaped molecule of carbon.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

lessons.title: Functional groups and naming

scenes.text: A chemist sees CH₃CH₂CHO and immediately says 'propanal'.
The name tells the number of carbons and the functional group.
IUPAC naming is a puzzle with simple rules.

steps.title: Functional groups
steps.body:
An atom or group that gives a compound its characteristic properties:

- Halo (–Cl, –Br): **chloro-/bromo-** prefix — chloropropane
- Alcohol (–OH): suffix **-ol** — propanol
- Aldehyde (–CHO): suffix **-al** — propanal
- Ketone (>C=O): suffix **-one** — propanone
- Carboxylic acid (–COOH): suffix **-oic acid** — propanoic acid
- Double bond: **-ene** (propene); triple bond: **-yne** (propyne)

steps.title: Naming steps
steps.body:
1. Count carbons in the longest chain: 1 meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex.
2. Choose the suffix/prefix from the functional group.
3. If a suffix starts with a vowel, drop the final 'e' of the alkane name: propane → propanol, propanone.

The carbon of –CHO and –COOH is counted in the chain.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — name these
steps.body:
- CH₃CH₂Br: **bromoethane**
- HCHO: **methanal** (formaldehyde)
- CH₃COCH₃: **propanone** (acetone)
- CH₃COOH: **ethanoic acid**
- CH₃CH=CH₂: **propene**
- HC≡CH: **ethyne**

steps.title: Solved example 2 — draw from a name
steps.body: Butanone: 4 carbons with a ketone in the chain: CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH₃. (A ketone needs at least 3 carbons, so 'methanone' and 'ethanone' do not exist.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not counting the carbon of –COOH in the chain (CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid, not methanoic acid).
- Writing 'propaneol' (drop the e).
- Confusing aldehyde (–CHO at the end) with ketone (C=O inside the chain).

activity.prompt: Match the compound with its IUPAC name.

quiz.q: Suffix for an aldehyde:
quiz.why: The suffix for an aldehyde is -al, for example propanal.

quiz.q: CH₃COOH is
quiz.why: CH₃COOH has two carbons and a carboxylic acid group, so it is ethanoic acid.

quiz.q: Functional group in propanone:
quiz.why: Propanone has a C=O group within the chain, which is a ketone group.

quiz.q: Name of C₂H₂:
quiz.why: C₂H₂ has two carbons and a triple bond, so it is ethyne.

quiz.q: The smallest ketone has
quiz.why: The C=O in a ketone must lie within the chain, so at least 3 carbons are needed. The smallest ketone is propanone.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

lessons.title: Chemical properties of carbon compounds

scenes.text: Neha's cooking pan turns black at the bottom when the gas flame is yellow.
After the air holes of the burner are cleaned, the flame turns blue and the soot stops.
Combustion is only one of four reaction types carbon compounds undergo.

steps.title: Four reaction types
steps.body:
- **Combustion:** C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat and light; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat and light. Saturated hydrocarbons usually burn with a clean **blue** flame; unsaturated ones give a **yellow sooty** flame. A yellow flame on a gas stove means incomplete combustion — clean the air holes.
- **Oxidation:** alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by **alkaline KMnO₄** or **acidified K₂Cr₂O₇** (oxidising agents): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH. (Purple KMnO₄ loses its colour.)
- **Addition:** unsaturated compounds add H₂ in the presence of **nickel or palladium catalyst** — **hydrogenation** of vegetable oils to make vanaspati ghee.
- **Substitution:** saturated hydrocarbons react with chlorine in **sunlight**: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (H atoms replaced one by one).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — test for unsaturation
steps.body: Burn two samples: the one with a yellow, sooty flame is likely unsaturated. A better lab test: unsaturated compounds decolourise bromine water by addition.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — health note
steps.body: Animal fats contain saturated fatty acids, said to be harmful for heart health; vegetable oils contain unsaturated fatty acids and are a better choice for cooking — though hydrogenated (saturated) vanaspati is less healthy than the oil it came from.

steps.title: Fuels and their flames
steps.body: Coal and petroleum contain carbon, hydrogen and also nitrogen and sulphur; burning them releases oxides of sulphur and nitrogen — major air pollutants. Charcoal or coal glows without a flame because a flame forms only when gaseous substances burn.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling oxidation of ethanol 'combustion'.
- Forgetting the catalyst in hydrogenation or sunlight in substitution.
- Saying saturated compounds give sooty flames (it is usually the unsaturated ones).

activity.prompt: Classify the reaction.

quiz.q: Hydrogenation of vegetable oils needs a catalyst such as
quiz.why: Hydrogenation of vegetable oils adds hydrogen across double bonds using nickel (or palladium) as a catalyst.

quiz.q: Substitution of methane by chlorine requires
quiz.why: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight in a substitution reaction, replacing hydrogen atoms with chlorine.

quiz.q: Alkaline KMnO₄ converts ethanol to
quiz.why: Alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid.

quiz.q: A yellow flame on a gas stove indicates
quiz.why: A yellow, sooty flame shows incomplete combustion, usually because the air holes are blocked. Cleaning them gives a blue flame.

quiz.q: Unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo
quiz.why: Unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, so they undergo addition reactions across them.

quiz.q: Which burns with a blue flame usually?
quiz.why: Saturated hydrocarbons like methane burn completely with a blue flame. Unsaturated or carbon-rich compounds give a yellow sooty flame.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

lessons.title: Ethanol and ethanoic acid

scenes.text: The pickle jar contains vinegar — a 5–8% solution of ethanoic acid.
The hand sanitiser by the door contains ethanol.
Two important carbon compounds, with very different uses and risks.

steps.title: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
steps.body:
- Colourless liquid, soluble in water; the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks; also used in tincture iodine, cough syrups, tonics and as a solvent.
- **Health:** drinking even small amounts causes drunkenness and harms health; long-term use causes many problems. **Methanol** (in illicit liquor) can cause blindness and death. Industrial alcohol is **denatured** (made unfit to drink) with methanol and coloured with dyes.
- **With sodium:** 2Na + 2CH₃CH₂OH → 2CH₃CH₂ONa (sodium ethoxide) + H₂.
- **Dehydration:** with **hot concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K** → CH₂=CH₂ (ethene) + H₂O.
- Ethanol is a clean fuel; mixed with petrol it is used as a fuel in many countries.

steps.title: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH)
steps.body:
- Commonly called **acetic acid**; 5–8% solution = **vinegar** (preservative in pickles). Pure ethanoic acid freezes at 290 K, so it is called **glacial acetic acid** in cold weather.
- It is a **weak acid** (does not ionise completely).
- **Esterification:** CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ (ethyl ethanoate, a sweet-smelling **ester**) + H₂O, with **conc. H₂SO₄** as catalyst. Esters are used in perfumes and flavourings.
- **Saponification:** ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium ethanoate (CH₃COONa). This is how soap is made from fats.
- **With a base:** NaOH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
- **With carbonates:** 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ (CO₂ turns lime water milky).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — distinguish ethanol and ethanoic acid
steps.body: Add sodium hydrogencarbonate: **ethanoic acid** gives brisk effervescence of CO₂; ethanol does not. Or test with blue litmus: ethanoic acid turns it red.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — identify X
steps.body: An organic compound X (C₂H₄O₂) gives effervescence with NaHCO₃ and a sweet-smelling compound with ethanol and conc. H₂SO₄. X is **ethanoic acid**; the sweet product is **ethyl ethanoate**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that conc. H₂SO₄ is a reactant in esterification (it is a catalyst; in dehydration it removes water).
- Calling vinegar pure acetic acid.
- Saying alcohol is safe in small quantities for teenagers — it is harmful, and illegal to sell to minors in India.

statements.s: Glacial acetic acid freezes at 290 K.
statements.why: Hence the name in cold climates.

statements.s: Esters have a sweet, fruity smell.
Ethanol reacts with sodium to give hydrogen.
Saponification makes alcohol from glucose.
statements.why: It is the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, used to make soap.

statements.s: Heating ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives ethene.

quiz.q: The ester formed from ethanoic acid and ethanol:
quiz.why: Ethanoic acid and ethanol form an ester named from the alcohol part first: ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₂H₅.

quiz.q: Vinegar is a solution of
quiz.why: Vinegar is a 5–8% solution of ethanoic acid in water, used to preserve pickles.

quiz.q: Ethanoic acid with NaHCO₃ gives
quiz.why: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate to give CO₂ gas with brisk effervescence.

quiz.q: Dehydration of ethanol at 443 K with conc. H₂SO₄ gives
quiz.why: Heating ethanol at 443 K with conc. H₂SO₄ removes water and gives ethene.

quiz.q: Denatured alcohol is made unfit to drink by adding
quiz.why: Denatured alcohol has poisonous substances like methanol added, so it cannot be drunk.

quiz.q: Saponification produces
quiz.why: Saponification is the reaction of an ester (fat) with sodium hydroxide, giving soap and alcohol (glycerol).

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

lessons.title: Soaps and detergents

scenes.text: Water alone cannot remove an oily curry stain from a school shirt.
Soap solution and scrubbing lift it out.
Soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail — they trap oil in tiny balls called micelles.

steps.title: How soap works
steps.body:
Soaps are **sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids**. Each molecule has:

- an **ionic (hydrophilic) end** that dissolves in water, and
- a long **hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail** that dissolves in oil.

In water, the tails bury themselves in the oily dirt while the heads face outward, forming a cluster called a **micelle**. Micelles stay suspended (an emulsion) and are rinsed away. Soap micelles do not come together because the ionic heads repel each other.

steps.title: Hard water and detergents
steps.body:
**Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble precipitate called **scum**, wasting soap and leaving deposits.

**Detergents** are usually ammonium or sulphonate salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Their charged ends do **not** form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so they work in hard water. They are used in shampoos and laundry products. (Some detergents are not biodegradable — a water pollution concern.)

steps.title: Solved example 1 — hard water test
steps.body: Equal amounts of soap solution are shaken with distilled water and with hard water. Distilled water gives plenty of foam; hard water gives little foam and a white curdy scum. More soap is needed with hard water.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why scrub?
steps.body: Scrubbing or beating clothes helps pull the oily dirt off the fabric so that micelles can form around it and carry it away.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the hydrocarbon tail faces water in a micelle (it faces the oil, inward).
- Thinking detergents form scum in hard water.
- Calling soap 'an ester' (soap is a salt; it is made from esters).

activity.prompt: Order the steps of how soap removes an oily stain.
items: Hydrocarbon tails attach to the oil droplet
Ionic heads face the water outside
A micelle forms around the oil

quiz.q: Soaps are salts of
quiz.why: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.

quiz.q: In a micelle the hydrophobic tails point
options: towards the oil at the centre
quiz.why: In a micelle the hydrophobic (oil-loving) tails point inward towards the oil at the centre, while the ionic heads face the water.

quiz.q: Scum forms when soap reacts with
quiz.why: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts in hard water to form an insoluble scum.

quiz.q: Detergents work in hard water because
options: they do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
quiz.why: Detergents do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, so they keep working in hard water.

quiz.q: Ionic end of a soap molecule is
quiz.why: The ionic end of a soap molecule is hydrophilic, which means it is attracted to water.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Carbon and its Compounds)

questions.q: Number of covalent bonds in methane:
questions.why: In methane each of the four hydrogen atoms shares a pair with carbon, giving 4 covalent bonds.

questions.q: IUPAC name of CH₃OH:
questions.why: CH₃OH has one carbon and an -OH group, so it is methanol.

questions.q: Which is unsaturated?
questions.why: C₂H₄ is ethene with a double bond, so it is unsaturated. CH₄, C₂H₆ and C₃H₈ are saturated.

questions.q: Glacial acetic acid is
questions.why: Glacial acetic acid is pure ethanoic acid. It freezes at about 290 K, which is just above room temperature in cold weather.

questions.q: Next member of the series CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈ is
questions.why: The series CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈ adds a CH₂ each time, so the next is C₄H₁₀.

questions.q: Hydrogenation of oils is an example of
questions.why: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to the double bonds of oils, so it is an addition reaction.

questions.q: Assertion: Covalent compounds are poor conductors. Reason: they do not form ions.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Covalent compounds do not form ions, so they have no charged particles to carry current.

questions.q: Functional group of propanal:
questions.why: Propanal is an aldehyde, whose functional group is –CHO.

questions.q: Which reaction forms a sweet-smelling substance?
options: Ethanoic acid + ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄
questions.why: Ethanoic acid and ethanol react with conc. H₂SO₄ as a catalyst to form an ester with a sweet, fruity smell. This is esterification.

questions.q: Case: In a village with hard water, Seema finds her soap does not lather and leaves white deposits on clothes. The deposits are
questions.why: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts in hard water to form scum, which are insoluble calcium or magnesium salts of fatty acids.

questions.q: Case continued: the best solution is to
questions.why: A detergent does not form scum with hard water ions, so it lathers and cleans in hard water.

questions.q: Number of structural isomers of butane:
questions.why: Butane, C₄H₁₀, has two structural isomers: n-butane and isobutane.

questions.q: Product of CH₃CH₂OH with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (heated):
questions.why: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ on heating oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH.

questions.q: A compound C₂H₆O reacts with Na to give a gas that burns with a pop. With hot conc. H₂SO₄ it gives C₂H₄. The compound is
questions.why: A compound C₂H₆O that reacts with sodium to give hydrogen and dehydrates to ethene with hot conc. H₂SO₄ is ethanol.

questions.q: Molecular mass difference between C₂H₅OH and C₄H₉OH:
questions.why: C₄H₉OH has two more CH₂ units than C₂H₅OH. Each CH₂ is 14 u, so the difference is 28 u.

questions.q: Why does the micelle cluster stay in solution rather than settling as oil?
options: Ionic heads on the outside interact with water and repel other micelles
questions.why: In a micelle the ionic heads face outward and are attracted to water. They also repel other micelles, so the oil stays dispersed as an emulsion.

questions.q: C₃H₆O can be (i) propanal or (ii) propanone. The structural difference is that
options: (i) has C=O at the chain end, (ii) has C=O in the middle
questions.why: Propanal has C=O at the end of the chain (an aldehyde), while propanone has C=O in the middle (a ketone). They have the same molecular formula, so they are functional isomers.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Life Processes
courses.summary: Nutrition (photosynthesis and human digestion), respiration (aerobic and anaerobic, human lungs), transportation in humans and plants, and excretion (kidneys, dialysis and plant excretion) — with labelled-diagram descriptions and experiments.
outcomes: Learners can explain photosynthesis and the experiments that show its requirements
Learners can trace digestion in humans with each enzyme and juice

lessons.title: Nutrition in plants: photosynthesis

scenes.text: A money plant on Asha's window grows towards the light and stays green.
Its leaves are tiny food factories using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
Her teacher shows how to prove, with iodine, that leaves make starch only where there is light and chlorophyll.

steps.title: Life processes and nutrition
steps.body:
**Life processes** are the basic functions that maintain living organisms: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Living things need energy and raw materials from outside — this is **nutrition**.

- **Autotrophic:** organisms make their own food from simple inorganic substances (green plants, some bacteria).
- **Heterotrophic:** organisms depend on others for food (animals, fungi).

steps.title: Photosynthesis
steps.body:
**6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O** (in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight).

Three events:
1. Absorption of light energy by **chlorophyll** (in chloroplasts).
2. Conversion of light energy to chemical energy and **splitting of water** into hydrogen and oxygen.
3. **Reduction of CO₂** to carbohydrates.

These need not happen one immediately after another: **desert plants** take in CO₂ at night (stomata open at night to reduce water loss) and use it in the day.

**Stomata** are tiny pores (mostly on the lower surface of leaves) for gas exchange; **guard cells** open and close them. Water comes from the soil through roots; nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, magnesium etc. are taken up as minerals. Food is stored as **starch**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — chlorophyll is needed
steps.body: Take a potted plant with **variegated leaves** (green and white patches). Keep it in the dark for 3 days (destarching), then in sunlight for 6 hours. Boil a leaf in alcohol to remove chlorophyll, rinse, add iodine: **only the earlier green parts turn blue-black** → starch forms only where chlorophyll was present.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — CO₂ is needed
steps.body: Two destarched potted plants are covered with bell jars. One jar contains **potassium hydroxide** (absorbs CO₂). After sunlight, a leaf from the KOH plant shows **no starch** with iodine; the other does → CO₂ is essential.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing for starch without removing chlorophyll first (the colour change is hidden).
- Writing that plants take in O₂ only at night — respiration happens all the time; photosynthesis only in light.
- Forgetting to destarch the plant before the experiment.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the variegated-leaf starch test.
items: Keep the plant in darkness for three days
Expose it to sunlight for about six hours
Boil the leaf in alcohol on a water bath to remove chlorophyll
Rinse and add dilute iodine solution
Observe: blue-black colour only where the leaf was green

quiz.q: Raw materials of photosynthesis:
quiz.why: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water, with light and chlorophyll, to make glucose and oxygen.

quiz.q: The pores for gas exchange in leaves are
quiz.why: Stomata are the tiny pores in leaves for gas exchange, controlled by guard cells.

quiz.q: Potassium hydroxide in the bell jar is used to
quiz.why: Potassium hydroxide absorbs CO₂, so the plant in that jar has no CO₂ available.

quiz.q: Desert plants take in CO₂
quiz.why: Desert plants open their stomata at night to take in CO₂ and save water, and fix it into an intermediate to use during the day.

quiz.q: The form in which plants store food is mainly
quiz.why: Plants store food mainly as starch, a reserve carbohydrate.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an event of photosynthesis?
quiz.why: Breaking glucose to release energy is respiration, not photosynthesis. Photosynthesis involves light absorption, splitting of water and reduction of CO₂.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

lessons.title: Nutrition in animals and human digestion

scenes.text: Farhan eats a samosa: potato starch, a little protein, and plenty of oil.
From mouth to intestine, juices break each nutrient into small, soluble molecules.
Let us follow the samosa through a 7–8 metre long tube.

steps.title: Heterotrophic nutrition
steps.body:
- **Holozoic** (eat and digest inside): humans, Amoeba. Amoeba engulfs food with **pseudopodia**, forming a **food vacuole** where it is digested.
- **Saprophytic:** break down food outside and absorb it (fungi like bread mould, yeast, mushrooms).
- **Parasitic:** obtain food from a host without killing it (Cuscuta/amarbel, ticks, lice, tapeworms).

steps.title: Human digestive system
steps.body:
- **Mouth:** teeth chew; **salivary amylase** converts starch to sugar. Tongue mixes food.
- **Oesophagus:** **peristalsis** (rhythmic contraction) pushes food down.
- **Stomach:** gastric glands release **HCl** (acidic medium, kills germs), **pepsin** (digests proteins) and **mucus** (protects the stomach lining). A **sphincter** controls exit to the small intestine.
- **Small intestine** (longest part): receives **bile** from the **liver** (makes food alkaline and **emulsifies fats** into small globules) and **pancreatic juice** (**trypsin** for proteins, **lipase** for emulsified fats). Intestinal glands finish digestion: proteins → **amino acids**, carbohydrates → **glucose**, fats → **fatty acids and glycerol**. **Villi** (finger-like projections) increase surface area for **absorption** into blood.
- **Large intestine:** absorbs water; waste leaves via the **anus**, controlled by the anal sphincter.

Herbivores eating grass have a longer small intestine to digest cellulose.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — role of HCl
steps.body: HCl creates an acidic medium that activates pepsin and kills many germs in food. Mucus prevents HCl from damaging the stomach lining; excess acid without enough mucus can cause acidity and ulcers.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why chew well?
steps.body: Chewing increases the surface area of food and mixes it with saliva so salivary amylase can start starch digestion. Bread chewed for a long time tastes sweet because starch is turned into sugar.

steps.title: Tooth decay
steps.body: Bacteria act on sugars in the mouth to produce acids; these soften the enamel and cause **dental caries**. Brushing after eating and avoiding frequent sweets helps (see also the pH lesson in Chapter 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying digestion of starch begins in the stomach (it begins in the mouth).
- Calling bile an enzyme (bile has no enzymes; it emulsifies fats).
- Placing villi in the large intestine.

activity.prompt: Match each juice or part with its role.
pairs: Begins protein digestion in the stomach
Digests proteins in the small intestine

quiz.q: Bile is produced by the
quiz.why: Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

quiz.q: Protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach:
quiz.why: Pepsin digests proteins in the acidic stomach.

quiz.q: Finger-like projections that absorb food:
quiz.why: Villi are finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase the surface area for absorption of food.

quiz.q: Amoeba captures food using
quiz.why: Amoeba captures food by extending pseudopodia (false feet) around it.

quiz.q: Fats are finally digested into
quiz.why: Fats are finally broken down into fatty acids and glycerol.

quiz.q: Cuscuta (amarbel) shows
quiz.why: Cuscuta (amarbel) takes food from a host plant, so it shows parasitic nutrition.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

lessons.title: Respiration

scenes.text: After a fast sprint, Priya's legs ache and she breathes hard.
Her muscles ran short of oxygen and made lactic acid for a while.
Respiration releases energy from food — with plenty of oxygen or, briefly, without it.

steps.title: Breaking down glucose
steps.body:
**Step 1 (cytoplasm, all organisms):** glucose (6C) → **pyruvate (3C)** + energy.

Then:
- **Anaerobic in yeast:** pyruvate → **ethanol + CO₂** + energy (fermentation).
- **Lack of oxygen in our muscles:** pyruvate → **lactic acid** + energy (causes **cramps**).
- **Aerobic (mitochondria):** pyruvate → **CO₂ + H₂O** + much more energy.

Energy is stored as **ATP** ('energy currency' of the cell), used for muscle contraction, protein synthesis, nerve impulses, etc. Aerobic respiration releases far more energy than anaerobic.

steps.title: Breathing in humans
steps.body:
Air path: **nostrils** (hairs and mucus filter dust) → **pharynx** → **larynx** → **trachea** (rings of cartilage keep it from collapsing) → **bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli** (balloon-like sacs with blood capillaries).

Inhaling: ribs lift, **diaphragm flattens**, chest cavity enlarges, air rushes in. Alveoli provide a huge surface for exchange (about 80 m² if spread out). **Haemoglobin** in red blood cells carries oxygen; CO₂ is carried mostly dissolved in blood. Lungs always hold some residual air so exchange is continuous.

**Aquatic animals** breathe faster than land animals because dissolved oxygen in water is much less than oxygen in air. **Plants** exchange gases through stomata and lenticels; at night they release CO₂; in daytime photosynthesis uses CO₂ and releases O₂.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — compare
steps.body: Aerobic: needs O₂; in mitochondria; products CO₂ + H₂O; much energy. Anaerobic: no O₂; in cytoplasm; products ethanol + CO₂ (yeast) or lactic acid (muscle); less energy.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — lime-water experiment
steps.body: Blow exhaled air through lime water using a straw; it turns milky faster than when air from a syringe/pump is passed. So **exhaled air contains more CO₂**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying anaerobic respiration happens only in yeast (our muscles do it briefly too).
- Confusing breathing (physical exchange of air) with respiration (chemical release of energy).
- Thinking plants respire only at night.

activity.prompt: Where does each happen?

quiz.q: Glucose is first broken into
quiz.why: Glucose is first broken into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. This step does not need oxygen.

quiz.q: Muscle cramps after exercise are due to
quiz.why: In heavy exercise muscle cells break pyruvate down without oxygen into lactic acid, which causes cramps.

quiz.q: Energy currency of the cell:
quiz.why: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell.

quiz.q: Rings of cartilage are found in the
quiz.why: The trachea has rings of cartilage, which keep the air passage from collapsing.

quiz.q: Aquatic animals breathe faster because
options: dissolved oxygen in water is low
quiz.why: Water holds much less dissolved oxygen than air, so aquatic animals breathe faster to get enough.

quiz.q: Yeast in anaerobic conditions produces
quiz.why: Yeast respiring without oxygen (fermentation) produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

lessons.title: Transportation in human beings

scenes.text: At a blood donation camp, Rahul's uncle has his blood pressure checked: 120/80.
His heart pumps blood through about 100,000 km of vessels.
Blood is the body's delivery system — and the heart is the pump with four rooms.

steps.title: Heart and double circulation
steps.body:
The heart has **four chambers**: two **atria** (upper, receive blood) and two **ventricles** (lower, thick-walled, pump blood).

- Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs → **pulmonary veins** → **left atrium** → **left ventricle** → **aorta** → body.
- Deoxygenated blood from the body → **vena cava** → **right atrium** → **right ventricle** → **pulmonary artery** → lungs.
- **Valves** prevent backflow.

Blood passes through the heart **twice** in one cycle — **double circulation**. Separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood gives an efficient oxygen supply, needed by birds and mammals to maintain body temperature. Fish have a **2-chambered** heart (single circulation); amphibians and many reptiles have **3 chambers**.

steps.title: Vessels, blood and lymph
steps.body:
- **Arteries:** carry blood away from the heart; thick, elastic walls (high pressure).
- **Veins:** bring blood to the heart; thinner walls with **valves**.
- **Capillaries:** one-cell-thick walls; exchange with cells.
- **Blood:** plasma (carries food, CO₂, nitrogenous wastes), **RBCs** (haemoglobin, O₂), **WBCs** (defence), **platelets** (clotting to stop bleeding).
- **Blood pressure:** normal about **120/80 mm Hg** (systolic/diastolic), measured with a **sphygmomanometer**. High BP (hypertension) can rupture capillaries — see a doctor if readings are often high.
- **Lymph:** fluid that escapes from capillaries into tissues; carries digested **fat** from the intestine and drains back into veins; helps in defence.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why ventricles are thicker
steps.body: Ventricles pump blood to the lungs and the whole body, so they need thick muscular walls. The left ventricle is the thickest because it pumps blood to the entire body.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — trace a red blood cell
steps.body: From the lungs: pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body capillaries → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all arteries carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
- Saying veins have thick walls.
- Mixing up atria (receive) and ventricles (pump).

activity.prompt: Trace oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the body.

quiz.q: The chamber that pumps blood to the whole body:
quiz.why: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body, so it has the thickest wall.

quiz.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs?
quiz.why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs. It is an exception to the rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood.

quiz.q: Normal blood pressure is about
quiz.why: Normal blood pressure is about 120 mm Hg (systolic) over 80 mm Hg (diastolic).

quiz.q: Cells that help blood clot:
quiz.why: Platelets help blood to clot, which prevents blood loss from wounds.

quiz.q: Fish have a heart with
quiz.why: A fish heart has 2 chambers (one atrium and one ventricle), and blood passes through it once per cycle.

quiz.q: Lymph carries digested
quiz.why: Lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the small intestine.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

lessons.title: Transportation in plants

scenes.text: A tall mango tree lifts water from the soil to leaves many metres up — without a pump.
Water evaporating from leaves pulls more water up like sipping through a straw.
Meanwhile sugar made in leaves travels down to the fruits and roots through another set of pipes.

steps.title: Xylem: water and minerals
steps.body:
**Xylem** vessels and tracheids form a continuous channel from roots to leaves.

- At the roots, cells take up ions actively; water follows, creating **root pressure** — important at **night**.
- During the day, **transpiration** (loss of water vapour through stomata) creates a **suction (transpiration pull)** — the main force moving water up tall plants.

Transpiration also helps in cooling the plant and in absorbing minerals.

steps.title: Phloem: food (translocation)
steps.body:
**Phloem** (sieve tubes and companion cells) carries soluble products of photosynthesis, mainly **sucrose**, amino acids and other substances from leaves to roots, fruits, seeds and growing parts.

Translocation uses **energy from ATP**: sucrose is loaded into phloem, raising osmotic pressure so water enters and pushes the material to where it is needed. It can move in **both directions** (up and down), unlike xylem's upward flow.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — compare xylem and phloem
steps.body: Xylem: water and minerals; mostly upward; mainly passive (transpiration pull). Phloem: food; up and down; active (uses ATP).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — experiment idea
steps.body: Place a cut celery stalk or balsam plant in coloured water; after a few hours, coloured streaks appear in the stem — showing the path of water in xylem.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying phloem carries water upward.
- Saying transpiration is useless water loss (it pulls water up and cools the plant).
- Forgetting that root pressure matters mostly at night.

statements.s: Xylem carries food from leaves to roots.
Transpiration pull is the main force for water movement in tall trees during the day.
Translocation in phloem uses energy.
statements.why: ATP is used to load sucrose.

statements.s: Phloem transport can be in both directions.
Root pressure is most important at noon.

quiz.q: Translocation of food occurs in
quiz.why: Translocation, the movement of food in plants, occurs in the phloem through sieve tubes.

quiz.q: Main force for upward water movement in daytime:
quiz.why: In the daytime the main force for upward movement of water is transpiration pull, caused by evaporation from leaves.

quiz.q: Food in phloem is mainly transported as
quiz.why: Food in the phloem is mainly transported as sucrose, a soluble sugar.

quiz.q: Transpiration helps in
options: absorption and upward movement of water, and cooling
quiz.why: Transpiration helps in absorption and upward movement of water and minerals, and also cools the plant.

quiz.q: Which uses ATP?
quiz.why: Phloem translocation is an active process that uses ATP energy. Transpiration, evaporation and diffusion do not use ATP.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

lessons.title: Excretion

scenes.text: Meera's grandfather visits the hospital twice a week for dialysis because his kidneys have failed.
A machine filters his blood, doing the job a pair of fist-sized organs normally does.
Excretion removes harmful nitrogenous wastes. Let us see how the kidney's tiny filters work.

steps.title: Human excretory system
steps.body:
Two **kidneys**, two **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and the **urethra**. Urine formed in the kidneys flows through ureters to the bladder, where it is stored until released through the urethra (under nervous control).

The filtering unit is the **nephron**:
1. **Glomerulus** (a cluster of capillaries) inside **Bowman's capsule** filters blood — water, glucose, amino acids, salts and **urea** pass into the capsule.
2. As the filtrate moves along the **tubule**, useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, most water) are **reabsorbed**.
3. The remaining liquid is **urine**. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much extra water the body has and how much waste must be removed.

About **180 L** of filtrate forms daily but only 1–2 L leaves as urine.

steps.title: Artificial kidney (haemodialysis)
steps.body: Blood is passed through long tubes with semi-permeable lining bathed in a dialysing fluid that has the same osmotic pressure as blood but **no nitrogenous wastes**. Wastes diffuse out and the cleaned blood returns to the body. Unlike a real kidney, there is **no reabsorption**. Kidney transplant from a matching donor is another option.

steps.title: Excretion in plants
steps.body:
- Oxygen (from photosynthesis) and CO₂ (from respiration) diffuse out; excess water is lost by **transpiration**.
- Wastes stored in **cell vacuoles** or in **leaves that fall off**.
- Some wastes stored as **resins and gums**, especially in old xylem.
- Some released into the soil around roots.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — trace urine
steps.body: Kidney (nephron) → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → out of the body.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the bladder makes urine (kidneys do).
- Saying dialysis reabsorbs glucose (it does not reabsorb).
- Calling excretion and egestion (removal of undigested food) the same thing.

activity.prompt: Complete the nephron sequence.
activity.text: Blood is filtered in the ___ inside Bowman's capsule; useful substances are ___ in the tubule; the remaining fluid is ___.

quiz.q: Functional unit of the kidney:
quiz.why: The nephron is the filtering and functional unit of the kidney.

quiz.q: Urine is stored in the
quiz.why: Urine is stored in the urinary bladder until it is passed out.

quiz.q: Main nitrogenous waste in human urine:
quiz.why: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in human urine. It is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

quiz.q: In dialysis, the dialysing fluid lacks
quiz.why: The dialysing fluid has no nitrogenous wastes, so wastes diffuse out of the blood into it.

quiz.q: Plants store some wastes as
quiz.why: Plants store some waste products as resins and gums in old xylem, and also lose them in leaves that fall.

quiz.q: Glomerulus is a
quiz.why: The glomerulus is a cluster of capillaries in the nephron that filters blood.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Life Processes)

questions.q: Which is a life process?
questions.why: Nutrition is a basic life process, along with respiration, transport and excretion.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own food are
questions.why: Organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis are autotrophs.

questions.q: Site of complete digestion of food:
questions.why: Digestion is completed in the small intestine, with bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice.

questions.q: The blood vessel with valves to prevent backflow:
questions.why: Veins have valves that stop blood flowing backwards, as the blood pressure in them is low.

questions.q: Gas released during photosynthesis:
questions.why: Oxygen is released during photosynthesis. It comes from the splitting of water.

questions.q: Enzyme in saliva:
questions.why: Salivary amylase in saliva begins to digest starch.

questions.q: Assertion: The left ventricle has the thickest wall. Reason: it pumps blood to all parts of the body.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, which needs high pressure, so its wall is thickest.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast gives
questions.why: In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) gives ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Water rises in tall trees mainly due to
questions.why: In tall trees water rises mainly due to transpiration pull, which draws water up the xylem like a suction.

questions.q: Case: In an experiment, a destarched plant kept with KOH in a bell jar shows no starch in its leaves after sunlight. The conclusion is
questions.why: KOH absorbs CO₂, so the plant got none. No starch was formed, which shows that CO₂ is necessary for photosynthesis.

questions.q: Case continued: why was the plant destarched first?
options: So any starch found must be newly made during the experiment
questions.why: The plant is destarched so that any starch found later must have been made during the experiment. This makes it a fair test.

questions.q: Emulsification of fats is done by
questions.why: Bile salts break large fat globules into small droplets (emulsification), which makes fat digestion easier.

questions.q: Double circulation means
options: blood flows in two directions in one vessel
blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle
questions.why: In double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: once in the pulmonary circuit and once in the systemic circuit.

questions.q: A person's urine contains glucose. Which process in the nephron is likely affected?
questions.why: Glucose is normally filtered and then fully reabsorbed in the tubule. Glucose in urine suggests reabsorption is not working fully.

questions.q: Why are alveoli suited for gas exchange?
options: Thin walls, huge surface area and rich blood supply
questions.why: Alveoli have thin walls, a very large total surface area and a rich blood supply, which make gas exchange efficient.

questions.q: Which pair is mismatched?
questions.why: Trypsin is made by the pancreas and works in the small intestine, not the stomach. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: A 3-chambered heart allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Animals like frogs can tolerate this because
options: their body temperature depends on surroundings, so they need less energy
questions.why: Frogs are cold-blooded, so their body temperature depends on their surroundings and they need less energy. Some mixing of blood is therefore tolerable.

questions.q: If 180 L of filtrate forms per day and 1.5 L of urine is passed, the percentage of filtrate reabsorbed is about

courses.title: Ch 6 · Control and Coordination
courses.summary: How the nervous system and hormones coordinate the body: neurons and synapses, reflex arcs, the parts of the brain, plant movements and plant hormones, and the human endocrine glands with feedback control.
outcomes: Learners can describe the structure of a neuron and how impulses travel
Learners can trace a reflex arc and explain why reflexes are fast
Learners can name brain regions and their functions
Learners can explain tropisms and the roles of plant hormones
Learners can name endocrine glands, their hormones and effects, and explain feedback

lessons.title: Neurons and nervous tissue

scenes.text: Sameer's hand brushes a hot tawa and jerks back before he even feels pain.
Messages raced along nerve cells faster than he could think.
Neurons are the wires of the body; let us see how they carry signals.

steps.title: Receptors and neurons
steps.body:
**Receptors** in sense organs detect stimuli: photoreceptors (eye), phonoreceptors (ear), olfactory receptors (nose), gustatory receptors (tongue), thermoreceptors and touch receptors (skin).

A **neuron** has:
- **Dendrites:** receive information (stimulus sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse).
- **Cell body:** contains the nucleus.
- **Axon:** carries the electrical impulse away from the cell body.
- **Nerve ending:** releases chemicals that cross the **synapse** (small gap) to the next neuron, muscle or gland, where a new impulse starts.

So signals travel as **electrical impulses within a neuron** and as **chemical signals across a synapse**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — path of a signal
steps.body: Dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending → (chemicals across synapse) → dendrite of the next neuron.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why chemical signals at synapses?
steps.body: Electrical impulses cannot jump the gap. Chemicals released at the axon end diffuse across and trigger a new impulse in the next cell. This also ensures one-way flow of information.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying impulses travel from axon to dendrite within a neuron (it is dendrite → axon).
- Saying the synapse is a physical connection (it is a tiny gap).
- Mixing up receptors (detect) and effectors (respond: muscles, glands).

activity.prompt: Order the path of information through a neuron.
items: Chemicals cross the synapse to the next cell

quiz.q: Part of the neuron where information is first acquired:
quiz.why: The dendrite is the part of the neuron that first receives information from the environment or other neurons.

quiz.q: The gap between two neurons is a
quiz.why: The gap between two neurons is called a synapse.

quiz.q: Gustatory receptors detect
quiz.why: Gustatory receptors, mainly on the tongue, detect taste.

quiz.q: Across a synapse, signals travel as
quiz.why: At a synapse the electrical impulse is passed on by chemicals called neurotransmitters.

quiz.q: Muscles and glands that respond are called
quiz.why: Muscles and glands carry out the response, so they are called effectors.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: Reflex actions and the nervous system

scenes.text: A ball flies towards Tara's face and she blinks instantly.
The message did not wait for the brain to decide; the spinal cord or brainstem handled it.
This quick, automatic response is a reflex, travelling along a reflex arc.

steps.title: Reflex arc
steps.body:
A **reflex action** is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, without thinking (pulling hand from a flame, knee jerk, sneezing, coughing, blinking, salivating).

**Reflex arc:** receptor → **sensory neuron** → **relay neuron** in the spinal cord → **motor neuron** → effector (muscle/gland).

The connections are in the **spinal cord**, so the response is fast. The information also goes on to the brain, which becomes aware of what happened. Reflex arcs evolved in animals whose thinking processes are not fast enough.

steps.title: Organisation of the nervous system
steps.body:
- **Central nervous system (CNS):** brain + spinal cord.
- **Peripheral nervous system (PNS):** **cranial nerves** (from the brain) and **spinal nerves** (from the spinal cord) connecting the CNS to all body parts.
- The brain is protected by the bony **skull (cranium)** and a fluid-filled balloon (cerebrospinal fluid) for shock absorption; the spinal cord is protected by the **vertebral column**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — trace the reflex
steps.body: Touching a hot object: heat/pain receptors in skin → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → arm muscles contract → hand pulls away.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — voluntary vs involuntary
steps.body: Writing, talking and walking are **voluntary** (controlled by the cerebrum). Heartbeat, breathing and salivation are **involuntary**; reflexes like sneezing are involuntary and very quick.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying reflexes are controlled by the cerebrum (most are by the spinal cord).
- Leaving out the relay neuron in the arc.
- Saying the brain is not informed at all.

activity.prompt: Arrange the reflex arc in order.
items: Relay neuron in the spinal cord

quiz.q: A reflex arc is usually completed in the
quiz.why: A reflex arc is completed in the spinal cord, so the response is quick without waiting for the brain.

quiz.q: CNS consists of
quiz.why: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and the spinal cord.

quiz.q: Which is a reflex action?
quiz.why: Sneezing is automatic and quick, so it is a reflex action. Reading, dancing and writing are voluntary.

quiz.q: The brain is protected by
quiz.why: The brain is protected by the bony skull and by the cerebrospinal fluid around it.

quiz.q: Nerves arising from the spinal cord are
quiz.why: Nerves that arise from the spinal cord are spinal nerves, part of the peripheral nervous system.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: The human brain

scenes.text: A tightrope walker balances, thinks about each step and keeps breathing calmly.
Different parts of her brain handle balance, thinking and breathing at the same time.
The brain has three main regions with distinct jobs.

steps.title: Regions and functions
steps.body:
- **Forebrain** — main thinking part. The **cerebrum** has areas for sensing (sight, hearing, smell, touch), association areas that link information, and motor areas that control **voluntary** muscles. It stores memory, thinking, reasoning, learning. Hunger is also sensed in the forebrain.
- **Midbrain** — controls certain involuntary actions such as reflex movements of the head, neck and eyes (e.g. change in pupil size).
- **Hindbrain**:
  - **Medulla:** controls involuntary actions — **blood pressure, salivation, vomiting**.
  - **Pons:** helps regulate breathing.
  - **Cerebellum:** **precision of voluntary actions, posture and balance** — walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, picking up a pencil.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — which part?
steps.body: (a) Solving a maths problem → cerebrum. (b) Balancing on a cycle → cerebellum. (c) Mouth watering at the smell of food → medulla (salivation). (d) Feeling full after a meal → forebrain.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — how muscles move
steps.body: When a nerve impulse reaches a muscle, special proteins in muscle cells change their shape and arrangement, making the cells shorter — the muscle contracts. Movement thus depends on changes at the cellular level.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing cerebrum (thinking) and cerebellum (balance).
- Saying the medulla controls voluntary actions.
- Forgetting that the forebrain also senses hunger.

activity.prompt: Match the brain part with its function.
pairs: Reflex movements of head, neck and eyes

quiz.q: Balance and posture are maintained by the
quiz.why: The cerebellum, in the hindbrain, maintains posture and balance.

quiz.q: Vomiting is controlled by the
quiz.why: The medulla controls involuntary actions like vomiting, salivation and blood pressure.

quiz.q: The main thinking part of the brain:
quiz.why: The forebrain (cerebrum) is the main thinking region, involved in reasoning, memory and voluntary action.

quiz.q: Walking in a straight line needs the
quiz.why: The cerebellum coordinates precise movements, so it is needed to walk in a straight line.

quiz.q: Muscle cells contract because
quiz.why: Muscle cells contract because special proteins change their shape and arrangement in response to nerve signals.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: Coordination in plants

scenes.text: Ravi touches a 'touch-me-not' (Mimosa pudica) leaf and its leaflets fold instantly.
A sunflower seedling on the windowsill slowly bends towards the light over days.
Plants have no nerves or muscles — yet they respond, using water movement and hormones.

steps.title: Two kinds of movement
steps.body:
1. **Not growth-related (fast):** e.g. Mimosa leaves fold on touch. Cells communicate electrical-chemically, and cells change shape by **changing the amount of water** in them (swelling/shrinking).
2. **Growth-related (slow) — tropisms:** directional growth in response to a stimulus.
   - **Phototropism:** shoots bend towards light (positive), roots away.
   - **Geotropism:** roots grow downwards with gravity (positive), shoots upward (negative).
   - **Hydrotropism:** roots grow towards water.
   - **Chemotropism:** growth of the **pollen tube** towards the ovule.
   Tendrils of a pea plant coil around support because the part away from the support grows faster (thigmotropism).

steps.title: Plant hormones
steps.body:
- **Auxin:** made at shoot tips; when light comes from one side it diffuses to the **shady side**, making those cells grow longer → shoot bends towards light.
- **Gibberellins:** help **stem growth**.
- **Cytokinins:** promote **cell division**; high in fruits and seeds.
- **Abscisic acid:** **inhibits growth**; causes **wilting of leaves** (a stress hormone).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — explain bending
steps.body: A seedling in a box with a hole on one side bends towards the hole: auxin accumulates on the darker side, cells there elongate more, so the stem curves towards light.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — classify
steps.body: Roots growing down: positive geotropism. Shoot growing up: negative geotropism. Pollen tube growing to ovule: chemotropism. Mimosa folding: touch response without growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Mimosa's folding a tropism (it is not growth-related).
- Saying auxin collects on the lighted side.
- Saying abscisic acid promotes growth.

activity.prompt: Growth-related tropism or non-growth movement?

quiz.q: Hormone that inhibits growth and causes wilting:
quiz.why: Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves. Auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin promote growth.

quiz.q: Growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule is
quiz.why: Growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule is a response to chemicals, so it is chemotropism.

quiz.q: Auxin causes bending towards light by
options: making cells on the lighted side grow faster
making cells on the shady side grow longer
quiz.why: Auxin collects on the shady side of the shoot and makes those cells grow longer. The shoot then bends towards the light.

quiz.q: Mimosa leaves fold because cells
quiz.why: Mimosa (touch-me-not) leaves fold because their cells change their water content and so change shape.

quiz.q: Hormone that promotes cell division:
quiz.why: Cytokinins promote cell division and are abundant in fruits and seeds.

quiz.q: Shoots show
quiz.why: Shoots grow upwards, against gravity, which is negative geotropism.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: Hormones in animals

scenes.text: As Kavya steps on stage, her heart pounds, breathing quickens and her hands feel cold.
Her adrenal glands have released adrenaline into the blood.
Hormones are chemical messengers that travel in blood to coordinate the body more slowly but widely.

steps.title: Endocrine glands and hormones
steps.body:
Endocrine glands release **hormones** directly into the **blood**.

- **Hypothalamus:** releasing hormones that act on the pituitary.
- **Pituitary:** **growth hormone** — deficiency in childhood causes **dwarfism**; excess can cause gigantism.
- **Thyroid:** **thyroxin** — regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; needs **iodine**. Iodine deficiency can cause **goitre** (swollen neck), so iodised salt is recommended.
- **Adrenal:** **adrenaline** — 'fight or flight': faster heartbeat, more oxygen to muscles, blood diverted from digestive system and skin to skeletal muscles, faster breathing.
- **Pancreas:** **insulin** — regulates blood sugar; too little causes **diabetes** (high blood sugar).
- **Testes:** **testosterone** — changes in boys at puberty.
- **Ovaries:** **oestrogen** — changes in girls at puberty.

steps.title: Feedback control
steps.body: Timing and amount of hormones are controlled by **feedback mechanisms**. Example: when **blood sugar rises**, the pancreas detects it and **releases more insulin**; as sugar falls, insulin secretion decreases.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — compare nervous and hormonal control
steps.body: Nervous: electrical impulses, very fast, short-lived, reaches only cells connected by nerves. Hormonal: chemicals in blood, slower, longer-lasting, reaches all cells, and every cell can respond.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — identify
steps.body: A child is unusually short for age; tests show low growth hormone → **pituitary** deficiency (dwarfism). A person has a swollen neck and lives in a region with iodine-poor soil → **goitre** (thyroid).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying hormones travel along nerves (they travel in blood).
- Calling insulin a thyroid hormone.
- Saying adrenaline slows the heart.

activity.prompt: Match the gland with its hormone or effect.

quiz.q: Iodine is needed to make
quiz.why: Iodine is needed to make thyroxin in the thyroid gland.

quiz.q: Diabetes is due to deficiency of
quiz.why: Diabetes results from too little insulin from the pancreas, which leaves blood sugar high.

quiz.q: Adrenaline is secreted by the
quiz.why: Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands, which lie above the kidneys.

quiz.q: Dwarfism results from deficiency of
quiz.why: Dwarfism results from too little growth hormone from the pituitary gland.

quiz.q: Hormones reach target cells through
quiz.why: Hormones are chemicals carried by the blood to their target cells.

quiz.q: When blood sugar rises, the pancreas
quiz.why: When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases more insulin, which lowers it. This is a feedback mechanism.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Control and Coordination)

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system:
questions.why: The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls voluntary actions?
questions.why: The cerebrum in the forebrain controls voluntary actions and thinking.

questions.q: Plant hormone for stem growth:
questions.why: Gibberellin helps the stem to grow longer. Abscisic acid inhibits growth, and insulin and adrenaline are animal hormones.

questions.q: Goitre is related to deficiency of
questions.why: Goitre is caused by lack of iodine, which the thyroid needs to make thyroxin.

questions.q: Roots growing towards water show
questions.why: Root growth towards water is hydrotropism, a response to water.

questions.q: Information travels across a synapse as
questions.why: Across a synapse, the information is carried by chemical signals (neurotransmitters).

questions.q: Assertion: Reflex actions are faster than voluntary actions. Reason: they are processed in the spinal cord without waiting for the brain's decision.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Reflexes are processed in the spinal cord by a short pathway without waiting for the brain's decision, so they are faster.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of the hindbrain?
questions.why: Thinking and reasoning are functions of the forebrain. The hindbrain controls breathing, blood pressure and balance.

questions.q: Hormone that helps the body respond in emergencies:
questions.why: Adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies, the fight-or-flight response.

questions.q: Case: A potted plant is placed near a window. After a week the shoot bends towards the window. The hormone responsible and where it collects:
questions.why: Auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot, away from the window, making those cells grow longer. So the shoot bends towards the light.

questions.q: Case continued: if the pot is laid on its side in darkness, the root will
questions.why: Roots respond to gravity by growing downward, which is positive geotropism. This happens even in darkness.

questions.q: The correct sequence in a reflex arc:
options: Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Receptor → motor neuron → sensory neuron → effector
questions.why: A reflex arc runs from receptor to sensory neuron, relay neuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron and effector.

questions.q: Which statement about hormones is correct?
options: They act slowly but their effects last longer
questions.why: Hormones are chemicals carried by the blood. They act slowly compared with nerve impulses but their effects last longer.

questions.q: A person cannot walk in a straight line and keeps losing balance after an injury. Which part is likely affected?
questions.why: The cerebellum controls balance and the precision of movement, so injury to it causes loss of balance and trouble walking straight.

questions.q: Why are animals' nervous signals unable to reach every cell, unlike hormones?
options: Impulses reach only cells connected to nerves; hormones reach all cells via blood
questions.why: Nerve impulses only reach cells that are connected to nerves. Hormones are carried by the blood to all cells.

questions.q: Mimosa leaf movement and phototropism differ because
options: Mimosa's is fast and not growth-related; phototropism is slow, growth-related
questions.why: Mimosa leaf movement is quick and does not involve growth, while phototropism is a slow growth movement of the shoot.

questions.q: A diabetic patient is advised regular insulin injections. Why can't insulin be given as a tablet? (beyond-syllabus reasoning)
options: Insulin is a protein and would be digested in the stomach and intestine
questions.why: Insulin is a protein. If swallowed as a tablet it would be digested by enzymes in the stomach and intestine before reaching the blood.

questions.q: Blood sugar falls after insulin release, and then less insulin is released. This is an example of
questions.why: Blood sugar falls after insulin is released, and then less insulin is released. A result that switches off its own cause is negative feedback.

courses.title: Ch 7 · How do Organisms Reproduce?
courses.summary: Why reproduction matters, asexual modes from fission to vegetative propagation, sexual reproduction in flowering plants, the human reproductive systems explained factually, and reproductive health including STIs, contraception and the law.
