questions.why: Drawing the wire three times as long makes its area one-third, since the volume stays the same. R ∝ l/A becomes 3 × 3 = 9 times, so 9R.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
courses.summary: Magnetic fields and field lines, the field around a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid, electromagnets, the force on a current-carrying conductor with Fleming's left-hand rule, and safe domestic electric circuits.
outcomes: Learners can describe magnetic field lines and their properties
Learners can use the right-hand thumb rule for straight wires, loops and solenoids
Learners can explain how an electromagnet is made and what affects its strength
Learners can apply Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of force
Learners can explain live, neutral and earth wires, fuses, short circuits and overloading

lessons.title: Magnetic field and field lines

scenes.text: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle deflect when current flowed in a nearby wire.
Electricity and magnetism turned out to be linked.
To picture a magnetic field we draw field lines, using iron filings or a compass.

steps.title: Field lines
steps.body:
A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where its force can be felt. It has both **magnitude and direction**. A compass needle (a small magnet) points along the field.

**Properties of field lines:**
- They emerge from the **north pole** and merge at the **south pole** outside the magnet; inside the magnet they go from south to north — so they are **closed curves**.
- The **closer** the lines, the **stronger** the field (crowded near the poles).
- **Two field lines never cross** — otherwise a compass at the crossing would point in two directions at once.

Iron filings sprinkled on paper over a bar magnet arrange themselves along the field lines.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why never cross?
steps.body: At any point the field has one direction. If two lines crossed, there would be two directions at that point, which is impossible.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — where is it strongest?
steps.body: Near the poles of a bar magnet field lines are crowded, so the field is strongest there.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying field lines start at S and end at N outside the magnet.
- Drawing field lines that cross.
- Saying field lines are open curves.

statements.s: Magnetic field lines are closed curves.
statements.why: N to S outside, S to N inside.

statements.s: Two field lines can intersect.
statements.why: The field would have two directions.

statements.s: Field lines are crowded where the field is strong.
Oersted showed that current produces a magnetic field.
Outside a magnet, field lines go from south to north.
statements.why: They go from north to south.

quiz.q: Outside a magnet, field lines go from
quiz.why: By convention, outside the magnet field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.

quiz.q: Field strength is shown by
quiz.why: Where field lines are closer together the magnetic field is stronger.

quiz.q: The scientist who found the magnetic effect of current:
quiz.why: Hans Christian Oersted found in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic effect.

quiz.q: A compass needle is
quiz.why: A compass needle is a small bar magnet that aligns itself along the magnetic field.

quiz.q: Magnetic field has
quiz.why: A magnetic field has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Magnetic Effects of Electric Current)

lessons.title: Fields of a straight wire, a loop and a solenoid

scenes.text: Kabir grips an imaginary wire with his right hand, thumb along the current.
His curled fingers show which way the magnetic field circles the wire.
Coil the wire into a loop or a long spring-like solenoid, and the field becomes stronger and more useful.

steps.title: Straight conductor
steps.body:
Field lines are **concentric circles** around the wire. Field strength **increases with current** and **decreases with distance** from the wire.

**Right-hand thumb rule:** hold the wire in your right hand with the **thumb along the current**; the **fingers curl in the direction of the field lines**. (Reversing current reverses the field — the compass deflects the other way.)

steps.title: Circular loop and solenoid
steps.body:
- **Circular loop:** near the wire the lines are circles; at the **centre** they become nearly **straight**. The field at the centre increases with current and with the **number of turns** n (fields of all turns add up) and decreases with larger radius.
- **Solenoid:** a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely like a cylinder. Its field pattern is like that of a **bar magnet**, with one end N and the other S. **Inside**, the field lines are **parallel straight lines** — the field is **uniform**.
- **Electromagnet:** a soft iron core placed inside a solenoid becomes strongly magnetised while current flows. Strength increases with more turns, more current and a soft-iron core. Used in cranes, electric bells, MRI-like equipment and relays.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — find the field direction
steps.body: Current flows vertically upward in a wire. Using the right-hand thumb rule (thumb up), the field lines seen from above circle **anticlockwise**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — make it stronger
steps.body: To strengthen a solenoid's field: increase the current, increase the number of turns, and insert a soft iron core.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the left hand for the thumb rule.
- Saying the field inside a solenoid is non-uniform.
- Using steel instead of soft iron for a temporary electromagnet (steel stays magnetised).

activity.prompt: Will the change make the magnetic field at the centre of a coil stronger or weaker?

items.text: Increase the radius of the loop
Move the compass farther from a straight wire

quiz.q: Field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are
quiz.why: The magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles around the wire.

quiz.q: The field inside a long solenoid is
quiz.why: Inside a long solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform.

quiz.q: Direction of field around a wire is given by
quiz.why: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.

quiz.q: A solenoid behaves like a
quiz.why: A solenoid carrying current behaves like a bar magnet, with a north and a south end.

quiz.q: Core used for an electromagnet:
quiz.why: Soft iron is used as the core of an electromagnet because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised.

quiz.q: Field at the centre of a loop increases with
quiz.why: The field at the centre of a coil increases with the number of turns, since the fields of the turns add up.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Magnetic Effects of Electric Current)

lessons.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor

scenes.text: An aluminium rod hangs between the poles of a horseshoe magnet.
When current flows through it, the rod swings out sideways; reversing current makes it swing the other way.
A magnet exerts a force on a current. Fleming's left hand tells the direction.

steps.title: The force
steps.body:
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force** (André-Marie Ampère suggested the magnet must exert an equal and opposite force on the conductor).

- The force is **largest when the current is perpendicular** to the field; it is zero when they are parallel.
- Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force.

**Fleming's left-hand rule:** stretch the **thumb, forefinger and middle finger** of the **left hand** mutually perpendicular. **Forefinger → field**, **middle finger → current**, then **thumb → force (motion)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — apply the rule
steps.body: Current flows towards the east in a wire placed in a magnetic field pointing north (horizontal). Forefinger north, middle finger east → thumb points **upward**: the force is vertically up.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — electron beam
steps.body: An electron beam moving west is like a conventional current towards the **east**. In a downward magnetic field, the force on it (by the left-hand rule) is found with forefinger down and middle finger east: the thumb points **north**, so the beam deflects north.

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: Electric motors, loudspeakers, electric fans, washing machines and mixers use this force. Inside the human body, weak currents in nerves create very small magnetic fields; **MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)** uses strong magnetic fields to make images of internal organs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the right hand for the force.
- Forgetting that electron flow is opposite to conventional current.
- Saying force is maximum when current is parallel to the field.

activity.prompt: Fleming's left-hand rule: match each finger with the quantity.

quiz.q: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of
options: force on a current-carrying conductor in a field
quiz.why: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

quiz.q: The force is maximum when current and field are
quiz.why: The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field, since the force depends on sin of the angle between them.

quiz.q: Reversing the current in the rod makes the force
quiz.why: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force on the rod.

quiz.q: In the left-hand rule, the forefinger shows
quiz.why: In the left-hand rule the forefinger shows the field, the middle finger the current and the thumb the force.

quiz.q: A device using this force:
quiz.why: An electric fan motor works on this force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Heaters, fuses and bulbs do not.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Magnetic Effects of Electric Current)

lessons.title: Domestic electric circuits

scenes.text: During Diwali, Riya's family plugs a heater, an iron and lights into one socket. Suddenly the power goes off.
The MCB in the meter box has tripped — it sensed too much current.
Domestic wiring has built-in safety: fuses, MCBs and the earth wire.

steps.title: Supply and wires
steps.body:
In India, mains supply is **AC at 220 V and 50 Hz**.

- **Live (phase) wire:** usually **red** (or brown in newer wiring) insulation — at high potential.
- **Neutral wire:** **black** (or blue).
- **Earth wire:** **green** (or green-yellow) — connected to a metal plate deep in the ground near the house.

The supply passes through the electricity meter and the **main fuse/MCB**. There are usually two circuits: a **5 A** circuit for lights and fans and a **15 A** circuit for heavy appliances (geysers, ACs, coolers). Appliances are connected **in parallel** so each gets 220 V and can be switched on or off independently.

steps.title: Safety devices and faults
steps.body:
- **Earthing:** the metal body of appliances (iron, toaster, fridge) is connected to the earth wire. If the live wire touches the body, current flows to earth (a low-resistance path), protecting the user from severe shock.
- **Short circuit:** live and neutral wires come into direct contact (damaged insulation or a fault) — current rises sharply.
- **Overloading:** too many appliances on one socket, or a sudden voltage increase — current exceeds the safe value.
- **Fuse / MCB** in series with the live wire melts or trips in such cases, cutting off supply and preventing fires and damage.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why parallel?
steps.body: In parallel, each appliance gets the full 220 V, has its own switch, and if one fails, the others keep working. In series, the current would be the same for all and one failure would stop everything.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — overloading
steps.body: An oven (2 kW) and a geyser (2 kW) on one 220 V, 5 A circuit draw about 4000/220 ≈ 18 A — far more than 5 A. The fuse would blow; heavy appliances belong on the 15 A circuit, and should not run together on one socket.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the fuse in the neutral wire.
- Using a thick copper wire in place of a fuse wire ('to stop it blowing') — this removes protection and can cause fires.
- Thinking the earth wire carries current all the time.
- Touching switches with wet hands.

activity.prompt: Home electrical safety checklist:
items: Do not plug many heavy appliances into one socket
Use 3-pin plugs with earthing for metal-bodied appliances
Never replace a fuse with a thick copper wire
Switch off the main supply before any repair

quiz.why: Earthing gives any leakage current a low-resistance path to the ground, so the user does not get a shock.

quiz.q: Heavy appliances like geysers are put on
quiz.why: Heavy appliances such as geysers draw a large current, so they are connected to the 15 A circuit.

questions.why: In Fleming's left-hand rule the thumb shows the force or motion.

questions.why: A heater and an iron together draw a large current. The MCB trips because the circuit is overloaded.

courses.summary: Ecosystems and their components, food chains and food webs, trophic levels and the 10% law of energy flow, biological magnification, ozone layer depletion, and managing the garbage we produce.
outcomes: Learners can identify biotic and abiotic components and types of ecosystems

lessons.title: Ecosystems and their components

scenes.text: Class 10-B sets up an aquarium with fish, water plants, snails, sand and light.
The fish eat, plants make food, snails clean up — the tank becomes a small, self-supporting world.
That is a mini ecosystem: living and non-living parts interacting.

steps.title: What is an ecosystem?
steps.body:
An **ecosystem** consists of all the living organisms in an area together with the non-living parts of the environment, interacting with each other.

- **Biotic components:** plants, animals, microorganisms.
- **Abiotic components:** temperature, rainfall, wind, soil, minerals, water, light.

**Natural** ecosystems: forests, ponds, lakes, grasslands. **Artificial (human-made)**: gardens, crop fields, aquariums.

steps.title: Roles of organisms
steps.body:
- **Producers:** green plants and blue-green algae make food by photosynthesis.
- **Consumers:** depend on producers directly or indirectly — **herbivores**, **carnivores**, **omnivores**, **parasites**.
- **Decomposers:** bacteria and fungi break down dead remains and wastes into simple substances that return to the soil — they **recycle nutrients**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — aquarium cleaning
steps.body: Why don't we clean ponds and lakes the way we clean an aquarium? Natural ecosystems have **decomposers** that break down wastes; an aquarium, being small and artificial, lacks enough decomposers.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — what if decomposers vanished?
steps.body: Dead plants and animals would pile up and nutrients would not return to the soil; producers would run short of minerals, and the whole ecosystem would suffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a crop field a natural ecosystem.
- Saying decomposers are producers.
- Forgetting abiotic factors (light, water, temperature) are part of the ecosystem.

activity.prompt: Biotic or abiotic component?

quiz.q: An artificial ecosystem:
quiz.why: A crop field is made by humans, so it is an artificial ecosystem. Forests, ponds and deserts are natural.

quiz.q: Decomposers include
quiz.why: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi, which break down dead remains.

quiz.q: Producers are
quiz.why: Producers are green plants that make food by photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which is abiotic?
quiz.why: Temperature is a non-living part of the environment, so it is abiotic. Fish, algae and mushrooms are living.

quiz.q: Decomposers help by
quiz.why: Decomposers break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients to the soil, where plants can use them again.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Our Environment)

lessons.title: Food chains, food webs and energy flow

scenes.text: In a forest, deer eat grass, and a tiger eats the deer.
The energy in the tiger's muscles began as sunlight caught by grass.
But at each step, most energy is lost — which is why there are far fewer tigers than deer.

steps.title: Food chains and trophic levels
steps.body:
A **food chain** is a series of organisms eating one another: grass → deer → lion; grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

Each step is a **trophic level**:
- 1st: **producers** (autotrophs)
- 2nd: **herbivores / primary consumers**
- 3rd: **small carnivores / secondary consumers**
- 4th: **large carnivores / tertiary consumers**

In nature, food chains interlink to form a **food web** (an organism may be eaten by many others).

steps.title: Energy flow
steps.body:
- Green plants capture about **1%** of the sunlight falling on leaves and convert it to food energy.
- **10% law:** only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next as organic matter; the rest is used for life processes and lost as heat.
- So food chains usually have only **3–4 trophic levels**; there are fewer organisms at higher levels.
- Energy flow is **unidirectional**: energy captured by autotrophs does not go back to the Sun, and energy passed to herbivores does not return to plants.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — 10% law
steps.body: Producers in a field store 10,000 J. Herbivores get **1000 J**, small carnivores **100 J**, large carnivores **10 J**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why eat plants?
steps.body: A vegetarian diet uses energy at the 2nd trophic level, so more energy from the same farmland is available to people than if plants are first fed to animals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 10% of energy is lost (it is 90% lost; 10% passes on).
- Drawing arrows from consumer to food (arrows point in the direction of energy flow: food → eater).
- Saying energy cycles back to producers.

activity.prompt: If producers fix 20,000 J of energy, how much reaches the third trophic level (small carnivores)?

quiz.q: Organisms at the first trophic level:
quiz.why: Producers are at the first trophic level of a food chain.

quiz.q: According to the 10% law, energy passed to the next level is about
quiz.why: By the 10% law only about 10% of the energy passes to the next trophic level. The rest is lost.

quiz.q: Energy flow in an ecosystem is
quiz.why: Energy flow in an ecosystem is one-way, from the Sun to producers and then to consumers. It is not recycled.

quiz.q: Herbivores occupy the
quiz.why: Herbivores eat producers, so they are at the second trophic level.

quiz.q: Food chains are short because
options: energy decreases sharply at each level
quiz.why: Food chains are short because energy falls sharply (about 10% passes on) at each level, so little is left for higher levels.

quiz.q: Plants convert about what fraction of incident sunlight into food energy?
quiz.why: Plants capture only about 1% of the sunlight that falls on them as food energy.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Our Environment)

lessons.title: Biological magnification

scenes.text: Farmers spray a pesticide on crops; rain washes some into a pond.
Tiny amounts enter plankton, then small fish, then big fish, then the birds and people who eat them.
At every step the chemical concentrates more. This is biological magnification.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
Some harmful chemicals (e.g. many pesticides) are **non-biodegradable** — they are not broken down and are not excreted easily. When they enter a food chain, they **accumulate progressively at each trophic level**.

Since **humans** often occupy the top level, the **maximum concentration** can build up in our bodies. Such chemicals have been found in food grains, fruits, vegetables, meat and even milk.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — compare concentrations
steps.body: Pesticide concentration in a pond chain: water (low) < plankton < small fish < large fish < fish-eating birds (highest).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — reduce the risk
steps.body: Use pesticides only as recommended, prefer integrated pest management and biodegradable alternatives, wash fruits and vegetables well, and support safe disposal of chemicals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy and chemicals both decrease up the chain (energy decreases; non-biodegradable chemicals increase).
- Thinking only animals at the top are affected (all levels absorb some).
- Confusing biological magnification with the 10% law.

activity.prompt: Order the organisms from lowest to highest pesticide concentration.

quiz.q: Biological magnification means
options: increase in energy up the chain
increase in concentration of harmful chemicals along a food chain
quiz.why: Biological magnification is the increase in concentration of harmful chemicals as they pass along a food chain.

quiz.q: Maximum concentration of pesticides is found in
quiz.why: Harmful chemicals build up along a food chain, so the highest concentration is found in the top consumers.

quiz.q: Chemicals that show magnification are usually
quiz.why: Chemicals that show biological magnification are non-biodegradable, so they are not broken down and stay in the body.

quiz.q: Humans are at risk because they
options: often occupy the top trophic level
quiz.why: Humans often feed at the top trophic level, so they may take in large amounts of accumulated chemicals.

quiz.q: A way to reduce biological magnification:
options: use pesticides only as needed and prefer biodegradable alternatives
quiz.why: Using pesticides only when needed and choosing biodegradable alternatives reduces the chemicals entering the food chain.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Our Environment)

lessons.title: Ozone layer and waste management

scenes.text: High above us, a thin layer of ozone shields life from the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.
In the 1980s scientists found it thinning, mainly due to CFCs from old refrigerators and aerosol sprays.
Global action and our daily choices about waste both shape the planet we live on.

steps.title: Ozone
steps.body:
Ozone (O₃) is a molecule of three oxygen atoms. At ground level it is a deadly poison, but in the **upper atmosphere** it **shields** the Earth from **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, which can cause skin cancer and damage living things.

**Formation:** UV radiation splits O₂ into free oxygen atoms: O₂ → O + O; then O + O₂ → O₃.

**Depletion:** a sharp drop was noticed from the 1980s, linked to synthetic chemicals like **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. In **1987**, the **United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)** reached an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels; CFC-free refrigerators are now standard.

steps.title: Managing garbage
steps.body:
- **Biodegradable** substances can be broken down by biological processes (vegetable peels, paper, cotton, leaves, dung).
- **Non-biodegradable** substances are not broken down this way (plastics, glass, metals, many pesticides); they persist and harm ecosystems.

**Good practice:** segregate waste at home (wet/biodegradable and dry/non-biodegradable), compost kitchen waste, reduce single-use plastic, reuse and recycle, carry a cloth bag. Disposable cups, packaging and changed lifestyles create more waste; switching from paper cups to kulhads at a large scale would also need clay and topsoil — every choice has trade-offs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body: Banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth → biodegradable. Plastic bottle, glass jar, aluminium can → non-biodegradable (but recyclable).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — explain
steps.body: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? More UV radiation would reach the Earth, increasing skin cancer, cataracts and harming plants and aquatic life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ozone is helpful at ground level (it is harmful there).
- Calling all plastics biodegradable.
- Saying CFCs were banned by a 1997 treaty (the UNEP agreement was in 1987).

activity.prompt: Biodegradable or non-biodegradable?

quiz.q: Ozone protects us from
quiz.why: The ozone layer protects living things from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation of the Sun.

quiz.q: Main cause of ozone depletion:
quiz.why: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) from refrigerators and aerosols are the main cause of ozone depletion.

quiz.q: Ozone forms when
options: O atoms combine with O₂ molecules
quiz.why: Ozone forms when UV light splits O₂ into oxygen atoms, which combine with O₂ molecules: O + O₂ → O₃.

quiz.q: UNEP agreement to freeze CFC production was in
quiz.why: In 1987 UNEP reached an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels.

quiz.q: A non-biodegradable substance:
quiz.why: Plastic is non-biodegradable, so it persists in the environment. Fruit peel, paper and cotton are biodegradable.

quiz.q: Best way to handle kitchen waste:
quiz.why: Kitchen waste is biodegradable, so composting it returns nutrients to the soil.

questions.q: A natural ecosystem:
questions.why: A pond is a natural ecosystem. A garden, an aquarium and a crop field are made by humans.

questions.q: Decomposers are
questions.why: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi, which break down dead organisms and wastes.

questions.q: Ozone is made of
questions.why: Ozone is O₃, a molecule made of three oxygen atoms. Ordinary oxygen, O₂, has two.

questions.q: Which is biodegradable?
questions.why: Paper is biodegradable because microbes can break it down. Glass, aluminium and plastic are not broken down easily.

questions.q: In grass → deer → tiger, the tiger is a
options: secondary consumer (top carnivore) at the 3rd trophic level
questions.why: In grass → deer → tiger, grass is the first level, deer the second and tiger the third. The tiger eats a herbivore, so it is a secondary consumer and the top carnivore.

questions.q: If a herbivore gets 1000 J, the next carnivore gets about
questions.why: By the 10% law only about 10% of energy passes to the next level, so 10% of 1000 J = 100 J.

questions.q: Assertion: Energy flow in ecosystems is unidirectional. Reason: energy captured by autotrophs does not revert to the Sun.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Energy captured by autotrophs flows to consumers and is lost as heat. It never returns to the Sun, so the flow is one-way.

questions.q: CFCs were widely used as
questions.why: CFCs were widely used as refrigerants in refrigerators and air conditioners, and in aerosol sprays.

questions.q: Which food chain is correct?
questions.why: Energy flows from the food to the eater, so a chain starts with a producer: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

questions.q: Case: A pond near farms has a fish-eating bird population with thin, fragile eggshells. Tests show high pesticide levels in birds but low levels in water. This is
questions.why: High pesticide levels in birds at the top of the food chain but low levels in the water show that the chemicals build up along the chain. This is biological magnification.

questions.q: Case continued: which organism in the pond would show the LOWEST pesticide concentration?
questions.why: The pesticide concentration rises up the food chain, so the lowest is in plankton and algae at the first trophic level.

questions.q: Why are there usually not more than four trophic levels?
options: Energy available becomes too little after a few levels
questions.why: Each step passes on only about 10% of the energy, so after three or four levels too little is left to support another level.

questions.q: If 1% of 1,000,000 J of sunlight is fixed by plants, how much energy reaches primary consumers?
questions.why: 1% of 1,000,000 J is 10,000 J fixed by plants. Primary consumers get about 10% of that, which is 1000 J.

questions.q: Which step correctly shows ozone formation?
options: O₂ → O + O, then O + O₂ → O₃
questions.why: UV light splits an O₂ molecule into two O atoms, and each O atom then combines with another O₂ molecule: O + O₂ → O₃.

questions.q: Removing all frogs from a food web of grass → grasshopper → frog → snake would most likely
questions.why: Without frogs, the grasshoppers are not eaten and increase, while snakes lose their food and decrease.

questions.q: Why is changing from disposable paper cups to clay kulhads at a very large scale not a perfect solution?
options: Making kulhads on a large scale uses fertile topsoil and resources
questions.why: Making kulhads on a large scale uses fertile topsoil and resources. So every option has some environmental cost.

Then he checks them here and corrects any slips.
Active recall beats rereading.

steps.title: Reactions (Ch 1)
steps.body:
- Combination: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat
- Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heat); 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electricity); 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (light)
- Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
- Double displacement: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl
- Redox: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
- Corrosion needs air + water; rancidity prevented by antioxidants, nitrogen, airtight storage

steps.title: Acids, bases, salts (Ch 2)
steps.body:
- Metal + acid → salt + H₂; carbonate + acid → salt + H₂O + CO₂; acid + base → salt + water
- pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; tooth decay below 5.5; acid rain below 5.6
- Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂
- Bleaching powder CaOCl₂; baking soda NaHCO₃; washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O; blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O

steps.title: Metals and non-metals (Ch 3)
steps.body:
- Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au
- Amphoteric oxides: Al₂O₃, ZnO
- Roasting (sulphide, excess air), calcination (carbonate, limited air), reduction with C; thermite Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃
- Electrolytic refining: impure anode, pure cathode, anode mud
- Alloys: brass Cu+Zn, bronze Cu+Sn, solder Pb+Sn; 22-carat gold

steps.title: Carbon compounds (Ch 4)
steps.body:
- Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; homologous members differ by CH₂ (14 u)
- Suffixes: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid; prefixes chloro-, bromo-
- Oxidation: ethanol → ethanoic acid (alk. KMnO₄ / acid. K₂Cr₂O₇)
- Addition: hydrogenation with Ni; substitution: CH₄ + Cl₂ (sunlight)
- Esterification: acid + alcohol (conc. H₂SO₄) → ester; saponification: ester + NaOH → soap/salt + alcohol
- Micelles; detergents work in hard water

Riya revises each process as a short sequence of steps.
Sequences are easy to recall and to write in exams.

steps.title: Life processes (Ch 5)
steps.body:
- Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O (light, chlorophyll)
- Digestion: mouth (amylase) → stomach (HCl, pepsin, mucus) → small intestine (bile, trypsin, lipase; villi absorb) → large intestine (water)
- Glucose → pyruvate (cytoplasm) → CO₂ + H₂O (mitochondria, O₂) / ethanol + CO₂ (yeast) / lactic acid (muscle)
- Heart: 4 chambers, double circulation; BP ~120/80 mm Hg
- Xylem (water, transpiration pull), phloem (food, ATP)
- Nephron: glomerulus filtration → tubular reabsorption → urine

steps.title: Control and coordination (Ch 6)
steps.body:
- Neuron: dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending → synapse (chemical)
- Reflex arc: receptor → sensory → relay (spinal cord) → motor → effector
- Cerebrum (thinking), cerebellum (balance), medulla (BP, salivation, vomiting)
- Plant hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid
- Glands: pituitary (GH), thyroid (thyroxin, iodine), adrenal (adrenaline), pancreas (insulin), testes, ovaries; feedback control

steps.title: Reproduction and heredity (Ch 7–8)
steps.body:
- Fission (Amoeba, Plasmodium), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Planaria), budding (Hydra, yeast), spores (Rhizopus), vegetative propagation
- Flower: pollination → pollen tube → fertilisation → ovule → seed, ovary → fruit
- Human: fertilisation in oviduct; placenta; menstruation if no fertilisation
- Contraception: barrier, hormonal, IUD, surgical; STIs
- Monohybrid F2 3 : 1 (1 : 2 : 1); dihybrid F2 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
- Sex: XX female, XY male; father's sperm decides

steps.title: Our environment (Ch 13)
steps.body:
- Trophic levels; 10% law; energy flow unidirectional
- Biological magnification of non-biodegradable chemicals
- Ozone: O₂ → O + O; O + O₂ → O₃; CFCs deplete it; UNEP 1987
- Segregate, compost, reduce, reuse, recycle

steps.title: Light (Ch 9)
steps.body:
- Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; m = −v/u; R = 2f; concave f < 0, convex f > 0
- Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; m = v/u; P = 1/f (m) in dioptres; convex P > 0, concave P < 0; P = P₁ + P₂
- n = c/v = sin i / sin r; air 1.0003, water 1.33, glass 1.52, diamond 2.42
- u is always negative (object on the left)

steps.title: Eye and colours (Ch 10)
steps.body:
- Near point 25 cm, far point infinity; accommodation by ciliary muscles
- Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens; presbyopia → bifocal
- VIBGYOR; violet deviates most, red least; rainbow opposite the Sun
- Twinkling, advance sunrise (~2 min) = atmospheric refraction; blue sky, red sunset = scattering

steps.title: Electricity (Ch 11)
steps.body:
- I = Q/t; V = W/Q; V = IR; R = ρl/A
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
- H = I²Rt; P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
- Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel

steps.title: Magnetic effects (Ch 12)
steps.body:
- Field lines: closed, never cross, crowded where strong
- Right-hand thumb rule (field around wire); solenoid like a bar magnet, uniform field inside
- Fleming's left-hand rule: forefinger field, middle finger current, thumb force
- Domestic: 220 V, 50 Hz; live, neutral, earth; fuse/MCB in live wire; 5 A and 15 A circuits

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- First 15 minutes: read the whole paper and mark easy questions.
- For numericals: Given → Formula → Substitution with units → Answer with unit and sign meaning.
- Draw labelled diagrams with a pencil and ruler; label arrows on rays.
- Keep 10 minutes to check.

steps.title: Top physics slips
steps.body:
- m = −v/u (mirror) vs m = v/u (lens).
- f in metres for power.
- Parallel resistance: take the reciprocal at the end.
- Fleming's LEFT hand for force.

questions.why: An oxide that reacts with both HCl and NaOH is amphoteric. Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, so X is aluminium.

questions.q: Why does a ray of light passing through the optical centre of a thin lens go undeviated?
options: Near the centre the two lens surfaces are nearly parallel, like a thin slab
The lens has no refractive index there
questions.why: Near the optical centre the two faces of the lens are nearly parallel, like a thin slab of glass. So the ray goes through almost undeviated.

questions.q: A household has a 5 A circuit. Which set can safely run together at 220 V?
options: A 2 kW heater and a 1 kW iron
Three 100 W bulbs and a 75 W fan
questions.why: A 5 A circuit at 220 V can carry up to 1100 W. Three 100 W bulbs and a 75 W fan total 375 W (about 1.7 A), which is safe. The other sets draw more than 1100 W.

questions.q: Ozone depletion would most directly increase
questions.why: The ozone layer absorbs UV radiation. If it is depleted, more UV radiation reaches the Earth.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
courses.summary: How Europe moved from dynastic empires to nation-states between 1789 and 1914: the French Revolution, liberal and conservative ideas, the revolutions of 1830 and 1848, the unification of Germany and Italy, symbols of the nation and the Balkan crisis.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a nation-state is and how the French Revolution created the idea of shared nationhood
Learners can compare liberal nationalism with the conservative order after 1815
Learners can sequence the unification of Germany and Italy with key people and dates
Learners can analyse allegories like Marianne and Germania and the Balkan problem

lessons.title: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation

scenes.text: Riya notices that the French flag, like India's, is a tricolour. Why do nations need such symbols?
Her teacher says the French Revolution of 1789 was the first clear expression of nationalism in Europe.

steps.title: From subjects to citizens
steps.body:
Before 1789, France was an absolute monarchy. The Revolution moved **sovereignty** from the king to the people.

- Ideas of **la patrie** (the fatherland) and **le citoyen** (the citizen) stressed a united community with equal rights.
- A new tricolour flag replaced the royal standard.
- The Estates General became the **National Assembly**.
- New hymns, oaths and martyrs were commemorated, all in the name of the nation.
- A centralised administrative system, uniform laws, and abolition of internal customs duties.
- Uniform weights and measures; **French** promoted as the common language (regional dialects discouraged).

steps.title: Napoleon and the Civil Code of 1804
steps.body:
Napoleon destroyed democracy in France (he became emperor) but made administration rational and efficient.

- The **Civil Code of 1804 (Napoleonic Code)** ended privileges based on birth, gave equality before law and secured the right to property.
- In conquered regions (Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy, Germany) he simplified divisions, ended feudalism, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, removed guild restrictions, and improved transport and communication.
- Initially welcomed, his rule soon became hated because of higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription into the French army.

steps.title: Sorrieu's utopian vision (1848)
steps.body: The French artist **Frédéric Sorrieu** prepared prints in 1848 imagining a world of "democratic and social republics". Peoples of Europe and America, grouped as nations with their own flags and costumes, march past the Statue of Liberty towards a shared future. A **utopia** is an ideal society that is unlikely ever to exist in reality.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was the French Revolution a turning point for nationalism? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Identify the shift:** power moved from monarch to the people (sovereignty of citizens).

**Step 2 – Give measures (any two):** ideas of la patrie and le citoyen; new tricolour; National Assembly; uniform laws, weights and measures; French as common language.

**Step 3 – Conclude:** these measures created a sense of collective identity – the core of nationalism.

steps.title: Solved example: “Napoleon was both a destroyer and a builder.” Justify (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Destroyer:** he ended democracy and made himself emperor; brought censorship, high taxes and forced conscription.

**Step 2 – Builder:** Civil Code of 1804 – equality before law, right to property, end of privileges by birth; abolished feudalism and guild restrictions; improved roads and communication.

**Step 3 – Conclude:** his reforms modernised administration but foreign rule bred resentment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Napoleon brought democracy – he **ended** it in France.
- Mixing up 1789 (Revolution) with 1804 (Civil Code).
- Thinking “la patrie” means “citizen”: la patrie = fatherland, le citoyen = citizen.
- Calling Sorrieu’s prints real events – they show an imagined (utopian) future.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: equality before law, right to property
an ideal society unlikely to exist

quiz.q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
quiz.why: The French Revolution began in 1789.

quiz.q: The Napoleonic Code is also called the
quiz.why: The Napoleonic Code, or Civil Code of 1804, removed privileges based on birth and established equality before the law.

quiz.q: Which was NOT a measure of the French revolutionaries?
quiz.why: The revolutionaries introduced a tricolour flag, French as the common language and uniform weights and measures. Restoring the Bourbon king was done by conservatives after 1815.

quiz.q: Why did people in conquered areas turn against Napoleon?
quiz.why: Napoleon's rule brought forced conscription (military service), censorship and high taxes. These outweighed the benefits, so people in conquered areas turned against him.

quiz.q: Sorrieu's 1848 prints showed
options: a utopian world of democratic and social republics
quiz.why: Sorrieu's 1848 prints showed a dream world of democratic and social republics, with people of many nations living together.

sources: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (topic reference)

lessons.title: Liberalism, conservatism and the revolutionaries

scenes.text: Arjun reads that a merchant travelling from Hamburg to Nuremberg in the early 1800s crossed 11 customs barriers and paid about 5% duty at each.
“No wonder traders wanted one economic nation!” he says.

steps.title: Liberal nationalism
steps.body:
In the early 19th century the new **middle classes** (industrialists, businessmen, professionals) stood for **liberalism** (from Latin *liber*, free).

- Politically: government by consent, end of autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government, inviolability of private property.
- But equality before law did not mean universal suffrage: in revolutionary France only property-owning men could vote; women and non-propertied men were excluded (the Jacobin period briefly allowed all adult men to vote).
- Economically: freedom of markets and the end of state-imposed restrictions on movement of goods and capital.

steps.title: Zollverein (1834)
steps.body: A customs union formed at the initiative of **Prussia** in 1834 and joined by most German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two. A network of railways further boosted mobility. A wave of economic nationalism strengthened wider nationalist feeling.

steps.title: The new conservatism after 1815
steps.body:
After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, European governments followed **conservatism** – preserving monarchy, Church and social hierarchy while keeping some modern changes (efficient bureaucracy, modern army).

- **Congress of Vienna (1815)**, hosted by Austrian Chancellor **Duke Metternich**, undid many Napoleonic changes: the Bourbon dynasty was restored in France; France lost territories; a series of states was set up on its boundaries; the German confederation of 39 states was left untouched.
- Conservative regimes were autocratic: they censored newspapers and books and suppressed liberal ideas.

steps.title: The revolutionaries: Giuseppe Mazzini
steps.body: Fearing repression, liberal-nationalists formed secret societies. **Giuseppe Mazzini** (born in Genoa, 1807) was a member of the **Carbonari**. Exiled in 1831, he founded **Young Italy** in Marseilles and **Young Europe** in Berne. He believed nations were the natural units of mankind and that Italy must become a unified republic. Metternich called him “the most dangerous enemy of our social order”.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain the economic case for nationalism in Germany (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Problem:** 39 states, each with its own currency, weights and measures and customs barriers – trade was slow and costly.

**Step 2 – Response:** Zollverein (1834) under Prussia abolished tariff barriers and cut currencies from over thirty to two; railways improved movement.

**Step 3 – Link:** a unified economic territory made the middle class demand a unified nation.

steps.title: Solved example: List three features of the Vienna settlement of 1815 (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Bourbon dynasty restored to power in France.

**Step 2:** France lost territories it had annexed under Napoleon; states were set up on its borders (e.g. Kingdom of the Netherlands, with Belgium, in the north; Genoa added to Piedmont in the south) to prevent future French expansion.

**Step 3:** Prussia got new territories on its western frontier; Austria got control of northern Italy; the German confederation of 39 states was left untouched.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying liberalism meant votes for all – in the 19th century it usually meant votes only for property-owning men.
- Confusing the Zollverein (customs union, 1834) with the Congress of Vienna (1815).
- Writing that Metternich was French – he was the Austrian Chancellor.
- Placing Young Italy in Rome – it was founded in Marseilles.

activity.prompt: Sort each idea: liberal or conservative (after 1815)?

items.text: Preserve social hierarchy and the Church

quiz.q: The Zollverein was started by
quiz.why: Prussia took the initiative in forming the Zollverein, a customs union, in 1834.

quiz.q: Who hosted the Congress of Vienna?
quiz.why: The Congress of Vienna (1815) was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor, Duke Metternich.

quiz.q: Young Italy was founded by
quiz.why: Giuseppe Mazzini founded the secret society Young Italy in Marseilles.

quiz.q: Liberalism comes from the Latin root liber, meaning
quiz.why: Liberalism comes from the Latin root liber, meaning free.

quiz.q: Which statement about 1815 conservatives is correct?
options: They wanted to preserve traditional institutions but accepted some modernisation
quiz.why: They kept monarchy, Church and hierarchy but accepted modern armies and bureaucracies.

lessons.title: The age of revolutions: 1830–1848

scenes.text: Meera learns that Polish composers turned folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols.
She wonders how music and language can fight an empire.

steps.title: 1830: France sneezes
steps.body: In **July 1830** liberals in France overthrew the restored Bourbon kings and set up a constitutional monarchy headed by **Louis Philippe**. The July Revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels, and **Belgium** broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Metternich remarked: “When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold.”

steps.title: Greek war of independence
steps.body: Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the 15th century. Nationalism sparked a struggle from **1821**. Greeks in exile and many West Europeans who admired ancient Greek culture supported it; poets and artists praised Greece as the cradle of European civilisation (the English poet **Lord Byron** organised funds and died of fever in 1824). The **Treaty of Constantinople (1832)** recognised Greece as an independent nation.

steps.title: Romanticism: culture and the nation
steps.body:
Romanticism was a cultural movement that rejected pure reason and stressed emotion, intuition and mystical feelings to build a shared heritage.

- German philosopher **Johann Gottfried Herder** said true German culture lay among the common people – **das volk** – in folk songs, poetry and dances.
- The **Grimm brothers** collected folk tales, seeing them as expressions of the German spirit, and opposed French domination.
- In Poland (partitioned and later ruled by Russia) the Polish language became a weapon: after the 1831 armed rebellion was crushed, clergy used Polish for church gatherings and religious instruction; **Karol Kurpinski** used operas and music (polonaise, mazurka) to celebrate the national struggle.

steps.title: Hunger, hardship and 1848
steps.body:
The 1830s were years of hardship: population rose, jobs were scarce, cottage industries suffered from cheap machine-made goods from England, food prices rose after bad harvests. In **1845** Silesian weavers revolted against contractors.

**1848 revolution of the liberals:** middle classes demanded constitutionalism with national unification. On **18 May 1848**, 831 elected representatives met at **St Paul's Church, Frankfurt** (the Frankfurt Parliament) and drafted a constitution for a German nation under a monarchy controlled by parliament. **Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia** rejected the crown, and the assembly was disbanded. Women were allowed only as observers in the visitors' gallery. Even so, conservatives gradually conceded some reforms – serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and Russia.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Narrow base:** it was dominated by the middle classes, which resisted the demands of workers and artisans, so it lost popular support.

**Step 2 – Royal opposition:** Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown and joined other monarchs to oppose the assembly.

**Step 3 – Outcome:** troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband.

steps.title: Solved example: How did culture help create national feeling? Use two examples (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Folk culture:** Herder and the Grimm brothers used folk songs and tales to define the German nation.

**Step 2 – Language/music in Poland:** Polish used in church and schools; Kurpinski's operas and folk dances became symbols.

**Step 3 – Conclude:** culture gave people a shared identity even without a state.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Greece became independent in 1821 – the struggle began in 1821; independence came by the Treaty of Constantinople, 1832.
- Saying the Frankfurt Parliament gave women voting rights – women were only observers.
- Mixing up the 1830 July Revolution (France, Belgium) with the 1848 revolutions.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order

events.text: July Revolution in France; Louis Philippe
Frankfurt Parliament meets in St Paul's Church

quiz.q: Which treaty recognised Greece as independent?
quiz.why: The Treaty of Constantinople (1832) recognised Greece as an independent nation.

quiz.q: Who said “When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold”?
quiz.why: Metternich said this, meaning that the revolution in France affected the rest of Europe.

quiz.q: Herder located true German culture in
quiz.why: Herder said that true German culture was to be found among the common people (das volk), in their folk songs, poetry and dances.

quiz.q: The Frankfurt Parliament met in
quiz.why: The Frankfurt Parliament met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt on 18 May 1848.

quiz.q: Assertion: Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament. Reason: He opposed a monarchy controlled by an elected assembly.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
quiz.why: Both are true. The King of Prussia rejected the crown because he would not accept a monarchy answerable to an elected assembly.

lessons.title: Unification of Germany and Italy; the strange case of Britain

scenes.text: Kabir compares maps of 1858 and 1871: dozens of states have become two big countries.
He discovers that one unification came through “blood and iron”.

steps.title: Germany: Prussia leads
steps.body:
After 1848, nationalism moved from democratic revolution to conservative power politics.

- Prussia took the lead. Its chief minister **Otto von Bismarck** used the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
- **Three wars over seven years** – with Austria, Denmark and France – ended in Prussian victory.
- In **January 1871**, the Prussian king **William I** was proclaimed **German Emperor** in a ceremony at **Versailles** (Hall of Mirrors).
- The new state emphasised modernising currency, banking, legal and judicial systems; Prussian practices became the model.

steps.title: Italy: from many states to one
steps.body:
In the mid-19th century Italy was divided into seven states; only **Sardinia-Piedmont** was ruled by an Italian princely house. The north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope, the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain. Even the Italian language had many regional and local forms.

- **Mazzini** had tried to build a unitary Italian republic (revolts of 1831 and 1848 failed).
- King **Victor Emmanuel II** of Sardinia-Piedmont and chief minister **Count Cavour** (who was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat) used diplomacy: an alliance with France helped defeat Austria in 1859.
- **Giuseppe Garibaldi** and his volunteers, the **Red Shirts**, marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860, winning local support to drive out the Spanish rulers.
- In **1861 Victor Emmanuel II** was proclaimed king of united Italy (Rome was added in 1870–71). Many peasants who had backed Garibaldi had never heard of “Italia”.

steps.title: Britain: nation-building without revolution
steps.body:
In Britain the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval but a long process.

- Before the 18th century there was no British nation; people saw themselves as English, Welsh, Scots or Irish.
- The English Parliament took power from the monarchy in **1688** (Glorious Revolution).
- The **Act of Union (1707)** between England and Scotland created the **United Kingdom of Great Britain** – in practice English dominance over Scotland, whose culture and Catholic clans were suppressed.
- Ireland, deeply divided between Catholics and Protestants, was forcibly incorporated in **1801** after a failed revolt led by **Wolfe Tone** and the United Irishmen (1798).
- Symbols of the new Britain: the British flag (Union Jack), the national anthem (God Save Our Noble King) and the English language.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare the roles of Cavour and Garibaldi (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cavour:** chief minister of Sardinia-Piedmont; a diplomat (not a revolutionary or democrat); built the alliance with France that defeated Austria in 1859.

**Step 2 – Garibaldi:** led the armed volunteers (Red Shirts) into the south in 1860, winning popular support.

**Step 3 – Combined result:** diplomacy plus popular military action led to Victor Emmanuel II being proclaimed king of united Italy in 1861.

steps.title: Solved example: “Unification of Germany was the work of Prussia.” Explain (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Liberal attempt of 1848 failed; Prussia took over the leadership of national unification.

**Step 2:** Bismarck used the army and bureaucracy; three wars in seven years with Austria, Denmark and France.

**Step 3:** William I of Prussia became German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871, and Prussian state power dominated the new nation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Germany was unified in 1861 and Italy in 1871 – Italy's king was proclaimed in **1861**, Germany's emperor in **1871**.
- Calling Cavour a revolutionary republican – he was a monarchist diplomat.
- Writing that the Act of Union (1707) united England and Ireland – it united England and Scotland; Ireland came in 1801.

lessons.title: Visualising the nation; nationalism and imperialism

scenes.text: Sana sees a statue of a woman holding a torch on a poster. “Why are nations drawn as women?”
She learns that 19th-century artists personified nations as female figures – allegories.

steps.title: Allegories: Marianne and Germania
steps.body:
An **allegory** is when an abstract idea (liberty, the nation) is expressed through a person or thing.

- **Marianne** (France): a popular Christian name chosen to represent the people's nation; features of liberty and the republic – red cap, tricolour, cockade. Statues were put up in public squares and her image was marked on coins and stamps.
- **Germania** (Germany): wears a crown of **oak leaves** – the German oak stands for heroism. In Philip Veit's painting her sword reads “The German sword protects the German Rhine”.

steps.title: Meanings of symbols
steps.body:
- Broken chains: being freed
- Breastplate with eagle: symbol of the German empire – strength
- Crown of oak leaves: heroism
- Sword: readiness to fight
- Olive branch around the sword: willingness to make peace
- Black, red and gold tricolour: flag of the liberal-nationalists in 1848, banned by the Dukes of the German states
- Rays of the rising sun: beginning of a new era

steps.title: Nationalism and imperialism: the Balkans
steps.body:
By the last quarter of the 19th century nationalism lost its idealistic liberal-democratic spirit and became a narrow creed with limited ends.

- The **Balkans** (modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro) was a region of ethnic variety whose inhabitants were broadly known as the **Slavs**. A large part was under the **Ottoman Empire**.
- As the Ottoman Empire weakened, Balkan peoples claimed independence using history, saying they had been independent but subjugated by foreign powers.
- Each state was jealous of the others and wanted more territory. The great powers – **Russia, Germany, England, Austro-Hungary** – competed for control. This rivalry led to a series of wars and finally the **First World War (1914)**. The area was called a “powder keg”.
- Anti-imperial movements in colonies later used the idea of nationalism to build their own nation-states.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was the Balkan region a source of tension after 1871? (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Ethnic variety:** many Slav nationalities with different histories.

**Step 2 – Ottoman decline:** the weakening empire encouraged each group to demand independence.

**Step 3 – Local rivalry:** each new state wanted more territory at the expense of others.

**Step 4 – Great-power rivalry:** Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary each sought control; the tensions culminated in the First World War.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain the symbolism in an image of Germania (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Crown of oak leaves – heroism.

**Step 2:** Sword with olive branch – readiness to fight but willingness to make peace; breastplate with eagle – strength of the empire.

**Step 3:** Broken chains / rising sun – freedom and the dawn of a new era. Together they show the nation as strong, free and new.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Germania wears a laurel crown – she wears **oak leaves**.
- Calling Marianne a real queen – she is an allegory of the French nation.
- Saying the Balkan problem was only local – great-power rivalry made it explosive.

quiz.why: The rivalry among Balkan states and the big powers led to the First World War in 1914.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Nationalism in India
courses.summary: India's national movement from the First World War to the early 1930s: satyagraha, Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and the Salt March, who joined and why, and how a sense of collective belonging was built.
outcomes: Learners can explain satyagraha and Gandhi's early movements
Learners can trace Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience with causes and outcomes
Learners can analyse how different social groups saw the movement
Learners can describe symbols, songs and images that built national identity

lessons.title: The First World War, Khilafat and the idea of satyagraha

scenes.text: Dadi tells Aman that her grandfather was in Amritsar on Baisakhi day in 1919.
“That day changed how ordinary people saw British rule,” she says.

steps.title: Impact of the First World War
steps.body:
- Huge rise in defence expenditure financed by war loans and increased taxes; customs duties raised and **income tax introduced**.
- Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918 – hardship for common people.
- Villages had to supply soldiers; **forced recruitment** caused anger.
- Crops failed in 1918–19 and 1920–21 in many areas, causing food shortages, accompanied by an **influenza epidemic**; 12–13 million people died in famines and the epidemic (Census 1921).

steps.title: The idea of satyagraha
steps.body:
**Mahatma Gandhi** returned to India in **January 1915** from South Africa, where he had fought racist rule with a novel method – **satyagraha**.

- It emphasised the **power of truth** and the need to search for truth.
- If the cause was true and the fight against injustice, physical force was not necessary; a satyagrahi could win by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor through non-violence.

**Early movements:** **Champaran (Bihar), 1917** – peasants against the oppressive plantation system; **Kheda (Gujarat), 1917** – peasants unable to pay revenue after crop failure and plague; **Ahmedabad, 1918** – cotton mill workers.

steps.title: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
steps.body:
- **Rowlatt Act (1919)** was hurriedly passed despite united opposition of Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners **without trial for two years**.
- Gandhi called a nationwide satyagraha – a hartal on **6 April 1919**.
- On **13 April 1919** (Baisakhi) a crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of **Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar**. Many were villagers unaware of martial law. **General Dyer** blocked the exits and opened fire, killing hundreds.
- Gandhi called off the movement as violence spread.

steps.title: Khilafat and the decision for Non-Cooperation
steps.body:
The Ottoman Emperor (Khalifa) was the spiritual head of the Islamic world. After the Ottoman defeat, a harsh peace treaty was expected. A **Khilafat Committee** was formed in Bombay in **March 1919**, led by brothers **Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**. Gandhi saw a chance to bring Hindus and Muslims together. At the **Calcutta session (September 1920)** he convinced Congress leaders to start a non-cooperation movement in support of Khilafat and swaraj; it was adopted at the **Nagpur session (December 1920)**.

In his book **Hind Swaraj (1909)** Gandhi argued British rule survived only because of Indian cooperation; if Indians refused, British rule would collapse within a year.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Gandhi call for a satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – What the Act did:** gave enormous repressive powers and allowed detention without trial for two years.

**Step 2 – How it was passed:** hurriedly, despite opposition of Indian members.

**Step 3 – Response:** Gandhi wanted non-violent civil disobedience against such unjust laws – starting with a hartal on 6 April 1919.

steps.title: Solved example: Suggest stages of Non-Cooperation as Gandhi proposed them (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Surrender titles awarded by the government.

**Step 2:** Boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods.

**Step 3:** If the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign would be launched.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating Jallianwala Bagh to 1920 – it was **13 April 1919**.
- Mixing up Champaran (indigo plantation peasants, Bihar) with Kheda (revenue relief, Gujarat).
- Saying Non-Cooperation was adopted at Calcutta – it was proposed there (Sept 1920) and adopted at **Nagpur (Dec 1920)**.

lessons.title: Differing strands within Non-Cooperation

scenes.text: In Awadh, Ramdei's family stops providing begar (forced labour) to the landlord.
In Assam, a plantation worker walks off the estate, believing “Gandhi Raj” is coming.

steps.title: In the towns
steps.body:
- Middle-class participation: thousands of students left government schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, lawyers gave up practice.
- Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party (party of non-Brahmans) contested.
- Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed, foreign cloth burnt. **The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922**, falling from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore.
- The movement slowed because khadi was more expensive than mill cloth, and alternative Indian institutions were not ready, so students and lawyers returned.

steps.title: Rebellion in the countryside
steps.body:
- **Awadh:** peasants led by **Baba Ramchandra**, a sanyasi who had been an indentured labourer in Fiji, opposed talukdars and landlords who demanded high rents and **begar**. The **Oudh Kisan Sabha** was set up in October 1920 headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others. In 1921 the movement turned violent in places (houses of talukdars attacked, bazaars looted).
- **Tribal peasants – Gudem Hills, Andhra Pradesh:** a guerrilla movement in the early 1920s under **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, who claimed special powers and was inspired by Gandhi but believed force was necessary. The colonial government had closed forest areas, preventing grazing and collection of fuelwood and fruits. Raju was captured and executed in 1924.

steps.title: Swaraj in the plantations
steps.body:
Under the **Inland Emigration Act of 1859**, plantation workers in Assam were not allowed to leave the tea gardens without permission (rarely given). Hearing of Non-Cooperation, thousands defied authorities, left the plantations and headed home, believing **Gandhi Raj** was coming and everyone would get land. They were stranded by a railway and steamer strike and beaten up by police.

Each group interpreted “swaraj” in its own way – for workers it meant freedom to move; for peasants, an end to rent and begar.

steps.title: Why Non-Cooperation was withdrawn
steps.body: In **February 1922**, a peaceful demonstration at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur) clashed with police and turned violent; police were killed. Gandhi felt the movement was turning violent and satyagrahis needed proper training. He withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain how the Non-Cooperation Movement spread in towns and why it slowed down (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Participation:** students left schools, teachers resigned, lawyers stopped practice; councils boycotted (except Madras).

**Step 2 – Economic boycott:** foreign cloth burnt; imports halved (₹102 cr → ₹57 cr between 1921–22); Indian textile production rose.

**Step 3 – Slowdown:** khadi was costlier; alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up.

**Step 4 – Result:** students and lawyers went back to government institutions.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare the peasant movement in Awadh with the Gudem Hills rebellion (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Awadh:** peasants against talukdars' high rents and begar; led by Baba Ramchandra; organised through the Oudh Kisan Sabha.

**Step 2 – Gudem Hills:** tribal peasants against closure of forests; led by Alluri Sitarama Raju through guerrilla warfare.

**Step 3 – Contrast:** both used Gandhi's name, but Raju believed in force, unlike Gandhian non-violence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Justice Party boycotted Madras elections – it **contested** them.
- Confusing the Inland Emigration Act (1859, plantation workers) with the Rowlatt Act (1919).
- Writing that Alluri Sitarama Raju was non-violent – he led an armed guerrilla movement.

quiz.why: The Awadh peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi.

quiz.why: The Inland Emigration Act of 1859 did not allow plantation workers in Assam to leave the tea gardens without permission.

quiz.why: Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922.

lessons.title: Towards Civil Disobedience and the Salt March

scenes.text: Ishaan wonders how a handful of salt could shake an empire.
He traces a 240-mile walk from Sabarmati to Dandi on a map.

steps.title: Between the movements (1922–1928)
steps.body:
- Some leaders (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru) formed the **Swaraj Party** within Congress to return to council politics.
- Younger leaders like **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Subhas Chandra Bose** pressed for more radical action and full independence.
- The worldwide economic depression made agricultural prices fall from 1926 and collapse after 1930, creating turmoil in the countryside.
- The **Simon Commission**, set up by the Tory government, arrived in **1928**. It had **no Indian member**, so it was greeted with the slogan “**Go back Simon**”.
- In **October 1929** Viceroy **Lord Irwin** announced a vague offer of “dominion status” and a Round Table Conference.

steps.title: Purna Swaraj and the Salt March
steps.body:
- At the **Lahore Congress (December 1929)**, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, the demand for **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence) was formalised. **26 January 1930** was celebrated as Independence Day.
- On **31 January 1930** Gandhi sent a letter to Irwin stating **eleven demands**; the most stirring was to **abolish the salt tax**, as salt was consumed by rich and poor alike.
- When Irwin did not respond, Gandhi began the **Salt March** with 78 volunteers from **Sabarmati** to the coastal town of **Dandi** – over 240 miles in 24 days – and violated the law by making salt on **6 April 1930**.

steps.title: Civil Disobedience: how it differed and what followed
steps.body:
- Unlike Non-Cooperation, people were asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to **break colonial laws** – salt laws, forest laws; foreign cloth boycotted, liquor shops picketed, peasants refused revenue and chaukidari taxes.
- The government responded brutally: when **Abdul Ghaffar Khan** (a devout disciple of Gandhi) was arrested in April 1930, crowds in Peshawar faced police firing; when Gandhi was arrested, industrial workers in Sholapur attacked police posts and government buildings.
- **Gandhi–Irwin Pact (5 March 1931):** Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London; the government agreed to release political prisoners.
- The **Second Round Table Conference (December 1931)** failed; Gandhi returned disappointed and relaunched the movement. It continued for over a year but by **1934** lost momentum.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was salt a powerful symbol? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Universal item:** salt is consumed by rich and poor alike – everyone felt the tax.

**Step 2 – Injustice:** the tax and the government monopoly over production were oppressive.

**Step 3 – Unity:** breaking the salt law was simple, legal-looking defiance anyone could join, uniting the nation.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish Non-Cooperation from Civil Disobedience (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Aim:** NCM (1920–22) sought swaraj and Khilafat; CDM (1930–34) sought Purna Swaraj.

**Step 2 – Method:** NCM = refuse cooperation (boycott schools, courts, councils, goods); CDM = refuse cooperation **and break laws** (salt, forest, taxes).

**Step 3 – Starting point:** NCM adopted at Nagpur 1920; CDM began with the Salt March 1930.

**Step 4 – End:** NCM withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922); CDM lost momentum by 1934.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Simon Commission had Indian members – it had **none**.
- Mixing 26 January 1930 (first Independence Day pledge) with 26 January 1950 (Constitution came into force).
- Writing that the Salt March began on 6 April – it began on **12 March 1930**; salt was made on 6 April.

lessons.title: How participants saw the movement; its limits

scenes.text: A Patidar farmer joins because revenue is too high; a mill owner joins hoping for protection from imports.
Their reasons differ – and so does their disappointment when the movement stops.

steps.title: Peasants, business and workers
steps.body:
- **Rich peasants** (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP) were hit by falling prices; for them swaraj meant a fight against high revenue. They were disappointed when the movement was called off in 1931 without revenue being revised; many refused to join when it restarted in 1932.
- **Poor peasants** wanted unpaid rent to be remitted; they often joined radical movements led by Socialists and Communists. Congress was unwilling to support “no rent” campaigns for fear of upsetting rich peasants and landlords.
- **Business classes** wanted protection against imports and a rupee–sterling exchange ratio that discouraged imports. They formed the **Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920)** and the **Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI, 1927)**, led by **Purshottamdas Thakurdas** and **G.D. Birla**. After the failed Round Table Conference and the spread of militant activities, they were less enthusiastic.
- **Industrial workers** largely stayed away except in the Nagpur region; Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands so as not to alienate industrialists.

steps.title: Women in the movement
steps.body: Women participated in large numbers – in protest marches, making salt, picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops; many went to jail. In urban areas they were mostly from high-caste families; in rural areas from rich peasant households. Gandhi said it was women's duty to look after home and hearth, and for a long time Congress was reluctant to give women positions of authority within the organisation.

steps.title: The limits: Dalits and Muslims
steps.body:
- **Dalits (“untouchables”)**: Gandhi called them **harijans** (children of God) and worked for their uplift, but many Dalit leaders wanted reserved seats and separate electorates. **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** organised Dalits into the **Depressed Classes Association (1930)** and clashed with Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference by demanding separate electorates. Gandhi went on a fast unto death; the result was the **Poona Pact (September 1932)**, which gave reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils but voting by the general electorate.
- **Muslims**: after Non-Cooperation–Khilafat, large sections felt alienated from Congress as it seemed closer to Hindu nationalist groups; relations worsened with communal clashes. In **1930 Sir Muhammad Iqbal**, as president of the Muslim League, reiterated the importance of separate electorates for Muslims.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did different social groups join the Civil Disobedience Movement? (5 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rich peasants:** to fight high revenue demands as prices fell.

**Step 2 – Poor peasants:** wanted rent remitted (Congress hesitated).

**Step 3 – Business classes:** wanted protection against imports and a favourable exchange rate; organised through FICCI.

**Step 4 – Women:** saw service to the nation as a sacred duty.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** each group had its own idea of swaraj, which explains both the movement's breadth and its tensions.

steps.title: Solved example: What was the Poona Pact and why was it signed? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cause:** Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits at the Second Round Table Conference; the British accepted the demand.

**Step 2 – Reaction:** Gandhi, feeling it would slow integration, began a fast unto death.

**Step 3 – Pact (Sept 1932):** Depressed Classes got reserved seats in legislatures but would be voted in by the general electorate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Ambedkar founded the Muslim League – he founded the **Depressed Classes Association (1930)**.
- Saying industrial workers joined everywhere – they largely stayed away except in Nagpur.
- Assuming all groups wanted the same thing – the exam often asks “why did groups feel differently?”

lessons.title: The sense of collective belonging

scenes.text: Before a school function, Tara asks where “Vande Mataram” came from.
Her teacher shows a painting of Bharat Mata and explains how images, songs and stories build a nation.

steps.title: Images, songs and folklore
steps.body:
- The identity of the nation was often symbolised in an image: **Bharat Mata**. **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay** wrote **“Vande Mataram”** in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland; it was included in his novel **Anandamath** and widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.
- **Abanindranath Tagore** painted a famous image of Bharat Mata as an ascetic figure – calm, composed, divine and spiritual.
- Nationalists recorded folk tales: **Rabindranath Tagore** collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths in Bengal; **Natesa Sastri** published a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales, *The Folklore of Southern India*.

steps.title: Flags and history
steps.body:
- During the **Swadeshi movement in Bengal**, a tricolour (red, green and yellow) was designed with **eight lotuses** representing eight provinces of British India and a **crescent moon** representing Hindus and Muslims.
- By **1921** Gandhi designed the **Swaraj flag** – a tricolour (red, green and white) with a **spinning wheel** in the centre, representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help. Carrying the flag during marches became a symbol of defiance.
- Nationalists reinterpreted history: they wrote about India's glorious past in art, science, mathematics, religion and law, urging Indians to take pride and change the miserable conditions under British rule.

steps.title: Problems with the images
steps.body: Images celebrated were often drawn from Hindu iconography, so other communities could feel left out – one reason why unifying people was difficult. By the 1940s, a section of Muslims felt alienated from the national movement.

steps.title: Solved example: How did nationalists use folklore and history? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Folklore:** they collected folk tales, songs and legends, seeing them as true traditional culture corrupted by outside forces (Tagore, Natesa Sastri).

**Step 2 – History:** they wrote about India's achievements in ancient times to counter British claims that Indians were backward.

**Step 3 – Effect:** this built pride and a shared identity.

steps.title: Solved example: Describe the Swaraj flag of 1921 (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** A tricolour of red, green and white.

**Step 2:** A spinning wheel in the centre stood for the Gandhian ideal of self-help.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Rabindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata – it was **Abanindranath Tagore**.
- Confusing the 1905 Swadeshi flag (8 lotuses, crescent) with the 1921 Swaraj flag (spinning wheel).
- Writing that Vande Mataram was written in 1947 – it was written in the 1870s.
