courses.title: Ch 3 · The Making of a Global World
courses.summary: Globalisation through history: the pre-modern world of silk routes, food and disease; the nineteenth-century world economy and colonialism; the inter-war economy and Great Depression; and the post-war Bretton Woods order.
outcomes: Learners can give examples of pre-modern global links (trade, food, disease)
Learners can explain the three flows of the 19th-century world economy and the role of technology
Learners can describe indentured labour and Indian entrepreneurs abroad
Learners can explain the Great Depression, its impact on India, and the Bretton Woods system

lessons.title: The pre-modern world

scenes.text: Neel eats noodles and wonders: did they come from China or Italy?
His sister adds that potatoes, chillies and tomatoes reached India only after Columbus's voyages.

steps.title: Silk routes
steps.body: The **silk routes** were land and sea routes knitting together vast regions of Asia and linking Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They existed before the Christian Era and thrived almost till the 15th century. Chinese pottery, textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia travelled one way; precious metals – gold and silver – flowed from Europe to Asia. Early Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers and Buddhism also travelled along these routes.

steps.title: Food travels
steps.body: Traders and travellers introduced new crops. Noodles may have travelled west from China to become spaghetti (or Arab traders took pasta to Sicily). After the discovery of the Americas, **potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes** reached Europe and Asia. In **Ireland**, poor peasants depended so heavily on potatoes that when disease destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation (the **Irish Potato Famine, 1845–49**).

steps.title: Conquest, disease and trade
steps.body: From the 16th century, after European sailors found sea routes to Asia and the Americas, the pre-modern world shrank. America's precious metals (especially silver) enhanced Europe's wealth. The Portuguese and Spanish conquest of America was helped not by firepower alone but by **germs such as smallpox**, against which the native Americans had no immunity – it spread deep and killed whole communities. Until the 18th century, China and India were among the world's richest countries.

steps.title: Solved example: “Pre-modern trade was not only about goods.” Explain (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Goods:** silk, pottery, spices, gold and silver moved along the silk routes.

**Step 2 – People and ideas:** missionaries, preachers and Buddhism travelled.

**Step 3 – Food and germs:** crops like potatoes spread worldwide, and diseases like smallpox shaped conquest.

steps.title: Solved example: How did smallpox help the Spanish conquer America? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Native Americans had no immunity because the disease was new to them.

**Step 2:** It spread ahead of the conquerors, killing whole communities and weakening resistance – a “biological weapon”.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying potatoes were native to India – they came from the Americas.
- Thinking silk routes carried only silk – they carried many goods, people and religions.
- Dating the Irish famine to the 1900s – it was 1845–49.

statements.s: Potatoes reached Europe from the Americas.
Smallpox was brought to Europe by native Americans.
statements.why: Europeans carried it to the Americas.

statements.s: The silk routes carried religions as well as goods.
statements.why: Buddhism and Christianity spread along them.

statements.s: China and India were poor until the 18th century.

quiz.why: The silk routes linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa by land and sea.

quiz.q: Which crop failure caused the Irish famine?
quiz.why: The Irish famine of 1845–49 was caused by potato blight, which destroyed the potato crop.

quiz.q: Which flowed from Europe to Asia on silk routes?
quiz.why: Precious metals like gold and silver flowed from Europe to Asia along the silk routes.

quiz.q: The conquest of America was helped most by
quiz.why: Germs like smallpox, to which the native people had no immunity, helped the conquest of America most.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an American-origin crop?
quiz.why: Rice is an Asian crop. Maize, groundnut and tomato came from the Americas.

lessons.title: The nineteenth century (1815–1914)

scenes.text: In the 1870s, refrigerated ships started carrying frozen meat from America and Australia to Europe.
Suddenly poor Europeans could add meat to a diet of bread and potatoes.

steps.title: Three flows
steps.body:
Economists identify three types of movement in international exchange: **(1) trade** (mainly goods like cloth or wheat), **(2) labour** (people migrating for work) and **(3) capital** (investments over long distances).

**World economy takes shape:** in Britain, the **Corn Laws** (restricting import of corn) were abolished under pressure from industrialists and urban dwellers. Cheap food imports flooded in, British agriculture could not compete, and vast areas went uncultivated. Food production expanded in Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia – railways, ports and canals were built, often with capital from London, and some 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century.

steps.title: Role of technology
steps.body: **Railways, steamships and the telegraph** were vital. Refrigerated ships (from the 1870s) made it possible to transport perishable foods like meat over long distances; animals were slaughtered at the starting point (America, Australia, New Zealand) and transported frozen. This reduced shipping costs and lowered meat prices in Europe, improving diets and supporting social peace at home and imperialism abroad.

steps.title: Colonialism and rinderpest
steps.body: In 1885 European powers met in Berlin to divide up Africa. In the **1890s** a fast-spreading cattle disease, **rinderpest**, arrived in Africa – carried by infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers in Eritrea. It killed about **90% of the cattle**, destroying African livelihoods. Colonial governments and planters used this to monopolise remaining cattle and force Africans into the labour market.

steps.title: Indentured labour and Indian entrepreneurs
steps.body:
- **Indentured labour:** a bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a specific time to repay his travel to a new country or home. Indians from eastern UP, Bihar, central India and dry districts of Tamil Nadu went to the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius and Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya. Living conditions were harsh, but workers found ways to survive, blending cultures – e.g. **Hosay** in Trinidad (from Muharram), **chutney music**, the Rastafarianism link with Indian migrants. The system was abolished in **1921**.
- **Indian entrepreneurs abroad:** **Shikaripuri shroffs** and **Nattukottai Chettiars** financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia; Hyderabadi Sindhi traders established emporia at busy ports.
- **Indian trade:** Britain's trade surplus with India was used to balance its deficits with other countries; Indian cotton textile exports declined while raw cotton exports rose; opium was exported to China.

steps.title: Solved example: How did refrigerated ships change the food economy? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Problem:** live animals were costly to ship, and meat was expensive in Europe.

**Step 2 – Change:** animals were slaughtered in America/Australia/New Zealand and shipped frozen.

**Step 3 – Effect:** lower costs and prices; poorer Europeans could eat meat, which kept social peace.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did indentured labourers call their new life a “new system of slavery”? Give two cultural responses (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Harsh conditions:** false information by recruiters, tough work, few legal rights.

**Step 2 – Response 1:** Hosay in Trinidad – a carnival from the Muharram procession joined by all races.

**Step 3 – Response 2:** chutney music in Trinidad and Guyana – a creative mix of Indian and Caribbean forms.

**Step 4:** The system ended in 1921 after nationalist opposition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing “trade, technology, transport” as the three flows – they are **trade, labour, capital**.
- Saying rinderpest killed humans – it is a **cattle** disease.
- Thinking indenture ended in 1947 – it was abolished in **1921**.

quiz.why: The three flows of the global economy are trade, labour and capital.

quiz.why: Rinderpest, a cattle plague, killed about 90% of cattle in Africa.

quiz.why: Hosay is an annual carnival of Trinidad, which grew out of Muharram processions of indentured Indians.

quiz.why: The system of indentured labour was abolished in 1921.

quiz.why: After the Corn Laws were abolished, cheap food was imported into Britain and it became cheaper than local produce, so some land went uncultivated.

lessons.title: The inter-war economy and the Great Depression

scenes.text: Neha's great-grandfather grew raw jute in Bengal. In the 1930s its price crashed by over 60%.
Peasants fell into debt, even as officials kept demanding the same revenue.

steps.title: War-time transformation
steps.body: The **First World War (1914–18)** was the first modern industrial war: machine guns, tanks, aircraft, chemical weapons. Industries were restructured for war goods; Britain borrowed large sums from US banks and the US public, turning the **US from an international debtor into a creditor**. After the war, Britain faced unemployment and lost its industrial dominance (e.g. Japanese and Indian industries grew).

steps.title: Mass production and consumption
steps.body: **Henry Ford** adapted the assembly line of a Chicago slaughterhouse to car-making in Detroit; the **Model T** was the first mass-produced car. Workers were paid **$5 a day** (from 1914). Fordist practices spread through the US and to Europe in the 1920s. Hire purchase (credit on easy instalments) spread demand for cars, refrigerators, washing machines and radios. US capital exports also boomed.

steps.title: The Great Depression (1929 to mid-1930s)
steps.body:
**Causes:** (1) agricultural overproduction – falling prices made farmers grow more, pushing prices further down; (2) in the mid-1920s many countries financed investment through US loans, and when US lenders panicked in 1928, countries dependent on loans faced crisis. The US raised import duties, and the **stock market crash of 1929** deepened the crisis: production, employment, incomes and trade fell. Banks collapsed – thousands of US banks went bankrupt in the early 1930s.

**India:** exports and imports nearly **halved between 1928 and 1934**; wheat prices fell **50%** in India in the same period. Peasants and farmers suffered most as the colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands. India became an exporter of **precious metals, notably gold**. Urban fixed-income groups (salaried employees) gained as prices fell.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain two causes of the Great Depression (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Overproduction in agriculture:** falling prices → farmers produced more to maintain income → glut → prices fell further; produce rotted.

**Step 2 – Dependence on US loans:** countries borrowed from the US; when US lenders withdrew (1928) and the stock market crashed (1929), these countries collapsed.

**Step 3 – Link:** together they turned a slump into a worldwide depression.

steps.title: Solved example: “The Depression hit Indian peasants hard but helped some urban groups.” Explain (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Peasants:** crop prices crashed (wheat −50%, raw jute −60%+) while revenue demand stayed the same; debts grew; savings and gold were used up.

**Step 2 – Urban fixed-income groups:** salaried people and landowners with fixed rents found everything cheaper, so they were better off.

**Step 3 – Politics:** rural unrest fed into the Civil Disobedience Movement (1931).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Depression started in 1939 – it began around **1929**.
- Writing that Britain became a creditor after WWI – the **US** became the creditor.
- Forgetting that India exported **gold** during the Depression.

quiz.why: After the First World War the USA became an international creditor, while Britain became a debtor.

quiz.why: Henry Ford paid his workers $5 a day from 1914.

quiz.why: Wheat prices in India fell by about 50% between 1928 and 1934.

quiz.why: During the Depression India exported large amounts of gold, which helped the world economy.

quiz.q: Who gained from falling prices in India?
quiz.why: Urban salaried people with fixed incomes gained, as falling prices let their money buy more.

lessons.title: Rebuilding a world economy: the post-war era

scenes.text: In July 1944, delegates met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA.
They wanted to avoid another depression and war – and created the IMF and the World Bank.

steps.title: Post-war settlement and Bretton Woods
steps.body:
The Second World War (1939–45) caused immense destruction. Lessons from the inter-war years: (1) an industrial society based on mass production needs mass consumption, so governments should ensure stable employment; (2) economic links with the outside world must be managed to achieve full employment.

- The **United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference** at **Bretton Woods (July 1944)** set up the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** to deal with external surpluses and deficits, and the **International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)** to finance post-war reconstruction. They are called the **Bretton Woods twins**; both started operations in 1947.
- Decision-making is controlled by the Western industrial powers; the US has an effective veto over key IMF and World Bank decisions.
- The system was based on **fixed exchange rates**; national currencies were pegged to the dollar at a fixed rate, and the dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce.

steps.title: Decolonisation, G-77 and the end of Bretton Woods
steps.body:
- Most colonies became independent after 1945 but remained poor. Many developing countries organised as the **Group of 77 (G-77)** to demand a **New International Economic Order (NIEO)** – real control over natural resources, more development aid, fairer prices for raw materials and better access to markets.
- From the 1960s, rising US overseas costs weakened the dollar; the fixed exchange-rate system collapsed and **floating exchange rates** were introduced in the early 1970s.
- **MNCs** (multinational corporations) expanded worldwide from the 1950s–60s; from the late 1970s they shifted production to low-wage Asian countries, especially **China** (after 1949, then opened from the late 1970s). India, China and Brazil later saw rapid transformation.

steps.title: Solved example: Why were the IMF and World Bank set up? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Context:** world war destruction and memories of the Depression.

**Step 2 – IMF:** to deal with external surpluses and deficits of member nations.

**Step 3 – World Bank (IBRD):** to finance post-war reconstruction (later development).

steps.title: Solved example: What was the NIEO and why did G-77 demand it? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Why:** decolonised countries found the Bretton Woods institutions served rich countries; their resources were still exploited by Western powers.

**Step 2 – What:** a New International Economic Order – control over their natural resources, more development aid, fairer raw-material prices, better market access for manufactured goods.

**Step 3 – Who:** the Group of 77 developing countries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing Bretton Woods in Europe – it is in **New Hampshire, USA**.
- Saying the Bretton Woods system used floating rates – it used **fixed** rates (floating came in the 1970s).
- Confusing G-77 (developing countries) with G-8/G-20.

courses.title: Ch 4 · The Age of Industrialisation
courses.summary: Industrialisation before and after factories: proto-industrialisation, the slow pace of change in Britain, hand labour versus steam, the decline and survival of Indian weaving, the growth of Indian factories and how goods were advertised.
outcomes: Learners can define proto-industrialisation and explain why merchants turned to the countryside
Learners can explain why steam power spread slowly and hand labour persisted
Learners can describe what happened to Indian weavers under the Company and after Manchester imports
Learners can explain the growth of Indian industry and the role of advertisements

lessons.title: Before the Industrial Revolution

scenes.text: In 17th-century England, a merchant from London rides out to a village to give wool to a poor peasant family.
The whole family spins and weaves at home – this is industry before factories.

steps.title: Proto-industrialisation
steps.body:
**Proto-industrialisation** is the phase of large-scale industrial production for an international market **before factories** – in homes, not in factories.

- Merchants could not expand production within towns because powerful **urban crafts and trade guilds** (associations of producers that trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices) and rulers granting monopoly rights restricted entry.
- So merchants turned to the **countryside**, giving money advances to peasants and artisans to produce for them.
- Poor peasants welcomed this: open fields were being enclosed, common lands disappeared, and income from proto-industrial work supplemented shrinking farm income.
- A **putting-out system** linked town merchants and rural producers. Example chain in cloth: a merchant clothier bought wool from a **wool stapler**, carried it to spinners; the yarn went to weavers, **fullers** and dyers; finishing was done in London before export.

steps.title: The coming of the factory
steps.body:
- The earliest factories in England came up by the **1730s**, but the number grew dramatically only in the late 18th century.
- **Cotton** was the first symbol of the new era; its production boomed (imports of raw cotton rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787).
- Inventions increased output per worker; **Richard Arkwright** created the **cotton mill**, bringing all processes under one roof and management, allowing careful supervision and quality control.

steps.title: Solved example: Why were merchants keen to shift production to the countryside? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Town barriers:** guilds controlled production and prices; rulers gave monopolies, blocking new merchants.

**Step 2 – Cheap rural labour:** peasants needed extra income as common lands were enclosed.

**Step 3 – Result:** merchants supplied raw material and advances; families produced at home → proto-industrialisation.

steps.title: Solved example: Describe the stages in producing cloth under proto-industrialisation (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Merchant clothier buys wool from a wool stapler and takes it to spinners.

**Step 2:** Yarn is taken to weavers, fullers and dyers in villages.

**Step 3:** Finishing done in London; cloth exported by merchants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking proto-industry happened in factories – it was **home-based**.
- Calling guilds trade unions of workers – they were associations of **producers/craftsmen and merchants** that controlled entry.
- Saying the cotton mill was invented by James Watt – it was **Richard Arkwright**.

activity.prompt: Order the cloth production chain
items: Wool stapler sells wool to the merchant clothier

quiz.q: Proto-industrialisation means
options: large-scale home-based production for international markets before factories

lessons.title: The pace of change; hand labour and steam power

scenes.text: A Victorian factory owner can buy a costly steam engine or hire cheap seasonal workers.
With migrants queuing at the gate, he chooses hands, not machines.

steps.title: How fast was change?
steps.body:
- The most dynamic industries were **cotton and metals**. Cotton led until the 1840s; then iron and steel led with the expansion of railways (England from the 1840s, colonies from the 1860s).
- New industries could not easily displace traditional ones; even at the end of the 19th century, **less than 20% of the total workforce** was employed in technologically advanced industrial sectors.
- Change in traditional industries was driven by ordinary small innovations, not only by steam.
- Technological change was slow: new machines were expensive, often broke down, and repair was costly. **James Watt** improved Newcomen's steam engine and patented it in **1781**; his industrialist friend **Matthew Boulton** manufactured it. But even by **1840** steam engines in England were rare – few users outside industry.

steps.title: Hand labour and the life of workers
steps.body:
- In Victorian Britain there was **no shortage of human labour**; poor peasants and vagrants migrated to cities in search of jobs, so wages were low and industrialists preferred hand labour.
- Many industries had **seasonal** demand (gas works, breweries, book-binders, ship repairers) – they preferred hand labour employed for the season.
- The upper classes (aristocrats, bourgeoisie) preferred **hand-made** goods – a symbol of refinement and class; machine-made goods were for export to colonies.
- In countries with labour shortage (e.g. America), mechanisation was preferred.
- Workers' lives: finding jobs depended on friends and relatives; many waited weeks, sleeping under bridges or in night shelters. When the **Spinning Jenny** (by **James Hargreaves**, 1764) was introduced, women who survived on hand-spinning attacked the machines because they feared unemployment.

steps.title: Solved example: Give three reasons why industrialists in Victorian Britain preferred hand labour (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Plenty of poor migrants → labour was cheap.

**Step 2:** Seasonal industries needed workers only for part of the year; machines would stand idle.

**Step 3:** Upper classes demanded hand-made goods of intricate designs and specific shapes that machines could not produce.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did women attack the Spinning Jenny? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** The Jenny let one worker turn several spindles and spin many threads at once.

**Step 2:** Women who lived by hand-spinning feared loss of work and wages, so they resisted it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming factories replaced hand work overnight – change was slow; most workers were still in traditional sectors in 1900.
- Saying Watt invented the steam engine from scratch – he **improved** Newcomen's engine (patent 1781).
- Forgetting that the spinning jenny was invented by **Hargreaves (1764)**.

statements.s: By 1900, most British workers were in technologically advanced industries.
James Watt patented his improved steam engine in 1781.
Seasonal industries preferred hand labour.
Aristocrats preferred machine-made goods.

quiz.why: Cotton and metals were the most dynamic industries in Britain.

quiz.why: James Hargreaves invented the Spinning Jenny in 1764.

quiz.why: Labour was scarce in America, so mechanisation was preferred there.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Steam engines were common in 1840 England

quiz.why: New machines were costly and often broke down, so many industrialists still preferred hand labour.

lessons.title: Industrialisation in the colonies: weavers and factories in India

scenes.text: Before 1750, Indian silk and cotton dominated the world market – Armenian and Persian merchants took goods via Punjab, Afghanistan and Persia.
By the 1800s the ports of Surat and Hoogly declined, and Bombay and Calcutta rose.

steps.title: The age of Indian textiles and the East India Company
steps.body:
- Pre-colonial trade networks linked Surat (Gujarat), Masulipatnam (Coromandel) and Hoogly (Bengal) with Southeast and West Asia. By 1750 this network was breaking down as European companies gained power.
- After the East India Company established political power (from the 1760s–70s), it eliminated existing traders and brokers and established direct control over weavers.
- It appointed paid servants called **gomasthas** to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine quality. Weavers were given **advances** and loans and were prevented from selling to other buyers.
- Gomasthas were outsiders who acted arrogantly; clashes between weavers and gomasthas were common. Many weavers deserted villages, refused loans or took up agriculture.

steps.title: Manchester comes to India
steps.body:
- By the 1800s Indian textile exports declined: in 1811–12 piece-goods were **33% of India's exports**; by 1850–51 only **3%**.
- Problems for weavers: (1) the export market collapsed, (2) the local market shrank, flooded with cheap Manchester imports, (3) raw cotton exports raised prices and weavers could not get good-quality cotton, (4) by the end of the 19th century, Indian factories competed too.
- Yet handloom production did not die: it survived because it adopted improved technology like the **fly shuttle** (by 1941 over 35% of handlooms in India had it) and produced finer or coarser cloth that mills could not match (e.g. saris with intricate borders).

steps.title: Factories come up
steps.body:
- The first cotton mill in **Bombay** came up in **1854**; the first **jute mill in Bengal in 1855**; first cotton mill of Ahmedabad in 1861; Elgin Mill at Kanpur in 1860; Madras mill in 1874.
- **Early entrepreneurs:** **Dwarkanath Tagore** (Bengal) made his fortune in the China trade and invested in industry; in Bombay **Dinshaw Petit** and **Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata**; **Seth Hukumchand** (Marwari) set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917; **G.D. Birla** also.
- European Managing Agencies (Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, Jardine Skinner & Co.) controlled large sections of industry.
- Workers came from nearby districts; industrialists employed a **jobber** to recruit workers – often an old trusted worker who got people from his village, helped them settle, and later demanded money and gifts and controlled their lives.
- **Peculiarities of growth:** early cotton mills produced coarse yarn; with the **Swadeshi movement** and World War I (1914–18) Indian factories grew as imports fell and they supplied army needs.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain the role of the gomastha (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Who:** paid servant of the East India Company.

**Step 2 – Work:** supervised weavers, collected supplies, examined quality of cloth.

**Step 3 – Effect:** prevented weavers from selling to other buyers; acted arrogantly, causing frequent clashes.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did handloom weaving survive into the 20th century? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Technology:** weavers adopted the fly shuttle (35%+ of looms by 1941), increasing productivity.

**Step 2 – Niche products:** intricate saris and borders (and some coarse cloth for the poor) that mills could not make.

**Step 3 – Demand:** both rich and poor markets for such goods remained.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the first Bombay cotton mill opened in 1914 – it was **1854**.
- Confusing the **jobber** (labour recruiter) with the gomastha (Company supervisor).
- Writing that handlooms vanished completely – they **survived and grew** in some segments.

lessons.title: Market for goods: advertising and the nation

scenes.text: Old Manchester cloth bundles carried labels showing "Made in Manchester" and pictures of Indian gods.
Calendars hung in tea shops and homes all year, keeping a brand in view.

steps.title: How new consumers were created
steps.body:
Advertisements make products appear desirable and necessary; they shape minds and create needs.

- **Labels:** Manchester industrialists put labels on cloth bundles – “Made in Manchester” in bold to signify quality; images of Indian gods and goddesses (Krishna, Saraswati) to give divine approval and a familiar feel; historic figures like emperors and nawabs to suggest a product worth respecting.
- **Calendars:** by the late 19th century manufacturers printed calendars that even non-readers could understand; hung in homes and shops, they advertised the brand daily.
- **Indian manufacturers** advertised the nationalist message – “If you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce” (Swadeshi). Images of Bharat Mata often appeared.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Manchester manufacturers use images to sell in India? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Quality label:** “Made in Manchester” in bold assured buyers.

**Step 2 – Gods and goddesses:** images of deities gave a sense of divine approval and familiarity.

**Step 3 – Royal figures:** pictures of emperors and nawabs suggested the product was respectable.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Indian manufacturers use advertising differently? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** They used a **nationalist** appeal – Swadeshi, buy Indian.

**Step 2:** They used national images like Bharat Mata to link buying with patriotism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking calendars were only for literate people – they were useful **even to those who could not read**.
- Forgetting that Indian advertisers used the **Swadeshi** message.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Print Culture and the Modern World
courses.summary: How printing began in East Asia, reached Europe with Gutenberg, created a reading public and helped religious and political change, and how print shaped Indian society, women, the poor and the national movement – and how governments tried to censor it.
outcomes: Learners can trace the history of print from China and Japan to Gutenberg
Learners can explain the effects of the print revolution in Europe, including on the Reformation and French Revolution
Learners can describe print in India: religious debates, women, the poor, caste reformers
Learners can explain colonial censorship including the Vernacular Press Act

lessons.title: The first printed books: East Asia and Gutenberg

scenes.text: Ananya reads that the oldest known dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868.
Hundreds of years later, a goldsmith's son in Germany built a press inspired by olive and wine presses.

steps.title: China, Japan, Korea
steps.body:
- The earliest printing technology came from **China, Japan and Korea** – **hand printing** by rubbing paper on inked wooden blocks. From **AD 594** books in China were printed this way. Both sides of thin porous sheets could not be printed, so the traditional **accordion book** was folded and stitched at the side.
- For a long time the imperial state in China was the major producer of printed material, printing textbooks for the civil service examinations.
- By the 17th century, urban culture bloomed in China; merchants used print for trade information; reading became a leisure activity; rich women began to read and some published poetry and plays. Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture (Western mechanical presses in the late 19th century).
- **Japan:** Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand printing around **AD 768–770**. The oldest Japanese book, the **Diamond Sutra (AD 868)**, has six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations. In 18th-century Edo (later Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted urban culture; **Kitagawa Utamaro** (born 1753) created the art form *ukiyo* (“pictures of the floating world”).

steps.title: Print comes to Europe; Gutenberg
steps.body:
- **Marco Polo** returned to Italy in **1295** after many years in China and brought woodblock printing knowledge; Italians produced woodblock books and the technology spread.
- Luxury editions were still handwritten on **vellum** for the rich. Hand-copying was expensive, laborious and time-consuming; manuscripts were fragile.
- **Johann Gutenberg**, son of a merchant, grew up on an agricultural estate seeing wine and olive presses, and learnt to polish stones as a goldsmith. Using this knowledge he designed the **printing press** – the olive press served as the model and moulds were used to cast metal types. By **1448** he had perfected the system. The first book he printed was the **Bible** – about **180 copies in three years**.
- Between 1450 and 1550 printing presses were set up in most European countries. In the second half of the 15th century, **20 million copies** of printed books flooded markets; by the 16th century, **200 million**. This shift from hand printing to mechanical printing led to the **print revolution**.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Gutenberg develop his press? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Background:** grew up seeing wine and olive presses; learnt to polish stones and make lead moulds as a goldsmith's apprentice.

**Step 2 – Design:** adapted the olive press as the model; used moulds to cast metal types for letters.

**Step 3 – Result:** perfected by 1448; printed about 180 copies of the Bible in three years.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was hand-copying unable to meet the demand for books? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** It was expensive, laborious and slow.

**Step 2:** Manuscripts were fragile and awkward to handle; demand from a growing readership could not be met.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying printing was invented in Europe – it began in **China (from AD 594)**.
- Writing that Gutenberg's first book was a dictionary – it was the **Bible**.
- Confusing the Diamond Sutra's country: it is the oldest **Japanese** book (868).

lessons.title: The print revolution and its impact in Europe

scenes.text: In 1517 a monk, Martin Luther, wrote 95 Theses criticising practices of the Church.
Printed copies spread so fast that a religious debate became the Protestant Reformation.

steps.title: A new reading public
steps.body:
- Print reduced the cost of books, and the time and labour needed fell; books flooded the market, reaching an ever-growing readership.
- Earlier, ordinary people heard sacred texts read out; books were few. Now a **reading public** emerged. But as literacy was low, publishers printed popular ballads and folk tales with pictures; oral culture entered print and printed material was read out to listeners – the line between **hearing and reading public** blurred.

steps.title: Religious debates and the fear of print
steps.body:
- Not all welcomed print: some feared it would spread rebellious and irreligious thoughts.
- **Martin Luther** wrote **95 Theses (1517)** criticising Church practices; printed copies spread widely. Luther translated the New Testament – 5,000 copies sold within weeks. He said: “Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.” This led to the **Protestant Reformation**.
- **Menocchio**, a miller in 16th-century Italy, read books and reinterpreted the Bible; he was hauled before the Roman Catholic Inquisition and executed. The Church began maintaining an **Index of Prohibited Books from 1558**.

steps.title: Reading mania; print and the French Revolution
steps.body:
- By the end of the 18th century literacy in parts of Europe reached 60–80%. **Chapbooks** (pocket-size books sold by pedlars called chapmen) in England and the **Bibliothèque Bleue** in France (low-priced small books on poor paper with blue covers) reached the poor.
- Almanacs, ballads, folk tales, romances, histories, and newspapers spread. Scientists like Newton published, and thinkers like Thomas Paine, Voltaire and Rousseau were read widely.
- **Print and the French Revolution** – three arguments: (1) print popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers who attacked tradition, superstition and despotism; (2) it created a new culture of dialogue and debate; (3) by the 1780s, literature mocked royalty and morality, spreading hostile sentiments against the monarchy. But print did not directly shape minds; people accepted some ideas and rejected others.
- **Nineteenth century:** children (Grimm brothers, children's presses), women as readers and writers (Jane Austen, Brontë sisters, George Eliot), lending libraries for workers; technological advances – **Richard M. Hoe** perfected the power-driven cylindrical press (could print 8,000 sheets per hour) by the mid-19th century; serialised novels; cheap “shilling series”; dust covers.

steps.title: Solved example: How did print help the Protestant Reformation? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Spread:** Luther's 95 Theses (1517) were printed in large numbers and read widely.

**Step 2 – Access:** his translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in weeks, letting people read scripture themselves.

**Step 3 – Result:** debate spread rapidly, leading to the Reformation; Luther called printing “the ultimate gift of God”.

steps.title: Solved example: Give three ways print contributed to the French Revolution (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Spread Enlightenment ideas of Voltaire and Rousseau against tradition and despotism.

**Step 2:** Created a culture of debate where values and institutions were questioned.

**Step 3:** Literature mocked the royalty and criticised its morality, turning people against the monarchy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying print **caused** the French Revolution directly – historians argue it helped create conditions; people interpreted ideas in many ways.
- Writing that the Index of Prohibited Books started in 1517 – it started in **1558**.
- Confusing chapbooks (England) with the Bibliothèque Bleue (France).

lessons.title: India and the world of print

scenes.text: In the 1800s, Rashsundari Debi, a young married woman in an orthodox household, learnt to read in secret in the kitchen.
Later she wrote an autobiography – Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali.

steps.title: Manuscripts and the coming of print
steps.body:
- India had a rich tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and vernacular languages, on palm leaves or handmade paper – expensive and fragile.
- The printing press first came to **Goa with Portuguese missionaries** in the mid-16th century; Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed tracts. By 1674 about 50 books had been printed in Konkani and Kannada. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in **1579** at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in **1713**.
- **James Augustus Hickey** began editing the **Bengal Gazette** in **1780**, a weekly magazine. **Gangadhar Bhattacharya**, a close associate of Rammohun Roy, was the first Indian to publish an Indian newspaper, the weekly *Bengal Gazette*.

steps.title: Religious reform and public debate
steps.body:
- From the early 19th century, intense debates around religion: reformers criticised practices like sati, child marriage, idolatry; others countered them.
- **Rammohun Roy** published **Sambad Kaumudi (1821)**; Hindu orthodoxy replied with **Samachar Chandrika**. In 1822 two Persian newspapers – **Jam-i-Jahan Nama** and **Shamsul Akhbar** – were published; the Gujarati newspaper **Bombay Samachar** also appeared.
- **Deoband Seminary (1867)** published thousands of **fatwas** telling Muslims how to conduct themselves.
- Among Hindus, vernacular texts reached many: the first printed version of Tulsidas's **Ramcharitmanas** came out from **Calcutta in 1810**; the **Naval Kishore Press (Lucknow)** and the **Shri Venkateshwar Press (Bombay)** published religious texts in vernaculars.

steps.title: Women, the poor and caste
steps.body:
- **Women:** writers wrote about women's lives; liberal husbands and fathers educated women at home. Some conservatives feared reading would make girls widows or that Muslim girls would be corrupted by Urdu romances. **Rashsundari Debi** wrote *Amar Jiban* (1876). **Kailashbashini Debi** and Tarabai Shinde and **Pandita Ramabai** wrote about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows. Hindi printing from the 1870s; journals for women discussed education, widowhood, widow remarriage and the national movement. Ram Chaddha's *Istri Dharm Vichar* taught wifely obedience.
- **Print and the poor:** very cheap small books sold at crossroads in Madras; public libraries from the early 20th century. **Jyotiba Phule**, Maratha pioneer of “low-caste” protest, wrote **Gulamgiri (1871)** about injustices of caste. **B.R. Ambedkar** and **E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)** wrote powerfully on caste. Kanpur mill worker **Kashibaba** wrote *Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal* (1938) linking caste and class exploitation.

steps.title: Solved example: How did print help religious reform debates in 19th-century India? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Wide circulation:** tracts and newspapers reached a wider public in local languages.

**Step 2 – Debate:** Rammohun Roy's Sambad Kaumudi (1821) argued for reform; orthodox Samachar Chandrika opposed it.

**Step 3 – Guidance:** Deoband Seminary (1867) issued fatwas; vernacular religious texts like Ramcharitmanas (1810) reached many.

steps.title: Solved example: How did print help women in India? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reading at home:** women learnt to read, sometimes secretly (Rashsundari Debi).

**Step 2 – Writing:** women wrote autobiographies and critiques (Amar Jiban; Pandita Ramabai on widows).

**Step 3 – Journals:** women's magazines discussed education, widow remarriage and the national movement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Hickey was Indian – he was British; Gangadhar Bhattacharya was the first Indian publisher of an Indian newspaper.
- Confusing **Gulamgiri** (Phule, 1871) with *Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal* (Kashibaba, 1938).
- Saying print came first to Calcutta – it came first to **Goa**.

lessons.title: Print and censorship

scenes.text: In 1908 Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote with deep sympathy about Punjab revolutionaries deported by the British in his paper Kesari.
He was imprisoned – and protests broke out across India.

steps.title: Colonial censorship
steps.body:
- Before 1798 the colonial state was not too concerned with censorship; early measures were aimed at Englishmen in India critical of Company misrule.
- By the 1820s, the Calcutta Supreme Court passed regulations to control press freedom; the Company encouraged newspapers that celebrated British rule.
- In **1835**, faced with petitions by editors, Governor-General **Bentinck** agreed to revise press laws; **Thomas Macaulay**, a liberal colonial official, formulated new rules restoring earlier freedoms.
- After the **revolt of 1857**, attitudes changed; enraged Englishmen demanded a clamp-down on the “native” press.
- **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, modelled on the **Irish Press Laws**, gave the government extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press. Newspapers were tracked; if a report was judged seditious, the newspaper was warned, and if ignored, the press could be seized and machinery confiscated.
- Nationalist newspapers grew in number despite repression, reporting colonial misrule. **Tilak** was imprisoned in **1908** after writing about Punjab revolutionaries in **Kesari**.

steps.title: Solved example: What was the Vernacular Press Act and why was it passed? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – When/model:** 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws.

**Step 2 – Why:** after 1857 the British feared vernacular newspapers spreading nationalist criticism.

**Step 3 – Powers:** censor reports and editorials; warn papers; seize presses and confiscate machinery if warnings were ignored.

steps.title: Solved example: How did nationalists respond to censorship? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Nationalist newspapers multiplied in all parts of India, reporting misrule and encouraging activities.

**Step 2:** Each crackdown (e.g. Tilak's 1908 imprisonment) provoked wider protest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that the Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1857 – it was **1878**.
- Saying Macaulay tightened censorship – in 1835 he formulated rules that **restored** earlier freedoms.

statements.s: The Vernacular Press Act was modelled on the Irish Press Laws.
Bentinck agreed to revise press laws in 1835.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Resources and Development
courses.summary: What resources are and how they are classified, sustainable development and resource planning, land use and land degradation in India, the major soil types and how to conserve soil.
outcomes: Learners can classify resources on four bases with examples
Learners can explain sustainable development, Agenda 21 and resource planning
Learners can describe India's land-use pattern and causes of land degradation
Learners can identify the six major soil types and methods of soil conservation

lessons.title: Resources: types and sustainable development

scenes.text: Kiran's village pond was once used by all; now a few farmers pump it dry.
Is the pond an individual, community or national resource – and who must save it?

steps.title: What is a resource?
steps.body:
Everything in our environment that can satisfy our needs, provided it is **technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable**, is a resource. Resources are a function of human activities – humans transform materials into resources.

**Classification:**
- **On the basis of origin:** biotic (from the biosphere, have life – humans, flora, fauna, livestock) and abiotic (non-living – rocks, metals).
- **On exhaustibility:** renewable (can be renewed by physical, chemical or mechanical processes – solar, wind, water, forests) and non-renewable (develop over very long geological time – minerals, fossil fuels; some are recyclable like metals, others not, like fossil fuels).
- **On ownership:** individual, community-owned (grazing grounds, burial grounds, village ponds, parks), national (all resources within political boundaries; land up to 12 nautical miles of the ocean – territorial waters), international (oceanic resources beyond 200 nautical miles – the Exclusive Economic Zone – belong to the open ocean; regulated by international institutions).
- **On status of development:** potential (found but not used, e.g. wind and solar in Rajasthan and Gujarat), developed (surveyed, quality and quantity determined), stock (have potential but no technology to access, e.g. hydrogen from water), reserves (subset of stock usable with existing technology but not yet used, e.g. water in dams for future).

steps.title: Development of resources and sustainability
steps.body:
Indiscriminate use of resources has caused depletion for the selfish needs of a few, accumulation in few hands (rich vs poor divide), and global problems like global warming, ozone depletion, pollution and land degradation.

**Sustainable development:** development should take place without damaging the environment and without compromising the needs of future generations.

- **Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit, June 1992** – first international Earth Summit; over 100 heads of state; adopted the Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity declarations, the Rio Convention and **Agenda 21** – a declaration to achieve global sustainable development in the 21st century, combating environmental damage, poverty and disease through global cooperation; every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.
- Gandhi: “There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed.”

steps.title: Solved example: Classify “wind energy in Rajasthan” on two bases (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Exhaustibility:** renewable (wind keeps blowing).

**Step 2 – Status of development:** potential resource – present in large quantity but not fully utilised.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish between stock and reserves (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Stock:** materials that can satisfy needs but humans lack the technology to use them; e.g. hydrogen and oxygen from water as fuel.

**Step 2 – Reserves:** a subset of stock that can be used with existing technology but is kept for the future; e.g. water in reservoirs, forests.

**Step 3 – Key difference:** technology – available for reserves, not for stock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all resources “free gifts of nature” – resources are a function of human activity.
- Mixing territorial waters (12 nautical miles) with the EEZ (200 nautical miles).
- Putting fossil fuels under “recyclable”.

lessons.title: Resource planning and land resources

scenes.text: Abandoned mine pits near Ranchi have left deep scars and heaps of overburden.
A local NGO plants trees on the dumps – one of many ways to fight land degradation.

steps.title: Resource planning in India
steps.body:
India has enormous diversity in resources: Jharkhand, MP, Chhattisgarh are rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water but lacks infrastructure; Rajasthan has solar and wind energy but lacks water; Ladakh is rich in cultural heritage but deficient in water and infrastructure.

**Process of resource planning:** (1) identify and inventory resources across regions – surveying, mapping, qualitative and quantitative estimation; (2) evolve a planning structure with appropriate technology, skill and institutions; (3) match resource development plans with overall national development plans. Resource planning has been a goal since the **First Five Year Plan**.

steps.title: Land use and degradation
steps.body:
**Relief:** about **43%** of India is plains, **30%** mountains and **27%** plateaus.

**Land use categories:** (1) forests; (2) land not available for cultivation – barren & waste land, land put to non-agricultural uses; (3) other uncultivated land (excluding fallow) – permanent pastures & grazing land, land under miscellaneous tree crops, culturable waste land (left uncultivated for **more than 5 agricultural years**); (4) fallow lands – current fallow (**1 year or less**), other than current fallow (**1–5 years**); (5) net sown area. Area sown more than once in a year plus net sown area = **gross cropped area**.

The **National Forest Policy (1952)** recommends **33%** of geographical area under forest; India is far below this.

**Land degradation causes:** mining (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, MP, Odisha – deforestation), overgrazing (Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra), over-irrigation (Punjab, Haryana, western UP – waterlogging, salinity and alkalinity), mineral processing like grinding of limestone for cement and calcite/soapstone for ceramics (dust).

**Solutions:** afforestation, proper management of grazing, planting shelter belts, stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes, control on overgrazing, proper management of waste lands, control of mining, treating industrial effluents before discharge.

steps.title: Solved example: A farmer left a field uncultivated for 3 years. Classify it (1 mark)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rule:** current fallow = ≤1 year; other than current fallow = 1–5 years; culturable waste = >5 years.

**Step 2 – Apply:** 3 years → **fallow other than current fallow**.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain how over-irrigation degrades land in Punjab (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Excess water:** canals and tube wells supply more water than crops need.

**Step 2 – Waterlogging:** water table rises; soil air spaces fill.

**Step 3 – Salinity/alkalinity:** evaporation leaves salts on the surface; fertility falls. Remedy: controlled irrigation, drainage, crop choice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying culturable waste = fallow for 2 years – it is land uncultivated **over 5 years**.
- Forgetting that the forest target is **33%** (National Forest Policy 1952).
- Confusing net sown area with gross cropped area.

lessons.title: Soils of India

scenes.text: Sunil's uncle grows cotton in Vidarbha. In summer the black soil cracks deeply.
In the rains it becomes sticky – but holds moisture for months.

steps.title: How soil forms
steps.body: Soil is the most important renewable natural resource – the medium of plant growth. It takes millions of years to form a few centimetres. Relief, parent rock (bedrock), climate, vegetation and other life forms, and time are factors; temperature changes, running water, wind, glaciers and decomposers contribute.

steps.title: Six soil types
steps.body:
- **Alluvial soil:** most widespread; whole northern plains (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra deposits), also Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor, and eastern coastal deltas (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri). Rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime – good for sugarcane, paddy, wheat, cereals, pulses. **Bangar** = old alluvium, more kankar nodules; **khadar** = new alluvium, more fine particles, more fertile.
- **Black soil (regur):** ideal for cotton; formed from lava rocks (climate and parent rock); Deccan trap (basalt) region – plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, MP, Chhattisgarh, extending south-east along Godavari and Krishna valleys. Very fine (clayey), high moisture-holding capacity; rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime; poor in phosphoric contents. Develops deep cracks in hot weather (self-aeration); sticky when wet.
- **Red and yellow soil:** on crystalline igneous rocks in areas of low rainfall in the eastern and southern Deccan plateau; Odisha, Chhattisgarh, southern Ganga plain, along the piedmont zone of the Western Ghats. Red due to **diffusion of iron**; yellow when **hydrated**.
- **Laterite soil:** from the Latin *later* = brick; develops under **high temperature and heavy rainfall**, a result of intense **leaching**. Low humus. Found in Karnataka, Kerala, TN, MP and hilly areas of Odisha and Assam. With manures and fertilisers good for tea, coffee; red laterite in TN, AP, Kerala suited to cashew.
- **Arid soil:** red to brown, sandy, saline; low humus and moisture; kankar in lower horizons restricts water infiltration; Rajasthan; can be made cultivable with irrigation (western Rajasthan).
- **Forest soil:** in hilly and mountainous areas with sufficient rain forests; loamy and silty in valleys, coarse on upper slopes; acidic with low humus in snow-covered Himalayan areas.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is black soil ideal for cotton? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Moisture:** clayey texture holds moisture for long, so cotton survives dry spells.

**Step 2 – Nutrients:** rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime.

**Step 3 – Aeration:** deep cracks in summer allow self-ploughing / aeration. Hence called “black cotton soil”.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish between bangar and khadar (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Bangar:** old alluvium, higher concentration of kankar nodules, less fertile.

**Step 2 – Khadar:** new alluvium, more fine particles, more fertile – renewed by floods each year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying laterite soil is rich in humus – it has **low humus** due to leaching.
- Calling black soil rich in phosphorus – it is **poor** in phosphoric content.
- Mixing up why red soil is red (iron diffusion) and yellow (hydration).

lessons.title: Soil erosion and conservation

scenes.text: From a train window, Divya sees deep ravines along the Chambal – once fertile fields.
Her teacher calls it “badland topography”.

steps.title: Soil erosion
steps.body:
Denudation of the soil cover and its subsequent washing down is **soil erosion**. Human causes: deforestation, overgrazing, construction and mining, defective farming (ploughing up and down slopes). Natural forces: wind, glaciers, running water.

- **Gully erosion:** running water cuts through clayey soils making deep channels (gullies); land becomes unfit for cultivation – **badland**; in the Chambal basin such lands are called **ravines**.
- **Sheet erosion:** water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope, washing away the topsoil.
- **Wind erosion:** wind blows loose soil off flat or sloping land.

steps.title: Soil conservation methods
steps.body:
- **Contour ploughing** – ploughing along contour lines decelerates water flow down slopes.
- **Terrace cultivation** – steps cut on slopes; common in the western and central Himalayas.
- **Strip cropping** – large fields divided into strips with grass left between crops to break wind force.
- **Shelter belts** – planting lines of trees; contributed to stabilising sand dunes and the desert in **western India**.
- Plugging gullies, check dams, afforestation, controlled grazing.

steps.title: Solved example: Suggest conservation measures for (a) hilly areas, (b) arid areas (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Hilly:** terrace farming and contour ploughing slow the runoff.

**Step 2 – Arid:** shelter belts of trees and strip cropping reduce wind speed; stabilise dunes with thorny bushes.

**Step 3 – Common:** afforestation and controlled grazing.

steps.title: Solved example: Differentiate gully erosion and sheet erosion (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Gully:** water cuts deep channels in clayey soils; creates badlands/ravines.

**Step 2 – Sheet:** water flows as a sheet over large areas, removing the topsoil uniformly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ploughing **up and down** slopes increases erosion; contour ploughing is **along** contours.
- Saying terrace farming is common in Rajasthan – it is common in the **Himalayas**.

quiz.why: Overgrazing is a human cause of soil erosion. Wind, rainfall and glaciers are natural forces.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Forest and Wildlife Resources
courses.summary: India's biodiversity and the IUCN categories of species, causes of forest and wildlife depletion, government conservation (Wildlife Act, Project Tiger, forest types) and community-led conservation like Chipko and Joint Forest Management.
outcomes: Learners can classify species using IUCN categories with Indian examples
Learners can explain the causes of depletion of flora and fauna
Learners can describe the Wildlife (Protection) Act, Project Tiger and types of forests
Learners can give examples of community conservation in India

lessons.title: Biodiversity and the categories of species

scenes.text: Aarav learns the Asiatic cheetah had become extinct in India by the mid-20th century.
He wonders which other animals are on the danger list.

steps.title: Flora, fauna and biodiversity
steps.body:
India is one of the world's richest countries in **biological diversity**, with about 8% of the world's species (an estimated 1.6 million). We humans, along with all living organisms, form a complex web of ecological systems in which we are only a part. Forests are primary producers on which other living beings depend.

At least 10% of India's recorded wild flora and 20% of mammals are on the threatened list (NCERT figure).

steps.title: IUCN categories with examples
steps.body:
- **Normal species:** population considered normal for survival – cattle, sal, pine, rodents.
- **Endangered:** in danger of extinction if negative factors continue – blackbuck, crocodile, Indian wild ass, Indian rhino, lion-tailed macaque, sangai (brow-antlered deer of Manipur).
- **Vulnerable:** population has declined and may move into the endangered category soon – blue sheep, Asiatic elephant, Gangetic dolphin.
- **Rare:** small population; may become endangered or vulnerable – Himalayan brown bear, wild Asiatic buffalo, desert fox, hornbill.
- **Endemic:** found only in particular areas isolated by natural or geographical barriers – Andaman teal, Nicobar pigeon, Andaman wild pig, mithun in Arunachal Pradesh.
- **Extinct:** not found after searches of known or likely areas – Asiatic cheetah, pink-headed duck.

steps.title: Solved example: Classify: Gangetic dolphin, Nicobar pigeon, pink-headed duck (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Gangetic dolphin – vulnerable (declining population).

**Step 2:** Nicobar pigeon – endemic (found only in Nicobar islands).

**Step 3:** Pink-headed duck – extinct.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish between endangered and vulnerable species (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Endangered:** already in danger of extinction if negative factors continue (e.g. blackbuck).

**Step 2 – Vulnerable:** population declining; likely to become endangered soon if factors continue (e.g. Asiatic elephant).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the Asiatic elephant endangered – NCERT lists it as **vulnerable**.
- Confusing **rare** (small population) with **endemic** (restricted area).
- Listing mithun as extinct – it is endemic to Arunachal Pradesh.

lessons.title: Causes of depletion of flora and fauna

scenes.text: A new reservoir floods a forest valley; deer and birds lose their home.
Ritika asks: development or destruction?

steps.title: Main causes
steps.body:
- **Agricultural expansion:** according to the Forest Survey of India, between 1951 and 1980 over **26,200 sq km** of forest was converted to agricultural land.
- **Shifting cultivation** (slash and burn) in tribal belts of NE and central India.
- **Large-scale development projects:** since 1951 over **5,000 sq km** of forest was cleared for river valley projects; e.g. the **Narmada Sagar Project** in MP would inundate **40,000 hectares** of forest.
- **Mining:** e.g. dolomite mining threatens the **Buxa Tiger Reserve** in West Bengal, disturbing natural habitats and blocking migration of the great Indian elephant.
- **Grazing and fuelwood collection**, enlargement of plantations (colonial period railways, agriculture, commercial forestry).
- Other factors: habitat destruction, hunting and poaching, over-exploitation, environmental pollution, poisoning, forest fires. Unequal access and consumption: the richest 5% of Indian society may cause more ecological damage than the poorest 25% because of high consumption.

steps.title: Solved example: “Development projects can deplete forests.” Explain with an example (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cause:** dams and river valley projects need large reservoirs that submerge forests.

**Step 2 – Data:** since 1951 over 5,000 sq km of forest cleared for river valley projects.

lessons.title: Government conservation and types of forests

scenes.text: Forest guards set camera traps in Corbett National Park.
Project Tiger, started in 1973, has helped tiger numbers recover in many reserves.

steps.title: Laws and projects
steps.body:
- In the 1960s–70s conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme. The **Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** was implemented: an all-India list of protected species was published; hunting was banned; trade in wildlife was restricted; habitats were given legal protection. National parks and wildlife sanctuaries were set up.
- **Project Tiger (1973):** tiger numbers had fallen to about 1,827 in 1973 (NCERT figure). Threats: poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey, growing human population. Tiger reserves include **Corbett (Uttarakhand), Sundarbans (West Bengal), Bandhavgarh (MP), Sariska (Rajasthan), Manas (Assam), Periyar (Kerala)**.
- Conservation also covers insects, and several projects protect specific animals.

steps.title: Types of forests (by administration)
steps.body:
- **Reserved forests:** more than half of the total forest land; regarded as most valuable for conserving forest and wildlife.
- **Protected forests:** almost one-third of total forest area; protected from further depletion.
- **Unclassed forests:** other forests and wastelands belonging to government and private individuals and communities.

Reserved and protected forests are called **permanent forest estates**. **Madhya Pradesh** has the largest area under permanent forests. Reserved forests dominate in J&K, AP, Uttarakhand, Kerala, TN, West Bengal, Maharashtra; protected forests in Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, HP, Odisha, Rajasthan; unclassed forests are a large share in all north-eastern states and parts of Gujarat (often managed by local communities).

steps.title: Solved example: Name three provisions of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** All-India list of protected species published.

**Step 2:** Hunting banned; trade in wildlife restricted.

**Step 3:** Habitats legally protected; national parks and sanctuaries established.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish reserved and protected forests (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reserved:** over half of forest land; most valuable for conservation; strict protection.

**Step 2 – Protected:** about one-third of forest area; protected from further depletion, with some limited use.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating Project Tiger to 1972 – the Act is 1972, **Project Tiger is 1973**.
- Saying unclassed forests are mainly in Punjab – they dominate in the **north-east** and Gujarat.

lessons.title: Community and conservation

scenes.text: In the Himalayan villages of the 1970s, women hugged trees to stop loggers – the Chipko movement.
Today Meena's village forest committee shares the benefits of a protected forest.

steps.title: People protect forests
steps.body:
- **Sariska Tiger Reserve (Rajasthan):** villagers fought against mining, citing the Wildlife Protection Act.
- **Alwar district (Rajasthan):** five villages declared **1,200 hectares** of forest as **Bhairodev Dakav “Sonchuri”**, with their own rules banning hunting and protecting wildlife from outside encroachment.
- **Chipko movement (Himalayas):** resisted deforestation; also showed community afforestation with indigenous species can succeed.
- **Beej Bachao Andolan (Tehri)** and **Navdanya**: showed diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible.
- **Joint Forest Management (JFM):** involves local communities in managing and restoring degraded forests; formally began in **1988** when **Odisha** passed the first resolution. Communities form village institutions to protect degraded forest land and get benefits like non-timber forest produce and a share in timber harvested.

steps.title: Sacred groves and traditions
steps.body:
Nature worship is an age-old tribal belief that all creations of nature must be protected; **sacred groves** (forests of God and Goddesses) were left untouched.

- **Mundas and Santhals** of Chota Nagpur worship **mahua** (*Bassia latifolia*) and **kadamba** (*Anthocephalus cadamba*) trees.
- Tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship **tamarind** and **mango** trees during weddings.
- Peepal and banyan are considered sacred by many.
- **Bishnoi** villages in Rajasthan protect herds of **blackbuck (chinkara), nilgai and peacocks** as part of the community.
- Monkeys and langurs are fed around temples.

steps.title: Solved example: What is Joint Forest Management? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** a programme involving local communities in the management and restoration of degraded forests.

**Step 2 – Origin:** formally started in 1988 with Odisha's resolution.

**Step 3 – Benefits:** members get non-timber forest produce and a share of timber for protecting forests.

steps.title: Solved example: Give two examples of traditional community conservation (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Bishnois in Rajasthan protect blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks.

**Step 2:** Mundas and Santhals worship mahua and kadamba; sacred groves are left untouched.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying JFM began in Uttarakhand – the first resolution was passed by **Odisha (1988)**.
- Writing that Chipko was about wildlife hunting – it was against **tree felling**.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Water Resources
courses.summary: Why water is scarce even in a water-rich country, multipurpose river valley projects – their benefits and costs – and India's traditional and modern rainwater harvesting systems.
outcomes: Learners can explain causes of water scarcity in quantity and quality
Learners can evaluate the benefits and problems of multipurpose river projects
Learners can describe regional rainwater harvesting systems of India
Learners can suggest ways to conserve water

lessons.title: Water scarcity and the need for conservation

scenes.text: In a dry summer, Lakshmi's street waits for a water tanker though the city is beside the sea.
How can a place surrounded by water face scarcity?

steps.title: How much usable water?
steps.body:
About three-fourths of the Earth's surface is covered with water, but only a small proportion is fresh water fit for use. **About 96.5%** of water is in oceans; fresh water is about **2.5%**, mostly as ice sheets and glaciers and groundwater. Fresh water is a renewable resource through the **hydrological cycle**.

India receives nearly 4% of global precipitation (NCERT figure) but per-person water availability is falling.

steps.title: Causes of scarcity
steps.body:
- **Over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access** among social groups.
- **Large and growing population** – more water for domestic use and more food (irrigated agriculture is the largest user).
- **Irrigation:** to grow more, farmers use wells and tube wells, lowering groundwater levels.
- **Industrialisation and urbanisation:** industries need water and hydroelectric power; cities have over-exploited groundwater through private wells.
- **Quality:** even where water is plentiful, it may be polluted by domestic and industrial waste, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers – unsafe for use.

Hence conservation is needed: to safeguard from health hazards, ensure food security, continue livelihoods and productive activities and prevent degradation of ecosystems.

steps.title: Solved example: “Water scarcity is not always due to lack of water.” Explain (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Quality:** water may be polluted by sewage, industrial effluents, pesticides – unusable.

**Step 2 – Distribution:** unequal access among social groups; some over-use while others lack.

**Step 3 – Over-exploitation:** cities and farms overdraw groundwater, creating shortages even in high-rainfall areas.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is irrigation linked with water scarcity? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Growing food for a large population needs more irrigated land, often in dry seasons.

**Step 2:** Wells and tube wells drawing groundwater lower the water table faster than recharge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fresh water is 25% of all water – it is about **2.5%**.
- Assuming scarcity happens only in deserts – quality and over-use cause scarcity in wet regions too.

statements.s: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans.
Fresh water is non-renewable.
statements.why: It is renewed by the hydrological cycle.

statements.s: Polluted water can cause scarcity.
Agriculture uses very little water.

quiz.why: Only about 2.5% of the Earth's water is fresh water.

quiz.why: Fresh water is renewed and recharged through the hydrological (water) cycle.

quiz.why: Pollution by industrial effluents, pesticides and sewage reduces the quality of water.

quiz.q: Cities over-exploit groundwater mainly through
quiz.why: In cities, groundwater is over-used mainly through private wells and tube wells.

quiz.q: Which is a reason to conserve water?
quiz.why: Conserving water helps ensure food security, health and livelihoods.

lessons.title: Multipurpose river projects: benefits

scenes.text: Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the "temples of modern India".
Rohan's grandfather remembers the Bhakra Nangal canals turning Punjab green.

steps.title: What a dam is and why multipurpose
steps.body:
A **dam** is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment. Dams were built in ancient India too – e.g. a sophisticated water-harvesting system channelling floodwaters of the Ganga at **Sringaverapura near Prayagraj** (1st century BC); **Chandragupta Maurya** built dams, lakes and irrigation systems; the **Bhopal lake** (11th century) was among the largest artificial lakes of its time; the **Hauz Khas** tank in Delhi (Sultanate period) supplied water to the Siri Fort area.

**Multipurpose projects** integrate several uses: irrigation, electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial use, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Bhakra Nangal** (Sutlej–Beas basin): hydel power and irrigation.
- **Hirakud** (Mahanadi basin): water conservation with flood control.
- **Sardar Sarovar** (Narmada, Gujarat) – irrigation and drinking water for Gujarat and neighbouring states; associated with the Narmada Bachao Andolan.
- Nehru saw dams as integrating agriculture with rapid industrialisation and growth of the urban economy.

steps.title: Solved example: List four purposes of multipurpose projects (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Irrigation and hydroelectricity.

**Step 2:** Flood control and water supply for homes and industries. (Also navigation, recreation, fish breeding.)

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Nehru call dams “temples of modern India”? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** They would integrate agriculture and village economy with rapid industrialisation.

**Step 2:** They supplied power for industry and water for irrigation and towns.

**Step 3:** They symbolised the modern, planned development of a newly independent nation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting Hirakud on the Narmada – it is on the **Mahanadi**.
- Saying dams are a modern invention – ancient India had sophisticated hydraulic structures.

lessons.title: Problems with big dams

scenes.text: Old Sunderlal's village now lies under a reservoir; he moved to a resettlement colony.
He joined the Narmada Bachao Andolan, which demanded justice for displaced people.

steps.title: Ecological and social costs
steps.body:
- Regulating and damming rivers affects their **natural flow**, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life.
- Dams **fragment rivers**, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning.
- Reservoirs on floodplains submerge existing vegetation and soil, which decompose over time.
- **Displacement** of local communities, who often give up land, livelihood and meagre access to resources without getting benefits.
- Movements: **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (against the Sardar Sarovar Dam – initially focused on environment, later on rehabilitation of displaced people) and the **Tehri Dam Andolan**.
- **Inter-state disputes:** e.g. the **Krishna–Godavari dispute** arose from objections by **Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh** to diversion of more water at **Koyna** by the Maharashtra government for a multipurpose project.
- **Induced floods:** dams meant to control floods have triggered floods due to sedimentation; release of water during heavy rain worsens floods downstream (e.g. Maharashtra and Gujarat 2006). Floods in reservoirs deposit less silt in fields.
- Overuse of irrigation water leads to **salinisation**; changes in cropping patterns towards water-intensive and commercial crops; increased earthquakes reported, water-borne diseases and pests; social gaps widen between rich landowners and landless poor.

steps.title: Solved example: Give four ecological problems of large dams (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Affect natural flow → poor sediment flow downstream, excessive sedimentation in the reservoir.

**Step 2:** Fragment rivers → aquatic animals cannot migrate to spawn.

**Step 3:** Submerge vegetation and soil on floodplains.

**Step 4:** Induced floods, salinisation of soils from over-irrigation.

steps.title: Solved example: What caused the Krishna–Godavari dispute? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Maharashtra planned to divert more water at Koyna for a multipurpose project.

**Step 2:** Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh objected, as it would reduce downstream flow for their farmers and industries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Narmada Bachao Andolan only opposed dams for environment – its focus shifted to **rehabilitation of displaced people**.
- Forgetting that dams can **cause** floods via sedimentation and water release.

lessons.title: Rainwater harvesting

scenes.text: In Phalodi, Rajasthan, Kamla's house has an underground tank (tanka) fed by the roof.
Its water, called palar pani, stays cool and lasts through summer.

steps.title: Traditional systems by region
steps.body:
- **Hill and mountain regions:** diversion channels like **guls or kuls** of the Western Himalayas for agriculture.
- **Rooftop rainwater harvesting** was commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in **Rajasthan**.
- **Flood plains of Bengal:** **inundation channels** to irrigate fields.
- **Arid and semi-arid regions:** agricultural fields converted into rain-fed storage structures that allowed water to stand and moisten the soil – **khadins** in Jaisalmer and **johads** in other parts of Rajasthan.
- **Tankas** in semi-arid and arid Rajasthan (Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer): underground tanks or tanks built inside the main house or courtyard, connected to the sloping roof by a pipe. Rain falling on rooftops travels down the pipe to the tank. The first spell of rain is usually not collected, to clean the roof and pipes. **Palar pani** (rainwater) is considered the purest form of natural water. Many houses built underground rooms adjoining the tanka to beat summer heat.

steps.title: Modern revival
steps.body:
- With the Indira Gandhi Canal providing perennial water, tankas are declining in western Rajasthan (unfortunately).
- **Gendathur**, a remote village in Mysuru (Karnataka), has rooftop rainwater harvesting in about 200 households – earning recognition for water richness.
- **Tamil Nadu** is the first state in India to make rooftop rainwater harvesting **compulsory** for all houses; legal provisions punish defaulters.
- **Bamboo drip irrigation (Meghalaya):** about 200 years old; water from streams and springs is diverted through bamboo pipes, reducing flow to 20–80 drops per minute at the base of the plant.
- **Shillong**, close to Cherrapunji and Mawsynram (very high rainfall), faces water shortage; nearly every household has rooftop rainwater harvesting.

steps.title: Solved example: Describe the tanka system (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Where:** arid and semi-arid Rajasthan – Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer.

**Step 2 – How:** underground tank in courtyard linked by pipes to the sloping roof; first spell of rain is let go to clean the roof.

**Step 3 – Use:** stores drinking water (palar pani) till the next rain; underground rooms alongside stay cool.

steps.title: Solved example: How does bamboo drip irrigation work? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Source:** water from streams and springs on hill tops is diverted with bamboo pipes.

**Step 2 – Network:** smaller bamboo channels carry water down to the plants; flow is controlled by changing pipe positions.

**Step 3 – Delivery:** 20–80 drops per minute reach the plant base – efficient irrigation on slopes (Meghalaya).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing khadins in Kerala – they are in **Jaisalmer, Rajasthan**.
- Saying Karnataka was first to make rooftop harvesting compulsory – it was **Tamil Nadu**.
- Confusing guls/kuls (Western Himalaya) with inundation channels (Bengal).
